# HAUNTED HOUSES

## INTRODUCTORY

### SPIRITUALISM AND MATERIALISM: A REPLY TO CAMILLE SAINT-SAËNS

Despite many convincing observations, the debate between psychists <term>psychists: those who study or believe in psychic and spiritual phenomena</term> and antipsychists <term>antipsychists: skeptics who deny the existence of psychic phenomena, often favoring materialist explanations</term> is still ongoing. Therefore, I believe it is useful to introduce this book with the following article, which was published in the *Nouvelle Revue* on December 15, 1900. It is particularly helpful because it presents the arguments of both opposing sides. 

My friend, Camille Saint-Saëns <note>Camille Saint-Saëns (1835–1921) was a world-famous French composer and conductor</note>, had just published an article praising the physical functions of the brain as an argument against the theory of a personal soul. If you compare the tone of that article with the letters published in *Death and Its Mystery* <note>original title: *La Mort et son Mystère*</note> (vol. ii, p. 34, and vol. iii, p. 8), you will see that during the nineteenth century, we were not yet close friends. 

Despite our different viewpoints, our relationship grew increasingly warm until he passed away on December 16, 1921. Those who seek truth and maintain their mental independence can learn to respect and care for one another despite their differences of opinion; such people are incapable of intolerance. This article, written in the final year of the nineteenth century, serves as a fitting introduction to the chapters that follow:

> MY DEAR FRIEND,
>
> I have just finished reading your insightful and engaging article in the *Nouvelle Revue*—though I am reading it a little late.

Your article struck me like one of those powerful symphonies for which you are so well known, where science and art compete to create the greatest possible effect on our minds. While you seem to touch only lightly on the subject in your article, you actually allow us to see into its true depths.

You are absolutely correct when you say that the words *spiritualism* <term>spiritualism: the belief that the soul or spirit continues to exist after death and can communicate with the living</term> and *materialism* <term>materialism: the theory that nothing exists except matter and its movements and modifications</term> are really just *words* nowadays. This is because we do not yet know the true nature of things, and because recent scientific discoveries suggest that the visible world is built upon an invisible world that acts as its foundation <note>original: "substratum"</note>. I thank you for highlighting my modest journey into the realm of the "Unknown," but I ask your permission to respond to your interpretation. You seem to worry that the origins of the word "psychic" have influenced my thinking. According to you, the facts organized in my book do not prove the soul's existence. You correctly accept these facts as authentic, but you argue they only prove this: "That the unknown force producing thought can project itself beyond the body’s limits, allowing one brain to act on another at a distance. It does not follow that this force is spiritual in nature or independent of the brain."

That is the argument I would like to examine and break down.

Let us, if you please, take a specific case and analyze it. A young woman, Miss Z. <note>original: "Mlle. Z."</note>, brought the following story to my office in Paris; I have removed the names to protect their privacy:

> When we first met, I was twenty years old and he was thirty-two. Our relationship lasted seven years, and we loved each other deeply.

[circum]stances, his poverty, and other factors forced him to marry; and among his awkward <note>original: "embarrassed"</note> explanations, I sensed a vague desire that our relationship should not be completely ended because of it.

I cut this painful interview short. Despite my great sorrow, I did not see my friend again; in my singular and absolute love, I had no wish to willingly share the man I loved so much with another woman.

I later heard indirectly that he had married and was the father of a child.

Some years after this marriage, on a night in April 1893, I saw a human form entering my room. The figure, which appeared tall, was wrapped in a white veil that hid nearly its whole face. I watched with terror as it moved forward and bent over me. I felt its lips touch mine. But what lips! I shall never forget the impression they made on me. I felt no pressure, movement, or warmth—only cold—the cold of a dead mouth!

Yet, I felt a sense of relief and well-being during this long kiss. At no point during this vision did the name or image of my lost lover come to my mind <note>original: "spirit"</note>. After waking up, I did not think about the dream until around noon, when I happened to look at a newspaper and read: "We hear from [town] X that the funeral of Mr. <note>original: "M." (Monsieur)</note> Y took place yesterday" (the article then described the deceased). The article concluded by attributing the death to an attack of typhoid fever <term>typhoid fever: a life-threatening bacterial infection common in the 19th century, often spread through contaminated water or food</term>, caused by the exhaustion of dedicated work.

"Dear friend," I thought, "when you were released from the rules of society <note>original: "worldly conventions"</note>, you came to me to tell me that you had loved me, and would still love me after death. I thank you, and I love you still."

->MISS Z.<- <note>original: "MLLE. Z." (Mademoiselle Z.)</note>

That is the event exactly as it happened. The old and convenient theory <note>original: "hypothesis"</note> of a simple hallucination no longer satisfies us today. What we must explain is why the death coincided with the apparition. Manifestations of this kind are so frequent that these coincidences can no longer be seen as accidental <note>original: "fortuitous"</note>; instead, they must be seen as a sign of cause and effect.

Both you and I, being free from prejudice, admit that Miss <note>original: "Mlle."</note> Z. saw and perceived the presence of her lover at the critical moment of his departure from this world. Hundreds of examples of the same kind exist. However, our interpretations differ. You only see brain activity <note>original: "a cerebral action"</note> of a dying person. I see a spiritual <note>original: "psychic"</note> action.

(I asked myself whether the narrator might have seen the newspaper the night before without remembering it, and whether the association of ideas had produced her dream; but she assures me it was only the next day that she read the paper. That theory <note>original: "hypothesis"</note> must, therefore, be excluded. There had been a real communication between the two beings.)

It is, of course, always difficult to distinguish between the work which belongs to the spirit or the soul and that which belongs to the brain. In our assessments <note>original: "appreciations"</note> and judgments, we are naturally guided by the inner feeling produced in us by the discussion of these occurrences <note>original: "phenomena"</note>. Now, do we not have in this case what is essentially a manifestation of the spirit? Two theories <note>original: "hypotheses"</note> present themselves. Either the lover, as indicated by the narrative, was already dead when he acted this way, or he was still alive, and at the moment of death this man thought of that woman—his friend from happier times <note>original: "sunnier days"</note>—and felt a regret, a remorse perhaps, and possibly a hope for the afterlife <note>original: "Beyond"</note>. That telepathic communication was perhaps not noticed <note>original: "perceived"</note> at once during the daily routine, but was delayed <note>original: "postponed"</note> to the hours of sleep and tranquility. It was not, of course, a case of a ghost <note>original: "phantom"</note> being physically moved from one city to another. It was a mental transmission, for which wireless telegraphy <term>wireless telegraphy: the early form of radio communication, using radio waves to send Morse code, which was a cutting-edge scientific concept at the time</term> provides us a physical comparison <note>original: "image"</note>. The distance was 62 miles, and we know that such a distance does not matter <note>original: "count"</note>.

When I was a student at the University of Kyiv <note>original: "Kieff"</note>, and already married, I had gone to spend the summer with my sister, who lived in the country not far from Pskov <note>original: "Pskow"</note>. While returning through Moscow, my beloved wife suddenly fell ill with influenza, and, despite her extreme youth, her health rapidly failed <note>original: "she was quickly broken up"</note>. Heart failure, like a bolt of lightning, took her life.

I shall not attempt to describe my pain and my despair. But I must submit to your expert judgment a problem which I sincerely hope to have solved.

My father lived at Poltava <note>original: "Pultowa"</note>. He knew nothing of the illness of his charming daughter-in-law, and believed that she was with me in Moscow. Imagine his surprise upon seeing her beside him as he was leaving the house, walking with him for a moment! Seized with fear and anxiety, he at once sent us a telegram to check on the health of my dear wife. It was the day of her death.

I would be grateful to you for the rest of my life for an explanation of this extraordinary fact.

In this case also, the observation was made after death. Do we not also find in this example the impression of a spiritual <note>original: "non-material"</note> origin for the phenomenon—of a moral or mental cause? This indicates not only the existence of unknown faculties in the human being, but even the existence of an intelligent agent. I cannot find anything in this class of facts pertaining to anatomy, animal physiology, or organic chemistry.

# HAUNTED HOUSES

In the first days of November 1869, I left Perpignan, my hometown, to continue my pharmaceutical studies in Montpellier. My family consisted of my mother and my four sisters. I left them very happy and in perfect health.

On the 22nd of the same month, my sister Hélène—a beautiful girl of eighteen, the youngest and most beloved member of the family—gathered some friends at her mother’s house. At about three o’clock in the afternoon, they set out with my mother for the Promenade des Platanes <note>original: "Promenade des Platanes," a well-known public park in Perpignan famous for its rows of plane trees</note>. The weather was beautiful. After half an hour, my sister was suddenly taken ill. “Mother,” she said, “I feel a strange shudder throughout my body. I am cold, and my throat hurts. Let us go home.”

That night, at 5:00 a.m., <note>The hours have been corrected from the first account after a careful examination of the details.</note> my beloved sister passed away in my mother’s arms. She was choked and overwhelmed by an attack of diphtheria <note>A serious and then-common bacterial infection that causes a thick covering in the back of the throat, making it hard to breathe</note> which two doctors were unable to treat.

I was the only man who could have represented the family at the funeral, and my family sent one telegram after another to me in Montpellier. But by a terrible stroke of misfortune, which I still deeply regret, none of them reached me in time.

During the night between the 23rd and the 24th, I had a harrowing hallucination.

I had returned home at 2:00 a.m. with a light heart, full of the joy I had experienced at a social gathering on the 22nd and 23rd. I went to bed feeling very cheerful and was asleep within five minutes.

About 4:00 a.m., I saw my sister’s face. It was deathly pale and bleeding, and a piercing cry—mournful and unceasing—struck my ear: “What are you doing, my Louis? Please come. Please come.”

In my restless and agitated sleep, I hailed a carriage <note>original: "took a cab," referring to a horse-drawn taxi</note>, but despite superhuman efforts, I could not make it move. And still, I saw my sister’s face and heard her voice in my ear: “Louis, what are you doing? Please come. Please come.”

I awoke suddenly; my face was flushed, my head felt feverish, my throat was dry, my breath was short and gasping, and I was sweating profusely. I jumped out of bed, trying to com—

At 11:00 a.m., I arrived at the dining hall <note>original: "refectory," a room used for communal meals, especially in educational or religious institutions</note> in a state of profound dejection. Questioned by my fellow students, I told them exactly what I had experienced. They teased <note>original: "chaffed"</note> me about it. At 2:00 p.m., I went to the Faculty <note>Referring to the university building where the medical or pharmaceutical department was located</note>, hoping to pull myself together over some work.

Coming out of the lecture, I saw a woman in deep mourning coming towards me. She raised her veil and I recognized my eldest sister. Feeling anxious about me, she had come, in spite of her own distress, to find out what had become of me. She told me of the tragic <note>original: "fatal"</note> event which nothing could have led me to expect, since I had had the best news of my family on the morning of the 22nd.

I assure you on my honor that this story is absolutely true. I express no opinion, but only state facts.

Twenty years have passed, but the impression is still vivid, especially now, and even if the features of my Hélène do not appear with the same clearness, I still hear her plaintive, oft-repeated, and despairing cry: “What are you doing, my Louis? Oh, come now, oh, come now!” <note>original French: “*Que fais-tu donc, mon Louis? Mais viens donc, mais viens donc.*”</note>

->Louis Noell<-
->(*Pharmacist at Sète*) <note>original: "Cette," the former spelling of the French port city Sète</note><-

There is the narrative of the psychic phenomenon. If you, my dear friend, do not feel that the body of the dead girl—twenty-three hours after her death—cannot have caused the impression; that there was something apart from the material organism; that, whether M. Noell’s spirit was carried <note>original: "wafted"</note> in his sleep to his dead sister, or that some telepathic action originated from her, we are face to face with an action of the soul and not of the body; that we are driven to think of the soul as personally existing, and not as an effect, a function, or a secretion of the brain: if you do not feel that, it is because you, the artist and thinker whom I know, have not given yourself time to weigh the problem.

# HAUNTED HOUSES

...her death? Any physical <note>original: "material"</note> explanation <note>original: "hypothesis"</note> is unlikely. We might suppose that she called her brother before her death, and that the call remained hidden <note>original: "latent"</note> in her brother's spirit until an hour of quiet enabled his brain to perceive it. On the other hand, we may suppose that the appeal was made after her death. We must consider every possibility.

The simplest solution <note>original: "expedient"</note> would be to deny it, and to declare that the young student simply had a nightmare which accidentally coincided with the death of his sister. That is indeed very simple. But does it satisfy you? Does it satisfy you when you are faced with hundreds of cases of the same kind? Does it satisfy you also in the cases where the person telling the story has "seen" from a distance all the details of a death, a suicide, an accident, or a fire? No. You have too scientific and rational a mind to be satisfied with this old theory of chance, and you know that the mathematics of probability <note>original: "calculus of probability"</note> makes it unacceptable. What then?

Then it follows that the psychic problem has been presented, and we may as well acknowledge it.

I do not claim to explain it. Science has not advanced that far. To admit a fact and to explain it are two different things. We are forced to admit facts even when we cannot explain them. Imagine a man passes the corner of a street and a flowerpot falls on his head. He is forced to admit the fact without immediately guessing how it happened, or how the horizontal and vertical paths met exactly at the spot occupied by his head.

No indeed, what we call matter and its properties are not enough to explain these facts. Therefore, they belong to another category—a category which we have every right to call "psychic"—and which leads us to admit the existence of souls, spirits, and intelligent spiritual beings, which are not simply brain functions <note>original: "cerebral functions"</note>...

> A hypnotist, much filled with mystical ideas, had a somnambulist <note>original: "somnambulist"; in 19th-century terminology, this referred to a person in a deep hypnotic trance who could perform actions or experience visions.</note> who during his sleep only saw angels and spirits of every kind. These visions confirmed the hypnotist more and more in his religious belief. As he always quoted the dreams of his somnambulist in favor of his system, another hypnotist of his acquaintance undertook to disillusion him by proving to him that his somnambulist had the visions described solely because their prototype <note>original: "prototype"; the mental image or model</note> existed in his own head. "And what are they doing?" asked the hypnotist. "They are sitting round a table eating." But he could not tell the dish of which they were partaking.

That is an example of mental suggestion, of which you know many cases. The will of the hypnotist acts upon the subject without the aid of words. We can, of course, call it the action of one brain upon another, but does it not seem as if the brain were only an instrument of the will? I should not congratulate the brain upon its thought any more than I should congratulate a telescope upon its view of Saturn. Is not the brain the organ of thought just as the eye is the organ of sight?

And what about seeing at a distance, or in dreams?

Was it the King himself who appeared to my husband? How did he learn the news? This provides significant matter for reflection.

We might suppose, along with Alfred Maury <note>Alfred Maury (1817–1892) was a French scholar famous for his study of dreams; he famously argued that external physical stimuli during sleep could trigger instantaneous, complex dream narratives</note>, that a physical shock produced the dream. However, this hypothesis does not explain premonition—seeing an event before it happens.

It is often objected that such dreams are modified and reorganized after the event has already occurred—albeit quite sincerely—within the imagination of the narrator. Of course, it is possible that various changes may occur in the memory of the dream. But this objection is dismantled by the observer’s own impression, for it is precisely the feeling of "having seen this before" which strikes the person most forcefully. Furthermore, some instances are so simple that no modification is possible. For example:

I dreamt that I was going on an errand on my bicycle when a dog ran across the road and I fell down, breaking the pedal of the bicycle <note>original: "machine"</note>.

In the morning, I told my mother about my dream. Knowing how often my dreams had come true in the past, she persuaded me to stay at home. I made up my mind not to go out; but about eleven o’clock, just as we were about to have a meal, the postman brought a letter saying that my sister, who lived five miles away, had fallen ill. Forgetting my dream and only anxious to have news of my sister, I hurried through my lunch and started off on my bicycle.

I proceeded without any trouble until I reached the exact place where I had seen myself rolling in the dust and breaking my bicycle the night before. Hardly had the memory of my dream occurred to me when an enormous dog suddenly jumped out of a neighboring farm and tried to bite my leg.

Living near Beauvais, when she wanted to spend some time with her children in Paris, she preferred to write to my uncle, and he met her at the station, from where <note>original: "whence"</note> he always brought her home in a carriage.

Well, on the afternoon of that day, as my uncle stood watching the passers-by from his doorstep, his eyes glanced mechanically toward the corner of New-Petits-Champs Street, and he saw a bus of the Northern Railway Company turning the corner and stopping at his shop.

In the bus were two ladies. One of them was my grandmother, who got off, while the vehicle continued on its journey with the other lady—the one he had seen in his dream—who was dressed in black and held a basket on her lap.

->LE NEUBOURG, EURE.<-

I will conclude these testimonies here, because one only needs to look around to find as many as one could possibly desire. Even the most precise and positive sciences are only established through conclusions drawn from our reasoning. Astronomy itself, that queen among the sciences, is based upon the theory of gravitation, of which its founder, Newton, said simply: “Things happen *as if* the heavenly bodies attracted each other directly in proportion to their masses, and inversely as the squares of their distances apart.” 

Well, faced with the phenomena of telepathy, with examples of mental vision at a distance without the help of physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> organs, and with the even more mysterious and incomprehensible fact of seeing the future in accurate detail with spiritual eyes, I say: “Things happen *as if* there existed a psychic, spiritual entity within the human organism, endowed with perceptive faculties as yet unknown.” This entity—this soul or spirit—acts and perceives through the brain, but it is not merely a material function of a material organ. This seems to me a logical conclusion arrived at by a sound and exact method. It seems to me superior both to denials <note>original: "negations"</note> and assertions <note>original: "affirmations"</note> that lack proof and are founded on blind faith. Faith, so-called miracles, and even martyrdom have never proved anything; they have been at the service of all causes—political and religious—including the most varied, contradictory, and sometimes the most absurd. Science alone can truly enlighten humanity.

->Camille Flammarion.<-

> You are the greatest of musicians, the pride of the Institute, and one of the deepest thinkers of our time—but you are not being logical.

Isn't it the spirit that acts in these phenomena? How can we find the properties of matter in them? It seems to me that this past exchange of ideas between two independent seekers is a very appropriate prologue to the present volume. I should add that Saint-Saëns himself provided an example of the independence of the soul relative to the body. He died on December 16, 1921, at the age of 86. On the previous October 16, he had lunched at my table at the Juvisy Observatory <note>Camille Flammarion's private astronomical observatory, established in 1883</note>, and we were all charmed by his conversation; his spirit was as young as it had been when he was twenty. Yet, he complained that his physical body <note>original: "organism"</note> was failing. He was unable to climb the tower to observe Venus and Arcturus in the company of our colleagues from the French Astronomical Society—including Prince Bonaparte, Count Gramont, Count de la Baume Pluvinel, General Ferrié, and other friends who had strongly urged him to join us. He suffered from pain in his legs. At the same time, *Le Ménestrel* <note>original: "The Minstrel"; a prominent French music journal published from 1833 to 1940</note> published (on October 21) an article he had written about Berlioz <note>Hector Berlioz, the famous French Romantic composer</note> that was full of a youthful spirit. While his body was failing, his soul remained in full force. Such a stark difference between the physical and spiritual elements is not rare.

## CHAPTER I

# EXPERIMENTAL PROOFS OF SURVIVAL

*Preliminary reply to certain criticisms—Ascertaining the facts—Blind and prejudiced denials—Laplace and the calculus of probabilities—The choice of precise observations.*

Serious and knowledgeable readers who understand the current state of our investigation, and who value the results we have achieved toward its solution, may think it is unnecessary for me to spend the first chapter of this book answering objections. These objections, raised by stubborn skeptics who refuse to accept the existence of <term>metapsychic phenomena</term> <note>A term used in the early 20th century to describe what we now call parapsychology or psychic research, such as telepathy or mediumship</note> at any cost, often lack any real substance. However, I believe a clear response to these denials is important. Most people are naturally unaware of these phenomena and are therefore likely to ignore them. If I can convince even one reader in ten that these closed-minded critics are mistaken, I will have provided a valuable service to public knowledge.

If we want to develop a firm and lasting conviction about the reality, nature, and significance of psychic phenomena, we must first realize how easily our senses—sight, hearing, touch, and the rest—can be deceived. Illusions can arise from a thousand unexpected causes, so we must be on guard against every possible mistake. Generally speaking, humans are poor observers; we do not look beneath the surface, we

...are content with mere approximations. The scientific method is needed here more than anywhere else if we wish to develop a well-founded conviction. Once we have taken these preventive precautions, the opinions of millions of other people cannot stop us from freely evaluating the facts we have observed. Let that be understood once and for all!

As for the issue of fraud, both intentional and unintentional, I have dealt with that in a long discussion of fifty pages in my work *The Unknown Natural Forces* <note>original: *Les Forces Naturelles Inconnues*, published by Flammarion in 1907</note>, so I do not need to repeat it here.

I am inclined to agree with Emile Boirac <note>A French psychologist and psychic researcher (1851–1917) who coined the term "déjà vu"</note> that the primary reason for the bias and mistrust toward psychic science among some of our contemporaries lies in how it was originally presented, and from which it has not yet been fully freed. It was originally called "Occult Science," or at least it formed part of that confused collection of trial-and-error observations, traditions, hypotheses, and speculations known by that name. These were mixed up with astrology, alchemy, <term>chiromancy</term> <note>The practice of palm reading to predict the future</note>, magic, and other early, undeveloped sciences of antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance. 

It is barely two centuries since psychic science began to emerge from that mass, and among those who devote themselves to it today, some of the mystical spirit of the old practitioners may still remain. This is all the more reason why we should take care to introduce the true spirit of modern science with increasing passion and vigor. This is how astronomy finally rose out of astrology, and chemistry out of alchemy; neither one has retained any stain of their "original sin." In the same way, psychic science—though it was cradled, so to speak, in magic and sorcery—already deserves (and will deserve even more in the future) to be described as an effective and positive science.

In these pages, we examine the greatest of all problems. Seeking knowledge of the soul and investigating our destiny is an all-consuming pursuit. A biographer recently remarked that if my life—after being devoted to investigating the astronomical world and demonstrating that life exists throughout the universe—served only to prove the existence of the human soul, it would have contributed to the progress of humanity. I sincerely hope that is the case.

Today, we require careful and rigorous discussion. The publication of the third volume of my <term>metapsychic trilogy</term> <note>original: "trilogie métapsychique"; Flammarion’s three-book series exploring the unknown powers of the mind and life after death</note>, *Death and Its Mystery*, which deals with manifestations "after death," has raised a storm of accusations from uninformed commentators. Some of these critics, while appearing sincere and balanced, speak as lightly and irresponsibly as anyone else; others show signs of bad faith and bitterness, which is as strange as it is useless.

Isn't it astonishing? Our legitimate and natural wish to know the nature of the soul—to know whether it really has a personal existence and whether it survives the inevitable destruction of the body—actually creates enemies for us. These adversaries use all their cleverness to invent a thousand obstacles to this free and independent research, attempting to delay it in every possible way! This organized opposition is almost hard to believe, and yet it exists.

Now is the right time to examine the subject with special attention, applying the principles of the proven scientific method. Let us return to the original events that sparked this debate.

### MANIFESTATIONS OF THE DEAD

Research into the nature of the soul and its existence after death must be conducted using the same methods used in any other science—without prejudice or preconceived opinions, and apart from any sentimental or religious influence. Are there, or are there not, manifestations of the dead? That is the question. Now, I declare that there are. *The Journal*, to which I had the honor of contributing during the time of its founder, my spiritual friend Xau <note>Fernand Xau (1852–1899) was a French journalist and the founder of the daily newspaper *Le Journal*</note>, having called attention to the solution of this long-standing problem, I now bring before its readers one of the two facts that have most convinced me of such survival. I defy the most skeptical of my opponents to explain it without assuming an action taken by the deceased person. Let them try, indeed.

There was an engineer who owned two factories: one in Glasgow and the other in London. In his service at the Scottish factory was a young man named Robert Mackenzie, who was particularly devoted and felt a deep sense of gratitude toward him. The employer did not live in Glasgow, but in London.

One Friday evening, the Glasgow workmen held their annual ball. Robert Mackenzie, who had no taste for dancing, asked permission to serve at the refreshment stall. Everything went well, and the entertainment continued into the Saturday.

On the following Tuesday evening, a little before eight o'clock in his house at Campden Hill <note>A residential district in Kensington, West London</note>, the engineer saw a manifestation which he relates as follows:

> "I dreamed that I was sitting at a desk, engaged in conversation with an unknown gentleman. Robert Mackenzie came toward me. Rather annoyed, I asked him whether he did not see that I was busy. He withdrew with a dissatisfied air, then came back again as if he strongly desired an immediate conversation. I reproached him even more rudely for his lack of tact. Just then, the person to whom I was talking took his leave, and Mackenzie advanced again. 'What does this mean, Robert?' I said in a tone of some irritation. 'Don't you see that I was busy?'"

> “This apparition, in my view, was caused by Mackenzie’s profound gratitude—since I had rescued him from a wretched state of misery—and his intense desire to keep my respect.”

That is the story told by the Glasgow manufacturer. Doesn’t the fact that this workman appeared after his reported suicide to reveal the truth prove survival after death?

We have hundreds of similar observations made by responsible people who simply describe what happened to them. The only way to avoid any explanation is to claim the stories are false, or that they were imagined or invented—in other words, that the witnesses are lying. Now, this Glasgow manufacturer was a personal friend of Edmund Gurney <note>Edmund Gurney (1847–1888) was a psychologist and a founder of the Society for Psychical Research</note>, one of the founders of the English Society for Psychical Research. Well, unless we accuse all these observers of fraud, or assume they are vision-impaired and that everyone is more or less mad or prone to hallucinations, we must accept these facts just as we are forced to accept the existence of a strange and unexplained flash of lightning. One cannot simply deny everything. We must honestly admit that this represents an entire field of knowledge currently unknown to scientific investigation. In the specific case I just described, the young man was accidentally poisoned in Glasgow during the night between Saturday and Sunday. He appeared the following Tuesday in London to his employer—who did not yet know of his death—to declare that he had not committed suicide. He had, therefore, been dead for forty-eight hours. In this case, we cannot accept the idea that a dream just happened to coincide with such a detailed event, nor can we blame chance or anything else.

### My Film

In 1861, on a pleasant summer evening, Mr. Harry Cower was sitting in his dining room in Sydney, Australia. He had no appetite and could not shake the gloomy thoughts that weighed on him.

Suddenly, he heard a sharp and very faint sound. The mirror over the mantelpiece had cracked. “That is strange!” said Mr. Harry Cower. A few weeks later, he learned that at the exact moment the mirror broke, his elderly aunt, Mrs. Dorothy Elizabeth MacClure, had died suddenly in Minneapolis, Minnesota, U.S.A.

Does this authentic fact not prove undeniably the reality of manifestations from the Beyond?

On another occasion, a man named Archibald B. Blackburn of Chicago was in Woodston, Ohio, in 1874. He saw his friend John William Hercules O’Sullivan, from New Tipperary, Massachusetts, appear before him. O’Sullivan’s face was twisted in pain. He seemed to have trouble breathing and was making strange gestures. “What is the matter?” asked Mr. Blackburn. “Help, I am drowning,” said O’Sullivan, and he vanished.

Blackburn, very distressed, went home. Eight days later, he heard that his friend had drowned in the Missouri River at the exact time and on the day when his spirit <note>original: "phantom"</note> called for help.

Those who deny these eloquent facts, says M. Flammarion, are either ignorant, illogical, or insincere.

Well, then, I deny them.

I deny them all, entirely <note>original: "*en bloc*"</note>, in the most categorical fashion.

I have read in the psychic books of M. Flammarion and other mystery-mongers <note>those who promote or deal in supernatural secrets</note> innumerable cases which strangely resemble the story of Harry Cower and Archibald B. Blackburn. I consider them devoid of any kind of documentary value. They all occurred at a legendary <note>original: "fabulous"</note> era, and guarantees of their truth are absolutely lacking. When I consider that we cannot be trusted to exactly describe a street accident which we saw ourselves, I say to myself that it is foolish to base a whole philosophy—a sort of religion—on ancient anecdotes told in their own way by people we know nothing about.

Besides, there is too much English spoken in these stories of another world. The spirits, specters, phantoms, and so on, are never natives of Pontarlier or Romorantin; it is always in England or America that they indulge in their little manifestations. Is the Beyond also an Anglo-Saxon colony?

Why, for instance, did not the late Bessarabo <note>Georges Bessarabo was the victim of a sensational "trunk murder" in 1920; his body was found in a trunk at a railway station.</note> appear to the President of the Criminal Court <note>original: "Assize Court"</note>, to the Jury, or even to Maître de Moro-Giafferi <note>Vincent de Moro-Giafferi (1878–1956) was a famous French criminal defense lawyer.</note>, to tell them under what circumstances he took up his quarters at the bottom of a trunk?

That would more surely overcome our skepticism than the collection of psychological hoaxes <note>original: "*psycho-canards*"; "canard" is French for "duck" but refers to a false or exaggerated story.</note> collected by the gentle and pensive Camille Flammarion.

->CLÉMENT VAUTEL.<-

It is by these pleasantries, this playing with words, and similar tactics, that our colleague <note>original: "*confrère*"</note> of the mainstream press <note>original: "Grand Press"</note> thinks he can explain away the posthumous apparition of Robert Mackenzie! I venture to remark that this "solution" bears no relation to the problem. It is equivalent to these simple words: "There is nothing in it." "Nothing"—that is, very little, considering all the facts established beyond a doubt.

As M. Clément Vautel declares that they "all [occurred at a fabulous epoch]..."

"Nonsense," they say, and they claim there is nothing but nonsense in all these stories. Death, mourning, pain, despair—none of this counts to them, and they can only laugh. This explanation for inexplicable things is extremely simple! Let us add that this treatment is quite typical; all the sciences were treated this way when they first began.

Furthermore, the objection itself is worthless, as an observation made in London or Rome is just as valid as one made in Paris. These facts are observed throughout the entire world, and France has no monopoly on them.

A few days later, on June 18, the following letter was sent to me from Boulogne <note>original: "Bologne"; likely Boulogne-sur-Mer</note> as a truly French observation:

>

She said, "Listen to this: that was the exact day father was exhumed! <note>Exhumation is the act of digging up remains, often done in common graves after several years to make room or move the deceased to a permanent location.</note>"

We may still assume this was a hallucination without an external cause. But how do we account for the coincidence of the vision with the exhumation of the narrator's father? Since the commencement of my inquiry in 1899, I have received more than 5,600 different reports of psychic observations, and I had already received 500 before I decided to begin the formal study. The narrative that approaches it most closely—concerning a delayed mental impression <note>original: "retarded cerebral impression"</note>—is the one that can be read in volume II of *Death and its Mystery* <note>A trilogy of books by Camille Flammarion exploring the soul and the afterlife.</note>, and which is mentioned above (page 6): the sister of Louis Noell, a beautiful girl of eighteen, was suddenly attacked by diphtheria during a walk at Perpignan. In the first place, the sincerity of the narrators may be doubted; there are always liars and jokers. In the second place, even when there is perfect sincerity, memory is not always faithful, and details can be rearranged or exaggerated. Furthermore, the problem is so serious in itself that we cannot and must not admit any observations except those which are indisputable. 

Beyond this, we must know how to interpret these observations. We must show that they cannot be accounted for by known human faculties and refuse to admit the actions of deceased persons unless no other hypothesis is possible. All these elements of study can only be combined in an observer if he is himself well-acquainted with this class of facts and, so to speak, knows what he is talking about.

In this connection, I may point out that the public generally allows the strangest confusions to creep into psychical <note>original: "metapsychic"</note> studies. To take a recent example: it appears that certain experiments undertaken in 1922 by three professors of the Sorbonne <note>The Sorbonne is the historic University of Paris, a prestigious center for academic research.</note> on the production of ectoplasm <note>In spiritualism, a substance or "organic product" alleged to flow from the body of a medium.</note> led to a negative or incomplete result. From this, the conclusion has been drawn that there are no manifestations of the dead. 

What singular reasoning! What do any organic products issuing from the mouth or the nose of "Miss A." or "Miss B." <note>Likely referring to pseudonyms for mediums under investigation, such as Marthe Béraud (Eva C.).</note> have to do with the immortality of the soul? Yet thousands of readers of the daily papers have agreed with such conclusions, which are as stupid as they are ridiculous.

Yes, we must know what we are talking about. If anybody came to me and said: "I have just been..."

I treat these correspondents the same way I treat those who constantly send me their various observations on astronomy and meteorology from every part of the globe.

When a person writes that they have observed an eclipse, an occultation <note>An astronomical event where one celestial body is hidden by another passing between it and the observer.</note>, a meteorite, a shooting star, a comet, a change on Jupiter or Mars, an aurora borealis <note>The Northern Lights.</note>, an earthquake, a storm, a peculiar lightning flash, a lunar rainbow, and so on, I assume the report is made sincerely and in good faith. However, this does not prevent me from examining and judging the information. One might object that the situation is not exactly the same, because an astronomical or meteorological observation might be made at the same time by other people, which provides a sort of control or verification. No doubt. But, regarding my opinion of the observer's sincerity, the case is precisely the same: I give them the benefit of the doubt while reserving all rights to investigate the claim freely.

## HAUNTED HOUSES

In cases of telepathy and similar phenomena, the same human beings are involved. They possess the same intellectual faculties. They are in a normal mental state and prove it through their own reflections. *From the outset* <note>original: "A priori" — a Latin phrase meaning "from the beginning" or based on theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note>, I have no more reason to distrust a <term>scholar</term> <note>original: "savant" — a highly learned person or scientist.</note>, a professor, a judge <note>original: "magistrate"</note>, a priest, a clergyman, a manufacturer, or a farmer when he tells me of a psychic fact than when he speaks of a physical observation. Yet, because these phenomena are rarer and less believable, I have set about investigating a large number of them, gathering information and making inquiries that have almost always resulted in the direct confirmation of the stories received.

That was also the practice of the Society for Psychical Research <note>The Society for Psychical Research (SPR) was founded in London in 1882 to investigate scientific claims of psychic phenomena.</note> in London. And in spite of certain variations in the narratives and certain gaps in memory, it is always found that the original event is real and not invented.

But, if impostors are rare, illusions are plentiful. They are <term>countless</term> <note>original: "Their name is legion" — a phrase from the New Testament (Mark 5:9) used to describe a vast number.</note> in this category of facts. The extent of human gullibility <note>original: "credulity"</note> is incredible! The style of these accounts is also very distinctive. Yet, counterfeit <note>original: "false"</note> money does not disprove the existence of the real thing.

What is perhaps most difficult is for a man to be entirely independent—to say what he thinks and knows without considering what opinion others hold of him. *To stake one's life on the truth* <note>original: "Vitam impendere vero" — a Latin motto used by the Roman poet Juvenal and the philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau.</note>, "to consecrate one’s life to Truth." It was a noble motto of Juvenal and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, but it usually produces nothing but enemies. For humanity is, above all, a coarse, crude, ignorant, cowardly, and hypocritical race.

What is perhaps even more curious is that the free search for truth is distasteful to everyone, for every mind has its little prejudices which it will not give up.

A person who dies in Marseille can appear at the same moment in Paris, in Algiers, in America, or in China, and can do so without physically moving.

A young girl waltzing with a beloved fiancé can suddenly see her dead mother enter the drawing room and call out that she is dying a thousand miles away.

A man passing along a street under his mistress's windows can appear to her in her room without ever leaving the street.

Thought can act upon the thoughts of another person without the help of the five senses.

One may see in a dream a country they have never seen before, and see themselves in that country as they will be ten years later.

The Future is as observable as the Past. The Present alone does not exist, since scientific analysis reduces it to less than a hundredth of a second.

Space and time, as they are presented to us by our measuring instruments, do not exist. Instead, there is infinity and there is eternity. <term>Laplace</term> <note>Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749–1827), a brilliant French mathematician and astronomer known as the "Newton of France."</note> reasoned correctly when he wrote in his *Analytical Theory of Probability* <note>original: *Théorie analytique des probabilités* (1812)</note>:

This argument of the immortal French astronomer confirms the ruling spirit of our present work on <term>metapsychical problems</term> <note>An early term for parapsychological research or the study of phenomena beyond known physical laws.</note>. # EXPERIMENTAL PROOFS

Certain objections have eventually become quite tiresome. Among these is the claim that, for an observation to have scientific value, we must be able to repeat it at will. This is essentially saying that a lightning flash never existed because one cannot recreate it on command; that the fall of a meteorite is unbelievable because we cannot reproduce it whenever we like; that an eclipse is a myth because one must wait for specific <term>luni-solar conditions</term> <note>The specific alignment and positions of the moon and sun.</note> for it to happen again; or that an earthquake never occurred because we cannot make it happen twice. This line of thinking confuses two entirely distinct categories: observation and experiment. We **observe** a spontaneous natural phenomenon; we **experimentally** manufacture a chemical compound. It is not uncommon to find this kind of logical error even among people accustomed to scientific methods. Astronomy and meteorology are observational sciences. Mechanics is an experimental science.

Must the manifestations of the dead be admitted into the category of facts scientifically proven through sufficient observation? That is the real question, and it is useless to complicate it by introducing side issues.

The amount of intellectual armor that was strapped on to defend against "manifestations of the dead" upon the publication of the third volume of my work leads me to insist upon the absolute reality of these events. The witnesses are countless. To refuse to believe them means accusing the narrators of poor observation, of suffering from illusions, or even of lying. While these accusations are sometimes applicable, they are not true in general. Let us examine, calmly and carefully, some of these accounts of manifestations of the dead. We may begin with one of the oldest.

This ancient testimony, which will be familiar to my readers because they saw it in *Uranie* <note>original: *Uranie* (1889), a popular astronomical and spiritualist novel by the author, Camille Flammarion.</note>, comes from a...

Some people, who are skeptics by temperament or by inclination, simply declare that they do not believe these stories and that there is no truth in them. However, that is not a serious solution. Minds accustomed to careful study cannot be satisfied with such light-hearted denials.

A fact is a fact. We cannot help admitting it, even when it is impossible to explain it within the current state of our knowledge.

It is true that medical records show there are many kinds of hallucinations and that certain nervous systems <note>original: "nervous organisations"; referring to a person's biological or psychological makeup.</note> are misled by them. But there is a massive gap between that fact and the conclusion that all unexplained psycho-biological phenomena are merely hallucinations.

The scientific spirit of our age rightly seeks to free all these facts from the deceptive mists of "supernaturalism," since nothing is truly supernatural. Nature, whose kingdom is infinite, includes everything.

Today, we see journalists who—either out of ignorance or bad faith—declare that all these accounts <note>original: "recitals"; meaning formal narrations or reports.</note> of apparitions and manifestations of the dead are reported by people of no intellectual merit. The evidence we can and must demand in these researches is not of the same kind as that to which we are accustomed in our laboratories and physical experiments. The dead are not at our disposal. We are forced to rely on the good faith of the storytellers—on their honesty and their conscience. 

If a kind woman writes to me, her tears falling on the paper, saying she has seen a vision of her husband who was buried only the night before, I can imagine she might be suffering from an optical illusion. However, I cannot believe she has invented a story to trap me, nor that the advice she seeks for comfort in her distress is merely an act. If someone falls ill as a result of seeing an apparition, I cannot view that circumstance as a trick played on my belief, and so on. 

None of these objections are serious. When our information shows we are dealing with honest people, does not simple common sense require us to accept their accounts? We should verify them as best we can and interpret them with careful attention, after ruling out cases of illusion and hallucination. I have published the precautions taken against jokers and imposters too often to need to list them again. Generally, these critics are unaware of their own shallow and poorly reasoned arguments.

The only theory that remains seriously worth considering is that of "illusion." However, this hypothesis is rarely applicable and often falls short from every point of view, as seen in the following case:

He was ill for several days in spite of his normally sound health, his strong constitution, and his very skeptical temperament. He did not know of the death, which had happened three hours before. His cry was heard by three witnesses. The vision was seen in a perfectly normal state—while awake in broad daylight and not in a dream—so that a hypnotic hallucination cannot even be imagined.

This narrative, accurate in its smallest details and confirmed by the Rector of St. Luke's, Mr. Davis—who sent it to Professor Adams of Cambridge—can hardly be treated as "nonsense" <note>original: "humbug"</note> or as "rubbish," as many critics wish me to do. Does not common sense permit us simply to turn our backs on these people? To deny such an observation is to deny everything.

We are often told that we must not believe everything we hear, and that there are tricksters and impostors about. This I have said myself a dozen times. But there are cases when invention is not imaginable, and this is one of them.

The word "coincidence" also often comes from the lips of critics. I should like to know what business that word has here. Is there no such thing as cause and effect? Is not the deceased <note>original: "defunct"</note> person the cause of the apparition?

Do you not think, dear readers, that it is time to become positive in our statements and to declare

On Friday, the 10th of January, 1879, after waking from my first sleep, I saw the moon shining through a south-facing window and lighting up my room. My eyes were drawn toward the panels of a cupboard built into the wall, which served as a press <term>press</term> <note>A "press" was a large cupboard or wardrobe used for storing linen or clothes.</note>. I was not at all startled, but thought I was simply seeing an illusion caused by the moonlight, so I turned over and went back to sleep.

The next morning at breakfast, I began to tell the story of the nighttime appearance, when, to my great surprise, my father abruptly left the table in a state of great distress and walked out of the room. I asked my mother for an explanation. She gestured for me to be silent. When the door was closed, she said to me: “Charles, I am going to tell you the strangest story I ever heard. This morning your father told me that he awoke in the night and saw his mother standing by his bedside, but when he tried to speak to her, she vanished.”

This conversation took place about 8:30 on the morning of Saturday, January 11. Before noon, we received a telegram saying that my grandmother had died during the night. But that was not the end of the story; my father later learned that my sister, who lived twenty miles away, had also seen my grandmother appear. Thus, three people, independent of each other, had the same vision. My father noted the exact hour—2:00 a.m.

I am certain that the moon was not far from its meridian <term>meridian</term> <note>The meridian is the highest point the moon or a star reaches in the sky; its position there helps confirm the specific time of night.</note> at the time of the apparition, and that it was about two o'clock, which is a significant confirmation of the time.

I considered it useful to provide the above account in full. It is significant because it records an observation made an hour and forty-five minutes after death, seen independently by three people. The death occurred fifteen minutes after midnight, and the apparition was seen at two o'clock.

What is the explanation?

It is obviously impossible here to imagine any sort of fraud.

The idea of an illusion or hallucination occurring to those independent witnesses seems impossible to me. The narrator declares that, for him and for his father, the phantom was objectively present, and the bonnet is presented as proof. It seems to me that the reality of the apparition may be interpreted as the deceased acting upon the spirits of her children, and that this mental suggestion translated itself into a visual image.

One evening, around 9:00 p.m., while everyone was still busy, my seventeen-year-old sister was walking down the hallway of our home. The following morning, the cook, a young woman about twenty-five, told my mother that the night before, after she had gone to bed, she had heard a breath and felt someone breathing on her face. Opening her eyes, she saw one of her friends from the country—a tall, beautiful girl in peasant clothing—standing by her bed. The cook mentioned that this girl had behaved poorly in the past and that she had often given her good advice. As it turned out, the girl had died the day before.

Can the old and somewhat cliché <note>original: "trite"</note> theory <note>original: "hypothesis"</note> of hallucination explain this case as well? Certainly not. There are two independent experiences here without any identifiable cause, as the death was unknown to both witnesses at the time. One could always assume the account was not true—that the story was made up, that the first girl was mistaken, or the second was lying. However, when these accounts are numbered by the thousands and come from every country in the world, we are called to examine them seriously.

Let us approach this examination with an open mind.

One can also cheat at cards or produce counterfeit coins. Rather than denying all these facts and ridiculing them, it would be wiser to seek the best interpretation—to discuss, respect, and study them. This approach provides guidance toward solving what is, especially today, the greatest of all problems.

These findings are of the highest philosophical significance <note>original: "import"</note>. Regarding psychic phenomena, I would like to quote what the mathematician Henri Poincaré said in 1911 about spiral nebulae <note>Galaxies that have a spiral shape, like our own Milky Way.</note>: “This spiral form occurs much too often to suppose it is due to chance. It is clear how incomplete any theory of the universe's origin <note>original: "cosmogonic theory"</note> is if it ignores it.”³ In the same way, psychic phenomena can no longer be ignored or dismissed by any philosophical theory. They must become an essential part of the study of humanity.

In the past, spiral nebulae were unknown. They were only discovered and studied slowly and gradually. At first, scientists did not believe in them, attributing them to optical illusions caused by instruments. When I entered the Paris Observatory in 1858 at the age of sixteen as a trainee astronomer, I heard people say they were false images created by Lord Rosse's telescope <note>William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse, who built the "Leviathan of Parsonstown," the largest telescope in the world at the time.</note>, which was supposedly shaped with optical flaws that produced those images. Today, however, they are considered an essential element of stellar astronomy <note>original: "sidereal astronomy"</note>. It seems to me that psychic phenomena hold the same position regarding the—

The scope of human reasoning is, in general, very narrow. 

There is no case of a scholar <note>original: "savant"</note> who was skeptical of these phenomena but took the trouble to examine them thoroughly and did not arrive at a conclusion in their favor. The following men all offer eloquent testimony: William Crookes, the physicist; Alfred Russel Wallace, the naturalist; Lord Lindsay; Cromwell Varley, the engineer; Johann Zöllner, the astronomer; Charles Richet, the physiologist; Cesare Lombroso, the physician; Enrico Morselli, the university professor; Professor Sir Oliver Lodge; and many others.

The critics who, from their position of arrogant ignorance, judge the researchers occupied in scrutinizing psychic phenomena—and treat those who admit the existence of the soul as simpletons—remind me of those geologists who, after examining the surface of the Earth to a depth of only one mile, make a definitive judgment on the interior of our planet, which has a diameter of 8,000 miles, and fix the temperature at the very center of our globe!

Science advances and progresses in all its branches. We have just quoted the opinion of Victor Hugo. We may read in his *Postscript of My Life*: “From Francœur to Flammarion, the number of stars seen by telescopes has increased from 60 million to 100 million.” The poet died in 1885. We seek truth sincerely and with complete independence of spirit. The science of the future perhaps holds unexpected discoveries in store, which may transform our whole philosophical structure.

What is the duration of this survival? Does it lead to the immortality of the soul?

In principle, there is no reason to suppose that if the soul survives the body by virtue of its own nature, it should be destined for future destruction. However, that is a metaphysical question outside the realm of scientific observation, to which this work is confined. Observation can only prove that which is happening at the same time as the observation itself. In these present researches, we do not prove immortality, but only survival for a certain period of time.

In the thirteen cases listed above, we only encounter a short survival, lasting a few minutes in Cicero’s story <note>original: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE); the author refers to a traditional account of a ghost appearing to a friend</note>, a few hours in Lord Brougham’s case <note>Henry Brougham (1778–1868), a British statesman who famously recorded seeing a vision of a friend at the exact moment the friend died in a different country</note>, and a few hours for the other observations. We see that, in general, these manifestations closely follow the death of the individual. This is what we already observed in Volume 3.

The essential condition for investigating natural phenomena, says Claude Bernard <note>Claude Bernard (1813–1878) was a French physiologist who pioneered the use of the scientific method in medicine</note>, is to maintain complete freedom of spirit in our studies, based on philosophical doubt. We must never depart from this principle.

The study of the soul is far from being completed. It has hardly begun, especially in the field of experimentation, where the ground has barely been cleared. Now that the principle of survival is established on proofs which cannot be logically refuted, we can go a little further in our <term>metapsychic</term> <note>metapsychic: a term used in the early 20th century for the study of phenomena like telepathy or ghosts that seem to transcend known physical laws; today we call this parapsychology</note> excursions. (The second-to-last of the preceding thirteen observations is a case in point: what is the "shade" <note>original: "shade," meaning a ghost or phantom</note> of an old woman that is perceptible even to a kitten?...)

# CHAPTER II

## HAUNTED HOUSES: A FIRST SURVEY OF THE SUBJECT

->*Truth and falsehood—Proven realities—Ancient and con-*<-
->*temporary observations—Legal recognition of haunted*<-
->*houses—Broken leases—Certainty of the phenomena of*<-
->*haunting.*<-

Who can believe in haunted houses? Only feeble and gullible <note>original: "credulous"</note> minds. They are nothing but old wives' tales <note>original: "nurses’ fables"</note>, useful only for scaring small children. Such is the general opinion—and such, it would seem, must be the verdict of common sense. How much is true? How much is false? "What is asserted without proof is denied without proof," <note>original Latin: *Quod gratis asseritur gratis negatur*</note> as Ernest Renan <note>Joseph Ernest Renan (1823–1892) was a French philosopher and historian famous for his work on early Christianity.</note> said to me one day while we were talking about the new dogma of Papal Infallibility which had just been affirmed by the First Vatican Council in 1870. What is asserted without evidence is simply dismissed. If the reality of haunted houses were not established by irrefutable proof, it would be our right, and even our duty, to deny their existence.

An old proverb assures us that there is no smoke without fire. No doubt there is often much more smoke than fire, but the popular saying remains true.

Even the most absurd legends have some origin.

Now, it is remarkable that stories of haunted houses are as old as the history of humanity itself.

In a large number of cases, especially in recent and contemporary times, critical analysis and judicial inquiries have found nothing in these ghost stories but purely human actions.

<summary>This page introduces a formal investigation into haunted houses, acknowledging widespread skepticism while arguing that the long history of such accounts suggests an underlying reality that requires proof.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's analysis of haunted houses, moving from potential fraudulent or natural explanations to the necessity of a rigorous scientific investigation of the phenomena.</meta>

# FIRST SURVEY OF THE SUBJECT

In the final analysis, these events often turn out to be more or less conscious deceptions by those suffering from hysteria, practical jokes, staged performances, and pranks, which sometimes deteriorate into malicious tricks. Someone may have wanted to scare the residents, avenge an injustice, drive down the value of a house to buy it cheaply, or simply harass cowards <note>original: "poltroons"</note> and gullible victims.

But not all cases can be explained this way. Besides, what was the very first haunted house? Imitation only happens when something already exists. Tricksters merely recreate scenes that have already terrified people. Those original scenes may have been real. On the other hand, they might have been nothing more than fearful <note>original: "timorous"</note> interpretations of very simple natural events—such as strange noises amplified by the silence of the night, which frighten people awake. Originally, there may have been nothing but the movement of stray animals—dogs, cats, rats, mice, or nocturnal birds—or simply the wind blowing through crumbling rooms, doors and shutters banging, or a piece of wall falling down for no obvious reason.

If the stories of haunted houses could be reduced to these explanations, such commonplace occurrences would not deserve a dedicated chapter in this book. But that is not the case. We must examine the facts without prejudice or preconceived ideas, but with the strictest caution <note>original: "circumspection"</note>. Only then can we reach a well-founded conclusion.

Much has been written about these stories, and much has been written against them. For my own part, I have been examining these reports for many years<sup>1</sup>...

Comparing, analyzing, and discussing so many observations, narratives, and commentaries that even twenty years ago I had, for my personal instruction, written a large volume which has remained unpublished.

There are real haunted houses. There are also fake ones. There are genuine banknotes; there are also counterfeit ones. There are truthful people; there are also liars. There are honest people and rascals. There are serious people and fools <note>original: "boobies"</note>. There are intelligent and unintelligent people.

To reject without examination everything that has been said about haunted houses would be as foolish as to accept everything without examination.

Old traditions and proverbs must not always be dismissed. "He roams about like a spirit in torment" is a saying so ancient that its origin is lost in the mists of antiquity. Where did it come from? What is its source?

Not all accounts must be rejected, despised, or suppressed. It is not all error, illusion, or trickery <note>original: "imposture"</note>. Here, as elsewhere, if we wish to learn, we must examine things without prejudice.

It is in this state of mind that we shall investigate this curious problem. There are too many reasons why living people might want to discourage others from living in a certain building for "haunted houses" to remain free from suspicion. There are too many ways to fake noises, move objects, and even create so-called apparitions for us to freely accept everything we are told. And, aside from trickery, there are sometimes natural causes—not of a psychic nature, but difficult to identify specifically. Finally, there is nonsense <note>original: "humbug"</note> and more or less morbid practical jokes of questionable taste, which can play a part even if no personal interests are involved. I can, if you like, give you an example of this: a story of a haunted house—or rather a flat—told by my friend Vibert, the painter, who died in 1902 <note>original: Jehan-Georges Vibert (1840–1902), a well-known French academic painter</note>. It took place in Paris, though I do not know exactly where or when. I have forgotten the names, but I have kept the memory of the facts. The police were notified, but their search proved useless; it was discovered quite by chance that the whole thing was a joke carried out by a studio full of painters.

Human ingenuity is great! I do not believe it is enough to establish the reality of a haunting just because the events observed remain unexplained, or because the phenomena are undeniable, recognized, and not—in general opinion—due to any identifiable cause. For this only proves that nobody knows the natural cause, not that a natural cause does not exist.

I believe that the only facts worth keeping are those which prove their own supernatural <note>original: "extra-natural"</note> origin, both in the category of haunted houses and in all other varieties of psychic phenomena.

I completely agree with the opinion expressed by the learned General. And, after all precautions have been taken, we shall soon have before our eyes typical and rigorously observed examples in which no doubtful element could have entered.

We were astonished by the cleverness of the supposed "tricksters" who could aim so perfectly from such a distance. The chance of such a feat was one in a hundred thousand, even at twenty-five paces—let alone from a mile away.

The good man had caught our interest, but we wished to question his neighbors. We visited several of them, including a prominent bookseller who lived on the corner. Like everyone else, he found the entire affair absolutely inexplicable, and he considered the accusation of trickery <note>original: "jugglery"</note> to be more absurd than anything else.

So says the Marquis de Mirville <note>Jules-Eudes de Mirville (1802–1873) was a French researcher and author known for his detailed studies of the supernatural from a Catholic perspective.</note> concerning that haunted house on the Rue des Noyers. We agree with Bozzano <note>Ernesto Bozzano (1862–1943) was an influential Italian researcher who specialized in analyzing and categorizing paranormal phenomena.</note> that this is the story of almost all the inquiries made into such cases.

In fact, the causes of these phenomena remain impossible to understand. They force skeptics to satisfy themselves with more or less absurd conclusions. These explanations remain harmless as long as the manifestations continue in full force, but they gain a sense of permanence and hide the truth once the manifestations stop and the impression of undeniable authenticity felt by onlookers begins to fade.

The remarkable incident of objects <note>original: "projectiles"</note> being formed in a way that allows them to pass through a narrow slit in a shutter—though marvelous—is not at all rare in this category of events. Indeed, the curious precision with which these objects hit their target is similar to many other cases of missiles which systematically and surely strike a specific mark. It is almost the rule in such cases. Everyone will understand the great theoretical importance of these episodes, since their origin implies a conscious intention served by supernatural faculties and powers. Therefore, we may excuse those who believe that the Devil is involved in the affair. Remember also that the Devil is even now associated with all Christian teaching.

At the same time, let us acknowledge our first impression of these strange actions, which is their triviality and vulgarity. Whatever the cause, they are peculiar forms of activity. “Intelligent forces in action!” they say; if so, they are surely very poor intelligences.

In the district, interpretations differ. The majority attribute the facts to the spirits of the dead. Others maintain that the parish priest of —— is an amateur conjurer, and that we are his victims. Others suppose trickery. My father-in-law, an orthodox pastor, summarily rejects <note>original: "regrets" — here meaning to dismiss or disapprove of</note> the stories in the name of certain Biblical passages. To me, for one, the observations are real, and trickery, as you may see, is inadmissible. Nor is the hypothesis of a hallucination possible; the stones and apples are quite objective. These facts seem to me to belong to the domain of the unknown, and to be worth including among those which you submit to the thinking public.

After all, are they more mysterious than those whose nature we can explain? Perhaps they are, only rarer and more difficult to prove. It shows a lack of sane philosophy to reject from the start <note>original: "a priori"</note> all that is outside the sphere of our ordinary thoughts. The world we see and think about can only be a feeble reflection of objective reality. You have discovered the mysterious link between the magnetic needle and solar storms. Other links, still more mysterious, must join the worlds and beings across all the grades we do not...

### HAUNTED HOUSES

...more particulars of the scenes at the house of d’O. We have stated everything we know.

It is quite true that strange noises are heard every evening from 6 o’clock until midnight on Saint-Paul Street <note>original: "Rue Saint-Paul"</note> in the house of the d’O. family. These noises resemble those produced by the successive firing of a double-barreled gun. They shake the doors, windows, and partitions. No light or smoke is seen, and there is no smell. These facts have been proven by the most distinguished and trustworthy people in our town, as well as by investigations conducted by the police and the gendarmerie <note>The French national police force</note> at the request of the d’O. family.

Mr. H. d’Orange believes there are physical causes, such as gases released from an ancient cemetery upon which the d’O. mansion is supposedly built. However, the house is built on solid rock, and there is no cellar connected to it.

For our part, we believe that these strange and currently unexplained facts, which for more than a month have disturbed the peace of an honorable family, will not always remain a mystery. We believe it is a very clever form of trickery, and we hope soon to see the "ghosts" of Saint-Paul Street appear in the police court.

In spite of this hope, nothing could be discovered, and the court has not had to deal with the unknown forces producing the raps and loud explosions.

As I said before, these events occurred at the house of Count d’Ourches and his sister. Mademoiselle d’Ourches was a <term>medium</term> <note>A person believed to be a bridge between the physical world and the spirit world</note> and was, as I have proposed to call it, *dynamogenic* <note>A term used in early psychic research to describe someone who generates or releases a specific type of vital energy or force</note>.

In connection with this haunted house in Poitiers, we may add that similar noises had already occurred in the same town and the same neighborhood. Joseph von Görres, the well-known author of a famous work called *The Mystics* <note>original: "La Mystique"</note>, reports that according to William of Auvergne <note>original: "Guillaume d’Auvergne"</note> (who died in 1249 and was the Bishop of Paris), a “rapping spirit” (<term>Poltergeist</term> <note>German for "noisy ghost"; a spirit characterized by physical disturbances like loud noises and moving objects</note>) had entered a house in the same Saint-Paul district of Poitiers, and that it threw stones and broke windows.

### FIRST SURVEY OF THE SUBJECT

One policeman even received a hit in his back at the very moment he was trying to explain to a comrade the trajectory <note>original: "parabola"</note> described by the stones in their fall.

In the evening, a calendar placed on a mantelpiece <note>original: "chimney-piece"</note> jumped up and flew through the air. Shoes placed on the floor also jumped about and landed with their soles upward.

When night came, the master of the house decided to keep watch.

He had hardly been alone when he heard a noise. It was a candlestick falling on the mantelpiece. While he was picking it up, a piece of decorative shell-work rolled across the floor. He stooped to pick it up, but the other candlestick fell onto his back. This continued for a good part of the night.

At the same time, the servant who slept upstairs called for help. She was found in such a state of terror that her honesty could not be doubted when she said she had been beaten. She was brought downstairs and put to sleep in a neighboring room. She was soon heard crying out again, and the sound of the blows she received could even be heard. The girl fell ill and had to return to her family.

On Sunday morning and the following day, Belgian coins <note>original: "sous and centimes"</note> were again thrown into the yard.

All these facts are confirmed by the people in the house, who are of a settled, calm, and deliberate character. These events are all the more inexplicable because the neighborhood is well-populated and a close watch has been kept for three weeks.

One can imagine how much the residents of the house suffer from this state of affairs. After first boarding up the windows facing the yard, they abandoned the rooms where these things happened. They are now, in a sense, camping in two or three rooms while waiting for their troubles to end.

These events—like those on Walnut Street <note>original: "Rue des Noyers," a famous 1860 poltergeist case in Paris</note>, Sandstone Street <note>original: "Rue des Grès," likely referring to another Parisian haunting case</note>, and in Poitiers—have defied the most active surveillance and the investigations of the police. In the presence of these many statements and numerous witnesses, denial is no longer possible. There must be some degree of exaggeration in the reports, but there must also be accurate facts at the core.

# HAUNTED HOUSES

These accounts have been personally confirmed by Colonel Mallet of Douai <note>Douai is a city in northern France; Mallet was a French officer interested in scientific anomalies.</note>, a man of genuine scientific achievements who conducted inquiries on-site and among the people involved. We can be certain that these events are real.

Let us admit that these occurrences are absurd, foolish, and meaningless—that they resemble the pranks of mischievous children. If that explanation could be applied, it would be the most natural one. Coins are thrown, shoes moved, objects displaced, and blows struck; there is the same triviality as in previous examples (after all, the lower levels of humanity are not necessarily more spiritual). Are they just boys' pranks? Yet nothing is discovered despite the most rigorous observation, and we shall see later that these movements also occur in hermetically sealed <term>airtight or completely isolated</term> rooms.

Before going any further, we might say that the involvement of the spirits of the dead does not seem to be indicated at all. One might sooner think of goblins <note>The author suggests these entities act more like legendary mischievous spirits than deceased humans.</note>.

We naturally think of electrical phenomena, such as lightning, but acting with a certain basic sense of purpose <note>original: "rudimentary intention"</note>.

The phenomena of haunted houses present us with two sides: on one hand, physical events without any apparent meaning; on the other, spiritual manifestations associated with certain biological properties of girls, young women, and youths. We can see how complex this problem is. Whatever the explanation may be, there are unknown, invisible forces at work. Could there be certain psychic entities in the atmosphere that are entirely lacking in intellectual or moral value? Our human race is full of such individuals. If the soul is not destroyed at death, what happens to the souls of those with severe intellectual disabilities <note>original: "idiots"</note>? And what of animal souls, which are sometimes superior to some human ones?
