As the town clock struck ten, each chime seemed to be echoed by a sound in the wall above the bed. We got a pickaxe and tore up part of the flooring where the knocking was occurring. The sounds moved to a different spot for a short time, but then they returned, sounding as if someone were hammering heavily on the edge of the hole we had just made in the floor.

<header>HAUNTED HOUSES</header>

...phenomena of haunting appear in every possible form.

I thought it appropriate to begin this first survey of our subject with these long-standing memories, which go back over fifty years. They possess the inherent value of showing that my study of these strange phenomena is not a recent hobby. Rather, my understanding is based on a lifetime of experience. I can only smile at those commentators who speak on every subject without actually knowing anything about it, misleading the public by claiming that stories of haunted houses are ridiculous and unworthy of attention. What is truly unworthy of attention is the shallow mindset of uninformed writers.

These memories from half a century ago have since been supplemented by hundreds of observations of various kinds, which confirm and expand upon them in many ways. Two major categories of phenomena demand our attention. On the one hand, there are noises, disturbances, the throwing of objects, the shifting of furniture, and the movement of things without contact and without any apparent cause—the physical facts of **telekinesis** <note>from the Greek words *tele* (distance) and *kinesis* (movement); original: "τηλε, distance, and κινησις, movement"</note>. On the other hand, there are "intelligent" manifestations, whether they come from unknown spirits, the spirits of the dead, or souls in distress. These are two very different categories, and everything must be studied, for we still know very little.

In the era of René Descartes <note>French philosopher and scientist (1596–1650) known for his "scientific method"</note>, science was organized around the direct observation of facts, using a method that stood in contrast to the abstract verbal debates of the past. Today, this organization is far from finished. It must continue by connecting physical facts with those of a psychic nature, which are no less significant.

He argues that modern science must expand to include psychic phenomena just as it once embraced physical observation during the time of Descartes.</summary>

Laplace <note>Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749–1827) was a brilliant French mathematician and astronomer often called the "Newton of France."</note> said on his deathbed: "What we know is very little; what we do not know is vast." What was true in Laplace’s time, a century ago, is even truer today, despite the progress of science—or rather, because of it—since every advance in our knowledge of the world opens new horizons before us.

This is especially true of <term>metapsychics</term> <note>an early 20th-century term for the study of paranormal phenomena, now known as parapsychology</note>, where we understand almost nothing. Here we have an entirely new world, which I believe it would be quite wrong to call "supernatural." Should Nature not embrace and include everything?

We have examined observations made in Paris in 1860 and 1849, at Poitiers in 1864, at Fives-Lille in 1865, at Port Glasgow in 1864, and elsewhere. We will have to choose from among hundreds of cases just to lay the foundation for our studies. Not a year passes without some report of a "haunted house." Before going further, let us look at a very interesting example. I have taken it from the *Review of Psychic Studies* <note>original: "Revue des Études Psychiques"</note>, edited by the capable and sincere writer, C. de Vesme (August 1904):⁷

The English poet Stephen Phillips, known mainly for his plays *Herod* and *Paolo and Francesca*, wanted to find the peace and quiet necessary to finish an important work. It is a method that is difficult to accept, but it is apparently the only one possible in certain desperate cases. This applies, for instance, when a house is apparently “phantom-generating” <note>original: “phantomogenic” — a term suggesting the physical environment itself triggers ghostly activity</note>—that is, it contains all the yet-unknown psychic conditions necessary in this provisional science of transcendental physics for producing the turbulent manifestations of occult entities. *That method consists of the entire demolition of the haunted building down to the ground.*

This practice, like many others, goes back to antiquity. Here is a quite respectable instance from the sixteenth century:

Ferdinand of Aragon, King of Naples, gave his secretary—the celebrated Giovanni Pontano—among other things, a very high square tower, which has since been called the *Pontaniana*. According to what Giulio Cesare Capaccio says in his *History of Naples* <note>original: *Historia Neapolitana*</note>, volume 1, page 61, this tower had to be demolished because it was inhabited by low, evil spirits <note>original Latin: *cacodæmona incoli*</note>.

It is logical to assume that before deciding to destroy a building of such importance—given its age and historical value—it must have been clear that no method other than this very radical one could be found for ending the haunting.

Another, more recent example is provided by Mrs. Crowe <note>The OCR reads “Mrs. Grove,” but this almost certainly refers to Catherine Crowe (1790–1872), the famous author of the cited book.</note> in her book, *The Night Side of Nature*, where we are told that Frederick the Great of Prussia had a haunted house in the village of Quercy pulled down and another one constructed at some distance from it.

Here is another, even more recent case:

Mrs. Ida Pfeiffer <note>Ida Pfeiffer (1797–1858) was a celebrated Austrian explorer and one of the first female travel writers.</note>, the famous traveler—an intelligent woman with a rather masculine character <note>In the 19th century, this was often a way of describing a woman who was courageous, firm, or intellectually rigorous.</note>—recorded in her *Voyage Round the World* (p. 340) the story of a tragic haunting <note>original: *infestazione*</note> which happened in 1853 in a small house belonging to the Residency of Cheribon (Java). This witness, stunned by the phenomena, used every means of discovering their cause and at length had to give it up. Finally, the Government put an end to it by demolishing the house.

Thus, experience shows that this radical remedy has been employed in order to destroy the energetic focus <note>original: "dynamic focus"</note> of the haunting, which then disappears. We see a similar idea in the history of sorcery, where not only were the witches burned, but also the objects accused of being cursed.

Does the principle, "When the cause is removed, the effect is removed" <note>original Latin: *Sublata causa tollitur effectus*</note> apply here also? Was the cause suppressed, or only the conditions necessary for its operation? Correlation is not logically equivalent to causation <note>original Latin: *Cum hoc* (with this) is not logically equivalent to *propter hoc* (because of this).</note>. The cause may be of a psychic, intelligent nature, while the conditions, on the other hand, are material.

This subject of haunted places <note>original Latin: *loci infesti*</note>, which is less rare than one thinks, is one of the most obscure in transcendental psychology. Spiritism, mediumship, and odic force <note>A hypothetical vital energy or life force proposed in the mid-19th century by Baron Carl von Reichenbach.</note>—what is truly at the bottom of it? For centuries, this obscure field has been explored in all directions, and hardly anything has been found. There is much digging, but we do not find the source. Even more than in medicine, we can say with Hippocrates: "Art is long, life is short" <note>original Latin: *Ars longa, vita brevis*</note>.

From the *Light and Shadow* <note>original Italian: *Luce e Ombra*, a prominent Italian journal of psychic studies founded in 1901.</note> report, we may conclude that the subject has been universally discussed.

The events in Egham mentioned above sparked several legal and humorous discussions regarding these accounts in the British press. Mr. Andrew Lang <note>Andrew Lang (1844–1912) was a prolific Scottish author, literary critic, and anthropologist known for his interest in folklore and psychical research.</note>, the well-known anthropologist, wrote an article for the *Morning Post* in which he recalled similar trials caused by disturbing spirits throughout history, and the legislation that was eventually established on this subject.

Alfenus <note>Alfenus Varus was a Roman jurist whose writings were included in the *Digest*.</note>, the author of the *Digest* <note>original Latin: *Digesta*, a collection of juristic writings compiled by order of the Emperor Justinian I</note>, is the primary authority for those who maintain that the tenant of a haunted house is required to prove something more than a "common fear" to obtain a legal cancellation of a lease.

Arnault Ferton, in his *Customs of Burgundy* <note>original French: *Mœurs de Bourgogne*</note>, is of the same opinion as Mr. Lang. He maintains that "phantoms which disturb the peace of the people and make the night sinister" are sufficient grounds for the termination of a tenancy contract. The Parliament of Granada <note>In this historical context, a "Parliament" refers to a high court of appellate jurisdiction rather than a legislative body.</note> adopted this viewpoint on several occasions.

Regarding the Middle Ages, Le Loyer <note>Pierre Le Loyer (1550–1634) was a French magistrate and demonologist who wrote extensively on specters.</note> quotes, in connection with the discussion of manifestations in Parliament, cases of houses where "spirits appear or make noises of all sorts, and disturb the tenants at night." He speaks of Daniel and Nicolas Macquereau, who rented a house on a lease, "and they passed no time when they did not hear the noise and clatter of invisible spirits, who allowed them no sleep or rest." The Parliament broke the lease, thus admitting that there could be places haunted by supernatural beings.

Now M. Maxwell, Advocate-General of the Court of Appeal at Bordeaux, has quoted decisions of several parliaments which, in the eighteenth century, canceled leases on account of haunting.⁹

Legal history includes more recent cases. The *Journal of Debates* <note>original French: *Journal des Débats*, a prominent French newspaper of the time.</note> from April 18, 1912, reports the following:

Mr. J. Denterlander owns a house in Chicago at 3375 South Oakley Avenue. The tax commission valued that significant property based on a rent of 12,000 dollars. Mr. Denterlander protested. Instead of being an asset to him, his house had been nothing but a nuisance. He had immense difficulty renting it because it was haunted. A young woman had died there under mysterious circumstances—likely murdered—and since then, every new tenant had been awakened by moans and cries. The tenants had been discouraged, and one after another had given notice to leave. For that reason, Mr. Denterlander asked for a tax reduction. After discussion, the commission agreed and lowered the valuation from 12,000 to 8,000 dollars. In doing so, they officially recognized the existence of ghosts.

The history of haunted houses is more than just a work of fiction.

Much has been written about the termination of leases and the decrease in the rental value of homes due to hauntings. I need only mention the remarkable legal argument presented in Naples by the lawyer Zingaropoli <note>Francesco Zingaropoli was a well-known Italian lawyer and psychical researcher who specialized in the legal aspects of the paranormal.</note> in defense of the Duchess of Castelpoto against the Baroness Laura Englen. There is a vast body of legal literature and theory on this question.

The most ancient law, which serves as the starting point of the dispute and the foundation for other discussions, is that of the lawyer Alfenus, reported in Book 19 of the *Digest* <note>original Latin: *Digesta*, a massive collection of Roman legal writings compiled by order of Emperor Justinian I.</note> (Title II, Law 27).

> "He was asked again whether someone who moved out because of fear should owe rent or not. He replied: if there was a reason why he feared danger, even if there was no danger in reality, he still should not owe rent; but if the cause of fear was not justified, he should owe it nonetheless." <note>original Latin: "Iterum interrogatus si quis timoris causa emigrasset, deberet mercedem, nec ne? Respondit: si causa fuisset cur periculum timeret, quamvis periculum vere non fuisset, tamen non debere mercedem; sed si causa timoris justa non fuisset, nihilominus debere."</note>

This fragment is commented upon by Godefroy <note>original: Gotofred. Denis Godefroy was a 16th-century jurist famous for his edition of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the body of Roman law.</note> (translated by Vignali, *Digest*, vol. iii, p. 133; Naples, 1857).

The fear must be *imminent*, and the tenant has the right to leave a dwelling as a result of a justified fear. I remember that when I was a young man, Ludovic Santonio—a very eloquent barrister in Paris, who was also my trustee and brother-in-law—obtained the cancellation of a client's lease. The client complained that he had not been able to enjoy the house he rented because of specters and ghosts which haunted it. Santonio argued that a tenancy was similar to a sale, and that it must transfer the risks associated with the rented property to the tenant. He quoted witnesses who were beyond dispute, drawing on the Holy Scriptures and quoting Matthew 8, Mark 5, and Luke 13, as well as a passage from Pliny the Younger, Book 7, Letter 27 <note>The original text cites "Book XXVII, Letter 7," but this is likely a mistake for Pliny’s famous ghost story in Book 7, Letter 27.</note>. He also recalled the story of the spirit of Samuel which appeared to Saul, and the striking passage by Saint Augustine in his treatise, *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead* <note>original Latin: *De Cura pro Mortuis Gerenda*</note>.

The commentaries and quotations of Godefroy show the importance attached to this question. In the Middle Ages, the issue was magnified and exaggerated by the dominance of demonological literature. These mysterious manifestations—the disturbances and troubles forced upon the inhabitants of a house—overwhelmed them beyond measure because of the deep-rooted conviction that they represented satanic intervention. One must go through the best-known demonological books—the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: *Malleus* (referring to the *Malleus Maleficarum*)</note> by Sprenger, the *Anthill* <note>original: *Formicarius*</note> by Nider, the *Magical Investigations* <note>original: *Disquisitiones Magicæ*</note> by Father Martin del Rio, and also the works of the Protestant theologians of that era, beginning with Martin Luther—to see how far the Devil's power was thought to extend. It was believed to be *everywhere*, and any event, even the simplest, could be caused by a malicious influence. This power was also considered all-knowing, aware of the past, the present, and the future.

Numerous quotations from both ancient and modern authors are recorded by Martin Delrio <note>original: l'Espagnol del Rio. Martin Delrio (1551–1608) was a Jesuit scholar and author of the influential treatise on magic and the supernatural, *Disquisitiones Magicae*.</note> in his *Disquisitions*.

Grimaldi Ginesio, in his *History of the Laws and Magistrates of the Kingdom of Naples* <note>original: *Istoria delle Leggi e Magistrati del Regno di Napoli*</note> (vol. 9, p. 4), discusses the *Pragmatic Commentary* regarding laws on "letting and hiring" <note>original Latin: *De Locato et Conducto*</note> published by the Count of Miranda on December 24, 1587. He writes as follows: "If it happens that in a rented house the tenant, driven by panic and terror, believes he is being attacked by those malignant spirits called in Naples the *Monacelli* <note>The *Monacelli* (literally "little monks") are mischievous or malevolent spirits in Neapolitan folklore, often blamed for unexplained disturbances in the home.</note>, he is allowed to leave without paying any compensatory penalties."

All the best-known French legal commentaries deal with this question at length, mentioning the legal precedents <note>original: jurisprudence</note> of the ancient parliaments of Paris and Bordeaux.

Troplong <note>Raymond-Théodore Troplong (1795–1869) was a French jurist and president of the Court of Cassation.</note>, in his work *On Exchange and Leasing* <note>original: *De la Permutation et de la Location*</note> (discussing Article 1702 of the Napoleonic Civil Code, which corresponds to Article 1577 of the Italian Code, paragraph 197), mentions "this hidden defect" <note>original French: *ce vice rédhibitoire*. In law, a "redhibitory vice" is a hidden defect that makes an item or property unfit for its intended use, potentially allowing for the cancellation of a sale or lease.</note>—the appearance of ghosts and phantoms in rented houses.

A certain person having rented a house, says Charondas <note>Louis Le Caron, known as Charondas (1534–1613), was a prominent French jurist.</note> in his *Legal Responses* <note>original: *Responsi*, Book VII, 232</note>, had hardly entered when he heard very loud and fearful noises from ghosts that appeared in the house, causing unbearable annoyance to himself and his family. During the night, several visions appeared to his sons and tormented them. On that account, the tenant demanded the landlord cancel and annul his contract. He argued that the owner knew before finalizing the lease that these phantoms and specters appeared in the house, having learned it from previous tenants who had abandoned the house for the same reason. 

"The facts having been fully proven, the application of the law was the only thing in question." The court did not wish to decide the specific question of whether spirits existed because *that question belonged to the realm of religion*. It judged, nevertheless, that it had jurisdiction regarding the fulfillment of agreements and contracts between people. However, it found nothing in Roman or French law to show that the fear of apparitions or ghosts was considered sufficient to cancel or annul the lease of a house, and judgment was delivered accordingly <note>This implies that the court ruled against the tenant, prioritizing the literal letter of the law over the tenant's fear of the supernatural.</note>.

See also Dalloz <note>Désiré Dalloz was a famous 19th-century French legal scholar and creator of a major legal encyclopedia.</note> in his *General Jurisprudence: Repertoire of...*

*Legal Precedents*, Paris, 1853, vol. 30, p. 313, par. 190 <note>original: *jurisprudence*</note>; Duvergier <note>Jean-Baptiste Duvergier (1792–1877) was a prominent French jurist and collector of legal decrees.</note>, No. 528; Troplong <note>Raymond-Théodore Troplong (1795–1869) was a French jurist whose works on the Napoleonic Code were highly influential.</note>, No. 197, etc.

This is the argument supported by the Italian lawyer.

We can see that legal experts agree with general public opinion. I point out these facts primarily to establish the following point:

*Haunted houses have been recognized for several centuries by European law.* <note>original: jurisprudence</note>

To deny the reality of haunted houses is a mistake often born of ignorance in such matters.

Haunting has always existed. Theologians have frequently commented on these phenomena because, for centuries, civilization focused on debating words rather than studying reality through observation or experiment. They explained everything as the work of demons. However, in our time, few people believe in demons. We require an explanation that can be more easily verified.

This initial survey has presented us with a number of very diverse examples—strange, inexplicable, trivial, or even childish, and often irritatingly mundane. Nevertheless, these events were real, observed, and verified by reliable witnesses who suffered so much that they abandoned the homes where they had once lived quite comfortably, asking for the cancellation of significant leases. What is the meaning of these incomprehensible occurrences whose triviality we find off-putting? They seem to reveal intentional acts, confused thoughts, or a lower form of intelligence. On our planet, we have no known example of thought existing without a brain. Yet certain effects of lightning are so unusual that they give the impression of a hidden intention, such as the case of the lady discussed at the Academy of Sciences <note>original: *Académie des Sciences*</note> (cited in *Concerning Death*, p. 311 <note>original: *Autour de la Mort*</note>).

<summary>The author highlights that European legal systems have long recognized haunted houses as a legitimate basis for breaking leases. He argues that while past generations attributed these disturbances to demons, modern inquiry should seek a more scientific understanding of these seemingly intentional, albeit trivial, phenomena.</summary>

<header>FIRST SURVEY OF THE SUBJECT</header>

On the other hand, the laws that govern the system of the world do not originate from a physical brain. There is a spiritual force <note>The author suggests that the "laws of nature" are not merely mechanical, but driven by an underlying intelligence or spirit.</note> within nature.

What is that "instinct" of a hen <note>original: fowl</note> that sits on her eggs for twenty days to hatch chickens? What is the perpetual renewal of countless millions <note>original: myriads</note> of living beings? The remarkable facts we wish to study here indicate extraordinary <note>original: fantastic</note> manifestations of this unknown spirit—a spirit that is likely beyond our understanding.

As we have said, this is only a preliminary survey. A more general exploration of haunted houses will be presented later.

We have a large number of facts for careful examination. They are so numerous that before entering this "forest" of information, we must first stop to consider some examples that have been precisely observed. We shall begin with one of the most typical and complete cases.

# CHAPTER III

## STRANGE PHENOMENA IN A CALVADOS CASTLE

As I have just mentioned, we are now entering the heart of our subject. The following account of the strange phenomena observed in 1875 in a Norman castle was written by M. J. Morice, a doctor of law. It was based on reports from the owner and witnesses and was published in the *Annals of Psychic Sciences* <note>original: *Annales des Sciences Psychiques*</note> in 1893. 

"No one can question the honesty and intelligence of this castle's owner," writes my learned friend Dr. Dariex, the editor of the *Annals*. "He is an energetic and smart man. He personally noted down every day all the extraordinary events that he and the other inhabitants of the castle witnessed, recording them exactly as they occurred. These witnesses, in turn, attested to the reality of these facts. However, the owner asked the narrator to ensure that *no names were printed*." (A restriction we may regret.) 

The following account has been shortened where possible, as the observations were numerous and lasted for a long time:

---
1. See *Annals of Psychic Sciences* <note>original: *Annales des sciences psychiques*</note>, 1893, p. 65.
---

Around the year 1835, there was an old castle in that parish belonging to the B. family.

The building was in such a state of decay that restoration was considered impossible. It was replaced by a new castle, built 150 yards to the north of the old one.

Mr. de X inherited the property in 1867 and moved in.

In October of that year, there was a series—

The state of fear became so great that the Abbé and his pupil went to stay with the parish priest.

Another incident: A friend or cousin, who was a military officer, wanted to spend a night in the particularly haunted room where nobody usually slept. He had his revolver and was determined to shoot at anyone who disturbed his sleep. He kept a light burning. He was awakened by the rustling sound <note>original: "frou-frou"</note> of a silk robe. He felt the coverlet over his feet being pulled away. He spoke to the nightly visitor without getting a reply and lit his candle, which went out again at once. Three times he lit it, and three times it went out. And still, the rustling and the interference with the bedclothes continued. He decided to shoot at the point indicated by the movement of the blankets, assuming that was the position of the intruder, and intended to hit the being point-blank. He fired, but without any result. Yet the bullets <note>original: "balls"</note> had not been removed from the cartridges, for they were found in the wall the next morning.

Does the strangeness of the phenomena described to me by the residents of La Constantinie and their neighbors justify rejecting them? People who contest the possibility of these spontaneous movements of material objects from the start <note>original: "a priori" (Latin: based on theoretical deduction rather than observation)</note> will, of course, not be convinced. I am inclined to think the opposite is more certain, and that the future will reveal many things. Nature is infinite, and we hardly know it.

Was it fraud? And was there a significant error in what the witnesses observed? The second theory cannot be accepted. The physical evidence is undeniable. Numerous items were broken right before the witnesses' eyes. The sound of these objects falling and the presence of the broken pieces, gathered exactly where they were seen to shatter, provide clear physical evidence <note>original: "objective confirmations"</note> for the testimony. These circumstances also rule out the possibility of a hallucination.

This leaves the theory of fraud. This naturally comes to mind. It might explain some of what happened, but it would seem to require many unlikely additional theories <note>original: "accessory hypotheses"</note> to explain every fact we have collected.

If a fraud was committed, who did it? Only three people can be suspected: the Faure ladies and their servant, Marie Pascarel. Most of the phenomena took place when these three people were present.

The movement of objects without contact was observed in many cases when the other residents of La Constantinie <note>La Constantinie is a small hamlet in the Corrèze region of France, the site of a famous 1888-1889 "poltergeist" case.</note> were absent and therefore could not have caused them. Among these instances are the events observed by the Mayor of Objat, as well as the tapping sounds, the damage, and the ransacking of the beds in various rooms when only the Faure ladies and their servant were home.

We can also rule out the Faure ladies. Setting aside their high social standing <note>original: "respectability"</note>, we must consider the obvious terror they lived in and the financial loss they suffered from the damage. Additionally, no link was ever found between them and the events. The disturbances stopped completely once Marie Pascarel left. Furthermore, some events occurred when the girl was alone with one of the Faure women. Finally, the physical weakness of the elder Madame Faure makes it impossible for her to have taken part in any fraud.

On the other hand, a clear connection was noticed between the presence of Marie Pascarel and the movement of objects without any visible contact. She was always present when the phenomena occurred. Some things even happened when she was entirely alone, such as the moving of the heavy barrels <note>original: "casks"</note> in the cellar and the fire in the bed. She was the apparent cause of these strange events. She was suspected by

We cannot, therefore, attribute fraud to anyone except Marie Pascarel <note>The young servant girl at the center of the investigation.</note>. Yet even in her case, this theory is difficult to accept. Some circumstances seem to make it possible, while others tend to rule it out. The former can be briefly summarized as follows:

She was always present at La Constantinie when an unexplainable phenomenon occurred. Her character had its flaws. She was not always polite to Mme. Faure <note>The mistress of the house.</note>. She was intelligent, bold, and interfered in matters that did not concern her. However, her honesty was never questioned. It was she who first reported the fire.

If the occurrences were caused by fraud, we may conclude that it was she who planned them and who cleverly deceived all the witnesses. Yet the circumstances that tend to rule out fraud are more numerous and significant than those suggesting it:

(1) **Lack of a clear motive.** Marie Pascarel was in a good position, and given the rural customs in Limousin <note>A former province in south-central France, known for its distinct cultural traditions.</note>, she could not easily find another job at that time of year. It was not, therefore, in her interest to risk being fired or to leave her job of her own choice. We should remember that at her age and in her social position, she could have no career other than that of a servant. Her main goal was to keep her job.

These considerations make the theory of fraud inspired by malice very unlikely. Still, I admit it is not impossible. But if it were true, we would have to attribute a remarkable level of boldness to Marie Pascarel. This young girl would have to have cleverly broken her mistresses' dishes and turned everything upside down just to harm and frighten them. Yet nothing suggests she had such evil intentions, which would have to have been very strong to persuade Marie Pascarel to risk being caught. On the other hand, the fire becomes impossible to explain with that motive. If she wanted to cause damage, why would she raise the alarm? Indeed, we would have to believe this young girl possessed an incredible amount of daring to think she set fire to Mme. Faure’s bed at a moment when everyone’s attention was heightened and her direct or indirect involvement was already being suspected.

We must also point out that these events only occurred in broad daylight. A person driven by malice, or simply by a desire to pull a prank <note>original: "mystification"</note>, would surely have chosen the night to act. She would have found more safety in the dark and would have more easily frightened her victims, as night and darkness make people prone to fear and belief. On the contrary, if Marie Pascarel was tricking people, she chose the middle of the day and the presence of many witnesses to carry out her hoaxes.

Was she driven by a desire to deceive? Or did she wish to create the impression that she possessed supernatural power? I do not think so.

In the first case, her hoaxes resulted in a significant increase in work for her, as she had to pick up the broken pieces and throw them away. She had to remake the beds and tidy the rooms after they were disturbed. She also risked being caught and fired under circumstances that would have ruined her reputation and made it difficult for her to find work with anyone else.

In the second case, she would have been seen as a witch. One only needs to know the low opinion the peasants of Limousin <note>A rural region in south-central France.</note> have of witches to realize how unwanted such a reputation would be for a young girl. The unfortunate Marie Pascarel did not, in fact, escape this danger; I witnessed the unfair hostility <note>original: "repulsion"</note> she provoked in others.

### (2) The need for extraordinary cleverness.

This factor is essential for fraud to even be possible. For several days, at any moment, objects moved without any apparent contact in the presence of numerous witnesses. An obvious fraud would have been detected immediately, especially since some witnesses, such as the Mayor, were watching closely for signs of trickery.

The testimony of this official <note>original: "magistrate"</note>, along with that of the Faure ladies, Mme. Madrias, and the male servant, is decisive. The Mayor placed several objects on the table. A stove-brush lay beside them. The brush was suddenly and forcefully thrown into the fireplace. When considering known physical forces, one might think of electricity in its many ever-changing <note>original: "protean"</note> forms. But what about the bloodstains? Maxwell, the researcher <note>original: "special student"</note> M. de Rochas, and to me—another student of these matters who remains in the dark.

I have enough experience with these phenomena to state with certainty that the servant was not the one responsible. The old Latin proverb, "With this, therefore because of this" <note>original: "Cum hoc, ergo propter hoc"; a logical fallacy suggesting that because two things happen together, one must cause the other.</note>, does not apply here any more than it does elsewhere.

On the other hand, the conclusion to be drawn from both the Calvados and Corrèze haunting cases is that invisible beings exist.

To suggest that the servant’s personality was unconsciously split while she was awake, granting her supernatural <note>original: "fantastic"</note> abilities, is a bolder claim than simply admitting that invisible beings exist. We must account for the deliberate <note>original: "intelligent"</note> movement of objects (see page 139): the crucifix being taken down, the mirror being unhooked, and the stove-brush being thrown right under the Mayor’s watchful eyes. None of these actions relate to the typical effects of sleepwalking <note>original: "somnambulism"</note>.

The sheer number of these observations is significant. I am well aware that Victor Hugo is not considered a great poet simply because he wrote 127,934 lines of verse. However, quantity does not, on its own, lessen the value of quality.

# CHAPTER 5

## HAUNTINGS: ANCIENT AND MODERN

->*A disturbed house in Auvergne—A psychic incident in Monaco—Physical phenomena and deaths—Death and clocks.*<-

It would be impossible to collect all the authentic examples of haunted houses in a single volume; it would require ten or twenty volumes instead. Even without counting the countless direct accounts I have received over many years from witnesses who have kindly written to me, the observations published by expert <note>original: "competent"</note> authors are often so distinctive that I am inclined to present them to my readers first for their own evaluation. These accounts reach back very far into the past.

One of the most ancient cases is that of Pausanias, the general of the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedæmonians"</note> at the Battle of Plataea. He was sentenced to starve to death in the temple of Athena <note>original: "Minerva," the Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena</note> in 477 B.C. His spirit, it is said, manifested itself for a long time afterward through cries and terrifying noises. Whether these are legends or genuine memories, ancient history is full of these stories of manifestations after death <note>original: "posthumous manifestations"</note>.

In a work still read today by all educated people, Pliny the Younger relates the classic story <note>original: "almost classical episode"</note> of the Athenian ghost, in which the philosopher Athenodorus bought a house at a very low price because it was haunted. During the first night, while he was reading and writing as usual, he suddenly heard what sounded like the dragging of chains across the floor. Looking up, he saw an old man of mournful appearance, bound in chains <note>original: "loaded with irons"</note>, who came closer, gestured for him to follow, and led him to a place

It is not uncommon for a portrait to fall at the exact hour of death of the person it represents. In volume three of *Death and Its Mystery*, we find a story by Alexandre Dumas <note>Alexandre Dumas (1802–1870) was a famous French writer, best known for *The Three Musketeers*.</note> about a fine pastel drawing falling at the moment of a death, and also of a painting falling under similar circumstances. After the death of Monsieur <note>original: "M."</note> de Curel, the Bishopric of Monaco was occupied by Monsignor Vié (from August 16, 1916, to July 10, 1918). On February 3, 1921, the episcopal palace was vacant and was in the charge of Canon Perruchot, who was then alone at the Bishopric. 

In passing through the great hall on the morning of that day, he saw the portrait on the ground with the glass broken. He immediately had the impression that this inexplicable fall—as the cord and nail were perfectly fine <note>original: "had nothing to do with it"</note>—might correspond to a misfortune. That same day, Father <note>original: "M. l’Abbé"</note> Foccart, the hospital chaplain <term>almoner</term>, passed by, gathered up the fragments of the frame, put the picture back together, and returned it to its place.

(The new Bishop of Monaco has since removed it and substituted his own.)

On page 351 of my book *Around Death* <note>original: "Autour de la Mort"</note>, I wrote that in 1913, at the exact hour an old relative died, her watch, which was hanging in her room, stopped. We often blame such things on chance, but these examples are quite frequent, and clocks do not generally stop in the middle of their operation without cause.

Mr. Duquesne, of Orsay, reported to me on June 25, 1922, an incident where a clock stopped upon the death of a person he had placed in the Salpêtrière <note>original: "Salpêtrière"; a famous hospital in Paris</note>, who had previously given him that very clock as a gift.

Mr. Lucien Jacquin, in Paris, told me in a letter dated October 1, 1922, that on the day his grandfather died, his grandfather’s clock stopped, much to the great astonishment of the entire family.

I believe that these singular manifestations are not as rare as one might imagine.

It was in my parents’ house at Épinal <note>A town in northeastern France.</note>. There was a clock on the mantelpiece, under a glass shade. The whole family was at the table, under the light of a hanging lamp. My father and mother were playing <term>bezique</term> <note>original: "bezique"; a popular 19th-century French trick-taking card game played with two decks of cards.</note>. The children were doing their school lessons. Only the tick-tock of the clock broke the silence which reigned in the semi-darkness of the room. One evening, about nine o’clock, a short rolling noise was heard inside the clock, and everyone looked up. “There,” said my father, “the clock is acting strange.” But nothing more happened, and the clock kept running. We decided to send for the clockmaker in the morning. He found nothing wrong, and the mechanism was in perfect order. He could find no explanation for the strange noise.

The next day—it was not a matter of sending a telegraph in those days—we heard of the death of my maternal grandfather, who had died that evening, perhaps at the very hour when that sinister rolling was heard. It was a curious coincidence that was talked about, but without anyone attaching much importance to it.

The next winter, however, there was a repetition of the same noise. My parents were startled. Would there be another death? There was. An uncle of mine died at the exact time when the clock made the noise. From then on, that clock was an object of anxiety in the family. At the slightest faint sound, frightened eyes turned toward the clock.

These, my dear old friend, are the things observed in a <term>milieu</term> <note>original: "milieu"; a person's social environment or surroundings.</note> where <term>psychic problems</term> <note>original: "psychic problems"; in this context, refers to the study of paranormal or spiritual phenomena.</note> received little attention. A large family was concerned with more practical matters.

I guarantee the absolute accuracy of what I have told you. My memory is very clear. And I must ask you to believe that I would consider it a sacrilege to associate the memory of my parents with a story about which there was even the slightest uncertainty.

->(Signed) ARTHUR LÉVY.<-

The following letter was sent to me from Paris on January 5, 1923:

> DEAR MASTER, <note>The correspondent is addressing Camille Flammarion (1842–1925), a famous French astronomer and researcher of psychic phenomena.</note>
> Being a student in Paris, I have the honor to request your kind judgment on an occurrence which interests me profoundly.
> On last December 19, I suffered the great sorrow of losing my mother at the age of forty-nine.
> On the night following her death, while three of us were in a room adjoining the death chamber <note>original: "death chamber"; the room where the person had just died.</note>, an old clock which had been silent for many years started running. Its striking mechanism rang out the hour of midnight in the clearest tones, even though the hands remained still at 11:20.
> What mysterious force set that rusty clockwork in motion?
> To you, dear Master, who have analyzed the human soul, I present this disturbing question, assuring you of my gratitude for the honor of a reply.

> 23, RUE SAINT-ANDRÉ-DES-ARTS,

The only answer to give in the current state of science is that we have a great number of similar examples, which prove their reality and rule out mere chance. They can only be explained through a comparative study. Was the soul of the deceased person not at work in this case?

Can we try to interpret these "coincidences" as symbolic?

What is a clock or a watch? It is an instrument for measuring time. Now, time is the essential element of life and leads ultimately to death.

In the universal psychic force which governs all things, there is an unknown intelligent principle associated with all events, both great and small—from the evolution of a world to the instinct of a bird or an insect.

Wouldn’t the stopping of an instrument that measures time correspond to the ending of a life? And wouldn't it then have a specific meaning or significance, rather than being a random effect of an unknown cause?

These physical effects associated with the dead are certainly difficult to understand. A stopped clock that starts ticking again; an object that falls. Pure chance—even when analyzed using the mathematical laws of probability <term>calculus of probabilities: the branch of mathematics dealing with the likelihood of random events</term>—does not explain these coincidences. A long time ago, in my book *The Unknown* <note>original French: "L'Inconnu," a famous work by Flammarion exploring psychic phenomena</note> (p. 175), I published a story about a coffee set falling with a great crash at the exact hour a family’s son died in Africa. In that letter, dated May 4, 1899, there was another incident that I did not publish then. Here it is:

> My grandparents had left the country and moved to La Rochelle <note>A coastal city in southwestern France.</note>.

> A new coffee service had been placed on the mantelpiece, just as the old one had been. Six years later, in 1841, my grandparents heard the same noise in the parlor. They ran to the room. The door and windows were shut, so there was no draft of air in this case either.
> 
> On entering the room, my grandparents were amazed to see the same phenomenon that had occurred at the death of their son. The coffee set lay in a heap of shattered fragments.
>

> 
> My grandfather—who is not inclined toward superstition but is actually quite skeptical of imaginary things—told these facts to my father and then to my mother. I heard it from them. The serious and strictly honorable character of the people involved leaves no room for doubt regarding their truthfulness.

> Niort (in the Deux-Sèvres region of France).

## MYSTERIOUS NOISES AT A PARSONAGE. THE TEACHER’S HOUSE. AN INVISIBLE COMPANION

If the haunted castle of Calvados impressed us particularly by its undeniable authenticity, the parsonage in the following story will give exactly the same impression.

In the report on Apparitions <note>original: "Phantasms," referring to the seminal work *Phantasms of the Living*</note>, published by the Society for Psychical Research and translated in the *Annals of Psychic Sciences* <note>original: "Annales des Sciences Psychiques"</note>, the celebrated naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace tells a remarkable story of a haunted house. The account was provided by a high-ranking official of the Church of England <note>original: "Anglican Church"</note> who lived in the house for twelve months, and who particularly observed the behavior of his dogs. During an attempted burglary at the parsonage, the dogs gave the alarm, and the clergyman got up after hearing their ferocious barking. However, during the haunting noises, they did not bark at all, even though the sounds were louder and more disturbing. Instead, the dogs were found huddled in a corner in a state of absolute terror. Let us read the account itself,¹ which is well worth our attention.

It is the observer himself who speaks—a learned clergyman and an upright, sensible man in full possession of all his mental faculties:

About eighteen years ago, having completed the two-year probationary period following my ordination as a deacon, I was searching for a curacy <term>curacy: the office or position of a curate, a member of the clergy who assists a parish priest</term>. Among others which—

At the end of that time, I was appointed to a church living <note>original: "benefice," a permanent Church of England appointment</note> in another part of England, and consequently resigned my position as curate <note>original: "curacy," the office of an assistant clergyman</note>. About 11 p.m., some rather violent blows were struck—as if with a stick held horizontally—on the table and sideboard of the room which served as a kitchen. At the same time, chairs danced, plates moved without breaking, and glasses knocked against each other, though they were found undamaged <note>original: "intact"</note> afterward.

About 1 a.m., three distinct, rather loud blows were struck in our own room on the woodwork of Mr. Salières’s bed.

The entire house was occupied by Mr. Salières, one of his brothers, and one of his sisters. The sister could not have been the cause of the noises, which only happened on the first floor <note>In France, the "first floor" refers to the level above the ground floor.</note>.

The rarity of authentic observations has no impact on <note>original: "bearing upon"</note> their reality, regardless of what certain strange <note>original: "queer"</note> debaters <note>original: "disputants"</note> might say.

Who are the witnesses consulted by the law? Naturally, those who have actually seen something.

What should we think of the following sentence:
“Since ten people saw the accused commit his crime and forty million did not, the accused is acquitted.”

Would the forty million inhabitants of France who had not seen the event have even the slightest weight against the evidence <note>original: "negative weight"</note>?

Yet this is the type of reasoning used by our opponents against these sincere investigations <note>original: "researches"</note>.

In an excellent article on haunted houses, Professor (Sir) William Barrett summarizes his views as follows:

1. Fraud and hallucination are not enough to explain all the phenomena.
2. The noises, movements of objects, and other physical phenomena seem to have some relation to an invisible intelligence which, despite its flaws <note>original: "imperfection"</note>, has some resemblance to our human intelligence.
3. These phenomena are usually associated with a person or a location, so that a base of operations <note>original: "point d'appui"; a French term literally meaning a "point of support" or a fulcrum</note> seems necessary for their production.
4. These phenomena are occasional <note>original: "sporadic"</note> and temporary, lasting some days or months, appearing and disappearing suddenly without a known cause.³

I agree with Barrett <note>Sir William Barrett (1844–1925), an English physicist and a founder of the Society for Psychical Research.</note> and Richet <note>Charles Richet (1850–1935), a Nobel Prize-winning French physiologist who researched spiritualist phenomena.</note> that the testimonies are too precise to be denied.

There are numerous cases, scrutinized under strict examination, which prove that objects move without contact and that noises occur for which no ordinary mechanical explanation can be found.

It is absurd to suggest that for weeks and months, several individuals—all in full possession of their faculties, conscientious, responsible, and scrupulously observant while living in a supposedly haunted dwelling—should have seen things that did not exist and heard loud, threatening noises that did not happen. If it were only a single case or involved only one person, we could respect the theory of illusions or hallucinations. However, that explanation is childish. We use the word "hallucination" as a convenient way to dismiss an unusual fact that disturbs our peace of mind. Such a tactic is the mark of a simpleton.

But let us not linger on useless arguments and instead continue our study. In any case, we can conclude from the events at the teacher’s house—just as we did from the occurrences at Calvados and Corrèze <note>Regions in France where famous haunting cases had been reported.</note>—that *invisible beings* do exist.

Phenomena related to hauntings take many forms. Some display an unintelligent triviality that is quite disconcerting. Others show some connection to the dead. Some appear to be completely independent of deceased persons, whether known or unknown. Others, yet again, show evidence of intelligence without being associated with anyone who was once alive. We are dealing with an invisible and unknown world. We must analyze these amazing occurrences with even greater care.

# CHAPTER VII

## THE EXTRAORDINARY VILLA OF COMEADA, COÏMBRA (PORTUGAL)

At Comeada, a suburb of Coïmbra—a town particularly famous for its secular University—certain strange <note>original: "fantastic"</note> phenomena occurred that are worth recording here:

At the beginning of October 1919, Mr. Homem Christo, a first-year law student who had been expelled from the University for refusing to conform to a religious custom and for taking part in an armed revolt, rented a house in Comeada. The house consisted of a ground floor and a first floor, where he moved in with his young wife and two maids. From the very first night, the lady complained of hearing strange noises in the house. Eight days later, one of their friends, Mr. Gomez Paredes, a second-year law student at the University, visited Comeada on business. He asked them for a night’s hospitality, which they readily granted. After they had spent the evening together, they each retired to their bedrooms around 1:00 a.m.

Hardly had he put out his candle when Mr. Gomez Paredes heard knocks on his windowpanes. He got up, lit his candle, and opened his window quite wide, but saw no one. He lay down again and put out his candle, but then he heard footsteps very close to him, and doors opening and closing all over the building. He lit the light again and searched everywhere—under the bed, behind the furniture, and so on. He found nothing and no one. He put out the light, and the noises started again. He lit it, and they stopped. Not wishing to disturb <note>original: "derange"</note> anyone, he endured the situation all night long. In the morning, he asked his friend, Mr. Homem Christo, whether he had heard anything unusual during the night.

“I heard nothing..."

It should be noted that everyone slept on the first floor, and no one was on the ground floor.

He went out to see if anyone was running away down a neighboring lane. Scarcely was he outside when the door slammed shut behind him and was locked. Outside, he saw no one. All this took place in complete darkness, for as soon as a light was struck <note>original: "a light was struck"; likely referring to lighting a match or a candle.</note>, nothing more was heard.

# CHAPTER VIII

## CHERBOURG OBSERVATIONS. WHAT IS THE AURA OF A DWELLING?

*Dr. Nichols and the fatal room—The malevolent <note>original: "maleficient"</note> ceiling of Oxford—The Cambridge obsession—Pierre Loti’s mosque at Rochefort.*

Not all manifestations of haunting show the same intensity or the same characteristics. The haunting I am about to describe has the personal interest of being closely connected to me. However, it contains no highly dramatic elements, except for the anxiety that naturally comes with these sensations.

Does any material trace remain in a home after the death of the people who lived there? Some observations seem to suggest so. In this field, as everywhere else, we find illusions, errors, misunderstandings, and even fraud <note>original: "trickery"</note>. But there are some undeniable facts. The following account is so well-documented <note>original: "presents an authenticity"</note> that it leaves no room for doubt, even though the explanation is no easier than in previous cases.

This minor event took place on the nights of April 26 to 27, 1918, and the following night, at No. 13, Rue de la Polle, Cherbourg. The house belongs to my friend, Dr. Bonnefoy, who was then the chief medical officer of the Naval <note>original: "Marine"</note> Hospital. I had stayed there in September 1914 with my wife, my secretary, Mademoiselle Renaudot, and our young cook, at the invitation of Madame Bonnefoy, president of the Red Cross and of the *Femmes de France* <note>original: "Women of France," a major French humanitarian organization and branch of the Red Cross</note>, who had asked us

I was deeply moved by it. Memories of the past constantly came to mind. I could see our friend again, as she appeared during her happy, active, and peaceful life devoted entirely to good deeds. I imagined her lying in this very bed, which had served as her deathbed for two days and three nights.

During the first night, from April 25 to 26, I could not sleep while thinking about her past and the current state of her home. I also felt rather unwell <note>original: "indisposed"</note>.

The following night, April 26 to 27, I promised myself a good night’s rest. I fell asleep around 11:00 p.m., having set aside my memories.

At 4:00 a.m. on the 27th, a loud noise woke me up. To the left of the bed, I heard terrible crackling sounds in the wall, which then moved toward the table and around the room. Then there was a softer sound, repeated several times, like someone turning over in bed. The wood of my own bed creaked as well. Finally, I heard the sound of light footsteps gliding along the left side of the bed, passing around it, and entering the sitting room <note>original: "drawing-room"</note> on the right. This was where Madame Bonnefoy used to listen to her husband—who was an excellent musician—playing the organ or the piano.

These sounds affected me so deeply that my heart felt as if it were choking me with its pounding, and my jaw went stiff.

Overcome with emotion, I got up, lit a candle, and sat down on a basket on the landing outside the room.

# HAUNTED HOUSES

At that moment, I tried to find a reason for the noises. They continued with even greater intensity, but there was nothing to be seen.

At 5:00 a.m., overcome by irrational terror and unable to endure it any longer, I went upstairs to the cook, Marie Thionnet, who slept on the third floor. She came back down with me. After her arrival, we heard nothing more. It may be helpful to note that the cook's personality did not at all match that of Madame Bonnefoy.

At 5:45 a.m., the doctor on the second floor got up and went into his dressing room. The noises he made while getting up and walking about did not in the least resemble the sounds I had heard an hour earlier.

During the day, I looked for a logical explanation for the phenomenon, such as cats or rats climbing along the walls. I examined the wall to the left of the bed. It was very thick, covered on the outside with slates, smooth, and overlooked a courtyard. It would have been a difficult path for cats or rats, as was the front wall on the Rue de la Polle <note>A street in Cherbourg, France</note>. Besides, the noises were very different from those produced by animals.

On Saturday, April 27, I went to bed at 10:45 p.m., feeling disturbed and nervous.

At 11:00 p.m., the noises started again, just as they had in the morning. In my state of fear, I immediately went upstairs to the cook. She came down and lay on the bed beside me. We left our candles burning. For half an hour the noises continued, with loud cracks coming from the wall on the left. Raps sounded on Madame Bonnefoy's portrait, or perhaps behind it, and the knocking was so loud that we feared the picture would fall. At the same time, the sound of footsteps glided through the room. The cook heard all of this as well and was deeply affected <note>original: "impressed"; meaning shaken or moved by the experience</note>. She is twenty-six years old.

At 11:30 p.m., the noises stopped. Because these occurrences <note>original: "manifestations"</note> were very unpleasant—especially since they were caused by something unknown and incomprehensible—I tried to calm myself during the following day. Supposing that the deceased woman might be connected to them, since it happened in her house, I begged her to spare me such painful emotions.

We stayed in the house until Saturday, May 4. Having heard nothing further and having calmed down, I then asked the deceased to reveal herself <note>original: "manifest herself"</note> and to let me know in some way what she might want.

### THE COOK'S ACCOUNT

On Saturday morning, April 27, 1918, around five o'clock, Mademoiselle <note>original: "Mlle."</note> Renaudot came for me to witness some noises in her room. I went down, but heard nothing.

The following night, April 27, a little after eleven, Mademoiselle Renaudot came again about the same noises, which had returned. I went down with her and heard noises behind the bedside table, as if someone were scratching the wood. Then I heard a sound as if someone glided very quickly over the floor from the table to the drawing room, and also as if someone had struck sharp blows behind the portrait of Madame <note>original: "Mme."</note> Bonnefoy. These noises lasted about half an hour. I admitted that I was very afraid, so much so that my teeth rattled. There were two lighted candles in the room, and we were wide awake, talking about the noises aloud and locating them as they occurred.

The following night I went down again at Mademoiselle Renaudot's request, as she did not dare to remain alone in the room because she was so disturbed, and I slept beside her. I heard some slight further noises, but was much less afraid. We slept very well, and then everything ceased.

It seemed as if my presence interfered with the noises, for they became fainter <note>original: "feebler"</note> after I arrived and then stopped entirely.

Nevertheless, I heard them only too well. They were very intense <note>original: "impressive"</note> and extremely unpleasant to me.

I also slept in Madame Bonnefoy's bed with Mademoiselle Renaudot on the nights of Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday; but we heard nothing more, fortunately for me, for I should not like to go through that half-hour of April 27 again.

->Signed, MARIE THIONNET.<-

CHERBOURG,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*May 7, 1918.*

It is useful to note that Mademoiselle <note>original: "Mlle."</note> Renaudot—a young astronomer at the Juvisy Observatory <note>The Juvisy Observatory was founded by Camille Flammarion in 1883.</note>, a distinguished mathematician, and at that time the Secretary to the Council of the Astronomical Society of France and editor of its monthly *Bulletin* during the war <note>This refers to the First World War (1914–1918).</note>—is a contributor to several scientific journals. She is accustomed to the physical <note>original: "exact"</note> sciences, not at all easily influenced, very skeptical of psychic phenomena, and most unlikely to be the victim of any illusion. This woman, who never knew fear and who passed entire nights in the solitude of astronomical observations under the silent dome, and who walked alone at midnight through lonely park avenues and dark streets, experienced a terrible fear for the first time in her life on that night.

What can be the explanation of this adventure? No normal cause can provide it—neither neighbors, nor cats, nor rats, nor mice, nor anything imaginable.

That the deceased lady was in some way associated with it is extremely probable, if not certain, since these events happened in her house, in the room of her girlhood where she lived for twenty years, and in her personal environment <note>original: "milieu"</note> near her deathbed. In hundreds of cases (which I have collected and compared), the same coincidences are found. However, we may agree that these noises signify nothing and show a triviality unworthy of a cultured spirit such as we knew in Madame <note>original: "Mme."</note> Bonnefoy.

The essential feature of this manifestation is that it filled the two observers with a real sensation of horror and anguish. This also happens in similar cases, for those who experience them do not wish to encounter them again at any price. They remember it as a practical joke in bad taste—extremely disagreeable and incomprehensible.

These pages were written in September 1918, a few months after the curious episode reported above. They were written in Cherbourg itself, but in another house with a view of the sea. I often used to sit on the shore, right by the incoming waves. Every day, the ebb and flow move the water before our eyes. A lady of my acquaintance became suddenly very unhappy simply because she had moved into a house that was actually quite pleasant and convenient. The feeling of emotional depression <note>original: "moral depression"; in this period "moral" often referred to mental or emotional states</note> that overwhelmed her reached an extreme level whenever she entered the main room of the house. Under the weight of this obsession, the lady eventually had to move to another house.

I was informed of these facts and, wanting to clear up the mystery, I began an inquiry into the previous inhabitants of the home. It was not long before I discovered that it had been occupied by a gentleman whose wife, suffering from a suicidal obsession <note>original: "suicidal mania"; a historical psychological term for an uncontrollable urge to end one's life</note>, had thrown herself headfirst from the window of that same main room and was killed instantly. Can we conclude from this that a kind of "saturation of the aura" <note>The idea that a person's energy or emotional state can "soak" into the physical environment</note> was produced, which was capable of being transmitted to the next person occupying the same room—even to the point of making her repeat the same suffering and the same suicidal impulse?

It is important to note that the new tenant was a stranger in the town and knew nothing of the people who had lived there before her.

This account from Dr. Nicolas <note>Likely Jean-Henri-Auguste Nicolas, a French researcher of psychic phenomena</note> cannot fail to attract our attention when considered alongside other similar observations.

*Seen and Unseen*, Miss Katherine Bates reports a curious personal observation communicated by her to the English S.P.R. <note>The Society for Psychical Research, a non-profit organization founded in 1882 to investigate paranormal phenomena</note>, and published in its journal (vol. 7, p. 282). On May 18, 1896 [she writes], I had gone to Cambridge to live at No. 35 Trumpington Street. My friend Miss Wales was away, and I had stayed alone for the night. When she came back the next day, I told her I had had a horrible night. I was haunted by recurring dreams about a man I had not seen or heard of for many years, but who at one time had been long and intimately linked with my life. In my dream, I saw him beside me. He was reproaching me for not marrying him and sarcastically mentioning the fact that, by refusing him, I had found myself sidetracked in life. I woke up and fell back asleep several times, but the same man always came into my dreams, and he always spoke the same words. 

During a sleepless interval, I felt his presence with such force that I cried: "Go away; leave me alone! I have nothing but kind feelings for you, but you persist in tormenting me, and you are proving that I would have been unhappy if I had married you. In the name of the Holy Trinity, I command you to leave me in peace!" After that prayer <note>original: "invocation"</note>, it seemed as if the evil influence faded, and I got back to sleep, though I only slept restlessly and fitfully. So, I felt a relief when the landlady's daughter brought me a cup of tea. 

Twice more during the same week, I had the same dream. It gave me such anguish that I said to Miss Wales: "This room seems haunted by that man, and I would like to know why. Is Peterhouse College <note>The oldest constituent college of the University of Cambridge</note> nearby? I ask you this because thirty years ago this man was educated at a college of that name." She answered "yes," and Miss Wales added that the college was close by.

The last time I dreamed of him I thought: "I cannot imagine why he should haunt this room to such an extent; could he have lived here?" To search for traces of this after twenty-eight years seemed impossible, but I asked Miss Hardwick how long her mother had kept those lodgings.

# CHAPTER IX

## A GENERAL SURVEY OF HAUNTED HOUSES

My primary goal has been to present to readers who are eager for the truth certain classic examples of haunted houses. We have already examined several detailed accounts of these strange occurrences. Such well-documented, comprehensive cases are quite rare. On the other hand, less detailed or partial accounts are very common. I have been collecting hundreds of these reports for a long time in preparation for this book. We will examine a few of them here, though space does not permit me to include them all.

Isocrates <note>Isocrates (436–338 BC) was an influential ancient Greek rhetorician and one of the ten Attic orators.</note> said to the Athenians in the fifth century BC: "Show such a respect for the truth on every occasion that your simple word carries more conviction than the oaths of others." Let us strive to think and act like Isocrates.

How can we avoid admitting that certain hauntings are objectively real, especially after reading the previous chapters and seeing that these observations have been confirmed with certainty? I am including this specific observation here because I believe it is particularly noteworthy. If I had known of it sooner, I would have published it in the third volume of my work, *Death and Its Mystery* <note>original: *La Mort et son Mystère*. This was a famous trilogy by Camille Flammarion exploring the survival of the soul after death.</note>, alongside similar cases. However, it fits perfectly here, as it demonstrates that hauntings and the physical appearance of invisible beings can begin at the very moment of death—a fact we already know from many consistent <note>original: "concordant"</note> reports.

Two thousand years ago, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an astronomer who promoted the geocentric model where the Earth remains stationary at the center of the universe.</note> said: "There is nothing more ridiculous, more stupid, or more laughable <note>original Greek: *πάνυ γελοιότατον* (pany geloiotaton)</note> than the idiotic hypothesis that the Earth moves." The following observation is as amazing as any that have come before it. Let us hear from the narrator.

One day, the jeweler’s wife told us in confidence that for some time she thought she had heard footsteps on the stairs, going up and down during the night.

We laughed and told her that her senses were playing tricks on her. But she insisted and pressed the matter, assuring us that she stayed awake for part of the night because of her small children; she was certain someone passed by on the stairs in the night; she was afraid of thieves; and her husband, when she mentioned it, had only laughed, just as we did. He carefully locked his door—a reinforced door—every evening and slept soundly afterward.

By repeating her story, the woman managed to catch my interest. My mother had trained me from a young age to overcome all fear. At various times during the night, I got up and searched the stairs from the cellar to the attic without finding anything at all. Due to the insistent pleas of the jeweler’s wife, I arranged glasses filled with water on the stairs on several occasions, but I found them untouched in the morning. Then I thought of another method. I took a ball of black thread and, in the dark of night, I stretched threads across the steps at irregular intervals. I found them all intact the next morning, ⁷ even while the woman insisted she had heard more footsteps on the stairs.

I became interested and even alarmed. I feared burglars, an attack on the jeweler, or something of that nature. I then obtained a hatchet, which I kept on my bed within arm's reach. I went to bed at ten o’clock as usual and sat reading until 2:00 a.m., ready to jump up at the slightest noise. But nothing happened.

The door to my room—the only entrance to our home—was made of solid oak at least two inches thick, typical of old houses from the 1600s <note>original: "seventeenth century"</note>. It was four feet wide and six-and-a-half feet high. Its frame was made of carved stone with sockets where the enormous door hinges pivoted. It was opened from the outside by a large, sturdy internal lock...

The key for this door weighed at least half a pound and turned a square bolt an inch and a quarter thick, with a latch of similar proportions. On the lock itself, above the keyhole, there was a type of spring-loaded hook that pressed against the stem of the bolt. In the evening, after turning the key in the lock, I would lift the hook, slide the bolt, and release the hook so that it rested against the key. This created a lock that was impossible to open from the outside. With such a sturdy door and lock, one could sleep in peace. It was not attractive, but it was solid and secure; under the circumstances, I paid very close attention to that lock. I want to emphasize this point.

One evening around 10:30 p.m., I had gone to bed after taking my usual precautions in case of an alarm. I remember reading Eugène Sue's *The Mysteries of Paris* <note>original: *Les Mystères de Paris*, a famous French adventure novel published in serial form in the 1840s</note> in an old magazine. I had just started a page beginning with the words, "The farm where Rodolphe took Fleur de Marie," when suddenly a terrifying shock burst the door open. It slammed against the wall with such force that I can still visualize it shaking on its hinges. My mother sat up with a start in her bed and cried out, "What is the matter?" Without answering her, I leaped from my bed with a hatchet in one hand and a candle in the other and rushed to the stairs. There, I found all my security threads <note>The narrator previously explained he stretched black threads across the stairs to detect intruders without their knowledge.</note> exactly where I had left them.

I hurried up the stairs, searched every corner, got the key from the attic <note>original: "garret," meaning a room directly under the roof</note>, opened the door, and went inside. There was nothing! I came back down, went into my room, and tried to shut the door. I then discovered that the lock and the bolt were still in the "closed" position. The door had been forced open despite being locked—and with incredible strength!

Only at that moment did I feel a sensation of true horror. My hair seemed to stand on end. The top of my head felt as if it were made of ice.

I closed the door and went back to bed, my whole body trembling, unable to take my eyes off the door.

My mother got up, and I told her what had happened. She sighed and said we would soon hear of a tragedy in the family. But nothing of the sort happened, either to us or the jeweler, and the event I have accurately reported *was not followed by any tragic coincidence*.

### AMONG HAUNTED HOUSES

[...sci]ence in its present state can provide an explanation. Yet, a dynamic consideration <note>original: "dynamical consideration"</note> demands our attention. Every physicist and mechanical expert knows the expression $mV^2$, and knows that the kinetic energy <note>original: "quantity of motion"; in classical physics, $mv^2$ was known as "vis viva" or living force, the precursor to our modern concept of kinetic energy</note> possessed by a moving body is calculated by multiplying its mass by the square of its speed. A double velocity is four times as powerful; a triple velocity, nine times; a fourfold velocity, sixteen times; and a fivefold velocity, twenty-five times as powerful. According to this formula, we might achieve any mechanical effect we desire simply by increasing the speed. It is not the bullet itself that kills, but its speed. If you throw a bullet at someone’s chest, the shock will hardly be felt through their clothing. I remember winning a bet in 1866, during a post-lunch shooting party, by firing through an oak plank with a cylindrical bullet made of Gruyère cheese, which I had used to load my gun. It was the conclusion <note>original: "epilogue"</note> to a discussion about Force and Matter (I recounted this story in my *Memoirs*, page 353).

A certain number of these noises and disturbances, like various strange effects <note>original: "freaks"</note> of lightning, could undoubtedly be explained by applying this formula. All modern scientific discoveries encourage us to believe that matter is electrical in nature, and that the cohesive forces between particles that give solid bodies their rigidity are electrical forces.

But let us not seek an explanation too eagerly, since no one knows what matter really consists of. A radioactive atom contains a formidable quantity of intra-atomic energy <note>now commonly known as nuclear energy</note>—enough to blow up an entire town.

Even when we cannot explain these phenomena, our scientific duty is to acknowledge them when they are accurately <note>OCR error: "not exactly"</note> observed. These more or less strange stories—scarcely credible, or rather, incredible—are not all inventions, frauds, illusions, or errors.

Here, as in all matters, it is best to examine things with an open mind, free from prejudice.

The conclusion to be drawn from all this is that there are unknown natural forces within and around us, and that despite its remarkable discoveries, science is only at the beginning of its journey. The invisible world is just as real as the visible world.

The phenomena of hauntings are extremely varied. They cannot all be explained in the same way, as they stem from different causes. Some are produced by the souls of deceased persons; others by invisible beings whose nature remains unknown to us; and others, still, by human organisms acting unconsciously. This last cause is frequent, and many have been led to regard it as the only cause, for the (insufficient) reason that a youth or a girl is almost always present when the phenomena occur—suggesting that the "Invisible" <note>The author uses this term to refer to the unseen realm or the forces acting from within it.</note> requires a living human form to manifest.

Every man who has personally investigated how much of these phenomena is true has come away from his study convinced. They have been forced to admit that the theories of hallucination and illusion were not enough to explain what they observed. This fact has been well known for some time, but people often pretend to ignore it. Who remembers, for instance, that as early as the 17th century, one of the most active Fellows <term>Fellows: formal members of a learned society, in this case, the elite Royal Society of London</term> of the Royal Society of London, Joseph Glanvill (1636–1680), discussed a collection of psychic facts in his book *Sadducism Defeated* <note>original: *Saducismus Triumphatus*; the title refers to the defeat of "Sadducism," a term used at the time for the skeptical denial of the existence of spirits or the supernatural</note>? These facts were similar to those we are studying here, but were observed in 1661. Therefore, the Royal Society preceded the Paris Academy of Sciences by two hundred years in giving these matters the attention they rightly deserved—

The most frequent phenomena are loud raps, scraping sounds <note>original: "frictions"</note>, footsteps, the movement of objects (even in locked rooms), and, more rarely, apparitions."

Another characteristic is their apparent absurdity and the lack of any known purpose in <term>motor phenomena</term> <note>Motor phenomena: Physical movements or actions performed by an unseen force, such as moving furniture or ringing bells.</note>, like bell-ringing, the putting out of lights, and the transportation of utensils, footwear, and headgear into the most unexpected places—or clothing being torn or sewn together. We must also note the great violence of the noises and the brutal throwing of objects without consideration for people or things. These displays are often vulgar, trivial, and sometimes carry evil intent, such as starting fires or causing destruction.

All this may seem trivial and mischievous. But if it results in proof of existence beyond the grave, we must confess that it is neither commonplace nor mischievous. Who, upon losing a beloved person and asking for any sign of survival, would not wish to see even the raising of a little finger?

The facts are real and incontestable. The belief in <term>haunted houses</term> <note>Haunted houses: Buildings where persistent supernatural phenomena, such as noises or sightings, are reported to occur.</note> is so ancient that in every language there are words to describe it: *spuken* <note>German: to haunt or ghost</note> in German, *haunting* in English, *spiritate* or *infestate* <note>Italian: to be possessed by spirits or infested</note> in Italian, and *hanter* <note>French: to haunt</note> in French, without counting numerous local terms. We have also seen that their reality is confirmed by numerous legal decisions.

"Haunted Houses!" The words alone, mentioned at random in a conversation, are capable of calling forth the most foolish mockery and the most unreasonable anecdotes. On the one hand, a whole category...
