Noises without an explanation—such as the wood-splitting sounds at Fougères—shocks that make the walls tremble, plaster falling from the walls, blows that respond in numbered sequences to questions, curtains waving, and the sound of furniture falling: none of these correspond to any physical reality. They are both subjective and objective phenomena, and it is difficult to categorize them theoretically. There is no doubt that hidden <note>original: "occult"</note> forces are at work, but what are they?

In haunted houses and during some fantastic manifestations, massive <note>original: "formidable"</note> noises are often heard. These include sledgehammer blows strong enough to knock down partitions, the rattling of doors and windows, and the sound of pottery or glass being thrown to the floor and shattered. Yet, when the results of all this commotion are examined, we generally find nothing broken, nothing demolished, and nothing moved from its place. However, the idea that these are merely illusions or hallucinations is ruled out because so many different people observe them at once.

In 1907, there was a "Universal Society of Psychic Studies" <note>original: "Société Universelle d'Études Psychiques"</note> in Paris, which was invited to conduct several investigations on the subject of our study. Let us look at the story of a haunted house on the outskirts of Beuvry, a large village of 7,000 inhabitants located five miles from Béthune, in the middle of the "Black Country" <note>original: a reference to the coal-mining region of northern France</note>: 14

After the regional newspapers of the Nord <note>a department in northern France</note> published an article concerning a haunted house in Douai,¹⁵ we traveled to the town on Sunday, January 13, to conduct an investigation. It had been vacant for some time, but for several months it had been occupied by the D. family, which consisted of the father (a postman), the mother, five children, and a young domestic worker <note>original: "servant"</note> of sixteen or seventeen years old.

These are the events that brought attention to that house. For about two weeks <note>original: "fortnight"</note>, Mrs. D. heard the front doorbell ring several times a day, but found nobody waiting to enter. At first, she thought it was a practical joke, but the bell-ringing soon increased in frequency and intensity, causing a disturbance in the house. In full view of the frightened family, the bell rang violently while the cord and the bell-pull moved along with it. The entire neighborhood <note>original: "quarter"</note> gathered, and over three hundred people witnessed the phenomenon.

The police were called in, but they could not find the cause. In fact, after three days, right in front of a policeman, the bell fell off the wall during one last ring and shattered on the ground.

This was the account from the newspapers. In Douai, we first visited the central police station. The facts were confirmed <note>original: "corroborated"</note>, but the public felt unable to determine a cause.

We went to 19 Rue des Écoles, but upon our arrival, we were met with a strict order <note>original: "formal injunction"</note> by Mr. D. to say nothing and to see no one. Although we were persistent, we could obtain no information. During our short interview with Mrs. D., we caught a glimpse of the famous bell. It is a simple bell with a cord hanging down in front of the door. (The broken bell had since been replaced.)

Therefore, it only remained for us to question the neighbors. We spoke to several people who were witnesses by sight or sound. All agreed on the reality and the loudness of the phenomenon. The bell did not merely tinkle, but rang for long periods. The cord was shaken as if by a hand.

A carpenter, Mr. Fournie, was trying on a cap when a long nail pinned it to his hand. The only thing to do was call the police.

Mr. Michelet, the local Police Commissioner <note>original: "Commissary"</note>, came to investigate. He believed he had discovered the source of the mysterious nail. His report simply accused the young woman herself, and he even persuaded her to confess.

This is a classic example of the mistakes often made when studying these subjects. It is not uncommon for a medium to secretly add fraudulent actions—whether clever or not—to their genuine abilities. These additions do not negate the reality of those actual abilities. I have personally verified this in the cases of Eusapia Palladino <note>original: "Eusapia"; a famous Italian medium known for physical manifestations</note>, Miss Huet, and others, as explained in my book *Unknown Natural Forces* <note>original: "Les Forces Naturelles Inconnues"</note>.

Naturally, this last part of her statement was not accepted. For the sake of everyone's peace of mind, the servant was considered the sole conscious and responsible culprit <note>original: "author"</note> for the damage.

A haunted farm in Brittany, located at Pleiber-Christ (Finistère) in the district <note>original: "canton"</note> of Saint-Thégonnec and the region <note>original: "arrondissement"</note> of Morlaix, attracted significant attention in 1909. We can read an interesting article about it from the March 1, 1909, issue of *The Morning* (*Le Matin*), which was later reprinted in the *Annals of Psychic Sciences* (*Annales des Sciences Psychiques*). This Breton haunted house is a classic example of its kind, where a mentally disturbed woman <note>original: "mad woman"</note> living in the house layered her own imaginary visions onto the genuine psychic phenomena we are investigating.

This episode occurred in 1909. Four years later, in 1913, similar events took place in the same department, region, and district, but on a different farm located in the community of Plouniour-Menez. These events caused a great sensation among the local people. The April 10, 1913, issue of *The Mysterious Life* (*La Vie Mystérieuse*) published a long report signed by Mr. Jean Mettois, who spent a day and a night at the farm. I have included an extract from his report below:

> As we entered the farmyard, the chickens were pecking away busily, seemingly indifferent to the tragedy of their surroundings, and the horses greeted us with neighing. Everything seemed calm and peaceful. The car horn sounded several times and the engine rumbled, but nothing moved. It felt as though we were not at the "Devil’s Farm," but rather in the castle of "Sleeping Beauty." Our noise did not seem to disturb man or beast.
>
> We knocked at the door of the main farmhouse but received no answer. We entered the traditional main room found in every Breton farm, with its large fireplace and pot-hook <note>original: "pot-rack"</note>, its box beds <note>original: "closed beds"; traditional Breton furniture where beds were built into wooden cabinets for warmth and privacy</note>, and its immense table, which took up nearly the entire space. Seated at this table was a woman of about fifty, her head resting in her hands. Our entrance seemed to awaken her from a trance-like state <note>original: "dream"</note>, and she said "Good day" in the Breton language. We were in the presence of the farmer’s wife.
> 
> My friend, who fortunately speaks Breton like a true Celt, explained the reason for our visit to the good woman.

On the fourth day, in the morning, he approached my father with his bag in his hand and his bundle on his shoulder.

"Master," he said, "I am leaving. If I remained here another day, I would go mad. If there were someone to fight, I would stay—but there is nothing, nobody. I am leaving at once, master."

After having finished a bottle of white wine as a farewell, they shook hands and parted. Angevin was sad and unsettled, and my father was somber and quiet.

"It is the first time I have run away from a job <note>original: "shirked." Meaning to avoid work or duty, in this case due to fear.</note>, master."

Those were Angevin’s last words. My father followed him with his eyes on the road leading from Mosnes to Amboise until he disappeared from view in the long avenue of poplars which line the road.

But the commotion went from bad to worse in the house. The invisible authors of the strange noises grew...

These occurrences happened for the most part when the master of the house was in Paris. He, therefore, could not have had anything to do with them.

In the evening, the two maids left the house, and the events happened exactly as if they were still present. It is enough to say that they are not to be considered suspects in this affair either.

Finally, the children were sent away, *successively* and *separately*, and the phenomena continued.

Then the sick lady herself was taken to another house, and the phenomena followed her there. The bed was pushed about and almost turned upside down. More than fifty credible <note>original: "creditable"</note> witnesses are certain of the facts and have testified in the courts of law.

What kind of phenomena are we dealing with?

Is it some mean-spirited practical joke, as is so often the case? Is it a servant <note>original: "domestic"</note> trying to make fun of a whole village by imitating ghost stories?

I do not think so, and here are my reasons:

Phenomena caused by fraud are generally produced at night, and always in the same place. Furthermore, they stop when the trickster is removed. In this case, they happened in the daytime as well as at night and continued even when every member of the family was absent.

It is therefore necessary to assume the conspiracy of several people. However, that only accounts for some of the clumsy physical phenomena, but not for the voice and its instantaneous changes of direction.

Further, a mirror was broken in such a way that it was impossible to reproduce artificially. In fact, this mirror showed a very clean circular hole with a bulge <note>original: "convexity"</note> *between the wood and the hole*, which indicated that the hole was made from the inside out, as in the case of an electric discharge.

Simple <note>original: "Artless"</note> people who claim to explain everything have not failed to say: "There was a ventriloquist hidden somewhere." Now, one only needs to have studied ventriloquism to dismiss this idea. It is impossible to produce effects of this kind from the bottom of the cellar to the first floor, and if anyone in the house was a master of this...

The phenomena are only produced when Mademoiselle <note>original: "Mlle."</note> Alice Cocat, Madame Massot’s niece, is present. For five years, she has been engaged to a nephew of Madame Massot, aged twenty-five, who is a working electrician and has served in the second regiment of artillery at Grenoble. # CHAPTER X

## CLASSIFICATION OF PHENOMENA: HAUNTINGS ASSOCIATED WITH THE DEAD

The general survey <note>original: "excursion"</note> we have just conducted of haunted houses has presented a wide variety of examples, which would be both interesting and educational to categorize. We will now attempt to do this. By doing so, we may succeed in identifying the causes and move closer to the long-sought explanation for these events.

In this classification, we must consider the production of physical forces that are not connected to the question of survival after death <note>The "problem of survival" refers to the scientific and spiritual debate over whether human consciousness continues after physical death.</note>. Other cases, however, are undoubtedly linked to survival, as we saw in the previous chapter—specifically in the first case described. This connection has been clear in several instances, and we are better prepared to accept it now that we have established solid experimental evidence of survival. We will begin this classification with hauntings associated with deceased persons, leaving other types for the next chapter.

We should not close our minds to either possibility. Some phenomena are clearly tied to the intentions of the deceased, while others are entirely independent of them.

The exclusively <term>anthropological theory</term> <note>In this context, the "anthropological theory" refers to the belief that all hauntings are products of the living human mind—such as hallucinations or subconscious physical effects—rather than external spirits.</note> has been disproven in this work through direct observation (see especially pages 66, 150–177, 183, 202, 210, 217, 231, and 247–261). These observations clearly demonstrate that this theory is insufficient. We must, therefore, distinguish between manifestations caused by the dying and those caused by the dead—both of which occur outside of our own minds.

He argues that evidence supports the survival of consciousness after death as a factor in certain hauntings.</summary>

Let us remember, above all, that throughout history and across all nations, these unexpected events have been attributed to the deceased. Was this merely a delusion born of ignorance or fear? All evidence suggests the opposite.

It would be unnecessary to repeat what was stated in the previous chapter. Every example mentioned could be matched by several similar cases. With a frequency too high to be a matter of luck <note>original: "fortuitous"</note>, deaths occurring elsewhere are instantly signaled by physical events. Broken mirrors are common in these reports and have even inspired a long tradition of folklore. This cannot be dismissed as self-suggestion or hallucination. Regarding this, I received a recent letter (April 30, 1922):

> I am a typesetter for a printing house. I was working at 20 Rue Turgot. A seventeen-year-old girl named Ida Schaub was working across from me. One day at noon, as she was preparing to leave work, she was powdering her face while holding a small mirror at eye level. Since I was on friendly terms with her, as I am with everyone in the shop, I was teasing her about her powder and her vanity <note>original: "coquetry"</note>. I was watching her when the mirror suddenly shattered into a thousand pieces in her hand, even though she hadn't moved. “Oh, my mother!” she exclaimed.
> 
> After walking thirty minutes to her home on Rue Trézel, she found her mother dead on the doorstep. She had died of a stroke <term>apoplexy</term> <note>Apoplexy was a historical term for a sudden loss of consciousness, typically what we now call a stroke.</note> and her body was still warm.
> 
> (Signed) AUGUSTE PAUTRÉ.
> 31 RUE MAZARINE.

Here we have a physical, objective fact where no hallucination is possible. Even if the effect was somehow produced by the girl’s own body <note>The author implies a physical force—today often called "telekinesis"—released by the girl's subconscious distress.</note>, the timing with her mother’s sudden death cannot be ignored. Was it just chance again? If so, "Lady Luck" <note>The original phrase "The little god must indeed have a broad back!" is a variation of a French idiom meaning that "chance" is forced to carry the blame for far too many things that are not actually random.</note> must have a very broad back to carry the weight of so many coincidences!

About a year and a half ago, my father, my sister, and a cousin who was staying with us were talking in the dining room. The three of us were the only people in the house when we suddenly heard the piano playing in the drawing-room <note>original: "salon"</note>. Greatly surprised, my sister took the lamp and went into the drawing-room; she clearly saw several keys pressing down together, sounding the notes, and rising up again.

She came back and told us what she had seen. At first, we laughed at her claim and suspected a mouse was behind the matter <note>original: "affaire"</note>, but since the lady has excellent eyesight and is not in the least bit superstitious, we thought it was strange.

However, a week later, a letter arrived from New York announcing the death of an old uncle who lived in that city. But, what was even more extraordinary, three days after the letter arrived, the piano started playing again.

Just as in the first instance, news of a death came a week later: the death of my aunt.

My uncle and aunt were a perfectly devoted couple. They were also greatly attached to their relatives and the Jura region <note>A mountain range on the French-Swiss border</note> where they were born.

The piano has not played since then.

The witnesses of this event will testify to it at any time you wish. We live in the countryside near Neuchâtel <note>A city in Switzerland</note>, and I assure you that we are not overly sensitive or "high-strung" people.

These are direct and unexpected observations. I can understand lies and illusions, but my inquiries have always proved the truthfulness <note>original: "veracity"</note> of the narrators.2

We look to electrical transmission for an explanation. What is electricity? We do not know. What is the magnetic force <note>original: "magnetic element"</note> that travels 93 million miles from the sun to move a compass needle? We are equally ignorant. What is the transmission of telegraphy or telephony through the air, over mountains, and over seas—signals that can be caught as they pass through a closed house? This is also a mystery.

Therefore, we should be humble before we resort to stubborn <note>original: "blind and deaf"</note> denials. Subjective experiences can take on objective forms. In my book *The Unknown* <note>original: "L'Inconnu," published by Flammarion in 1900</note>, one can read in the chapter on "Phantasms of the Dying" a letter from a resident of Valabre (in the Vaucluse region of France), who wrote (Letter 714):

> I must have been twelve years old. My poor father, one of the heroes of the Battle of Sidi-Ibrahim <note>A famous 1845 battle between French forces and Algerian resistance</note>, had spent the night and part of the day at the bedside of his mother, who was seriously ill. He had left her, and about 4:00 p.m., one of my uncles went to find him to tell him that his mother was worse and had expressed a wish to see her two young grandsons. My father wanted to bring us along. My younger brother obeyed, but I resisted so wildly that nothing could shake my resolve—all because I was terrified of the dead.
> 
> I therefore remained alone in the house with my mother, who, after supper, wanted to put me to bed. But I refused—

---

The account of the premonition associated with Lord Dufferin <note>Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood (1826–1902), a prominent British diplomat and Viceroy of India</note>, though widely reported, is still awaiting final verification. I am aware of three different versions of the story: 
1. The version I published myself (Volume II, page 231). 
2. The version found in *Liliana* by Sienkiewicz <note>Henryk Sienkiewicz, the Nobel Prize-winning Polish author of "Quo Vadis," who died in 1917</note> (Madrid, 1921, page 154). 
3. The version published by Stainton Moses <note>A famous English cleric and spiritualist</note> in the journal *Light* (1892, page 181, and 1907, page 64), which was also reproduced in Bozzano’s *Premonitory Phenomena* <note>original: "Phénomènes prémonitoires"</note> (Paris, 1914, page 397). 

It sometimes happens that the same story is told in several different ways, which is why I much prefer first-hand accounts written by the witnesses themselves. However, we must not allow ourselves to be swayed by the dishonest <note>original: "mendacious"</note> denials of people with a biased interest in the matter.

I went to bed without even closing the window, for it was a warm night in August, and I slept very soundly.

Suddenly, I was awakened by a hellish <note>original: "infernal"</note> uproar—a frightening noise of saucepans being thrown about, dishes breaking, and plates shattering into pieces, which I heard clattering on the concrete floor of the kitchen. You would have thought a whole troop of cats was overturning everything in the house. This last thought reassured me. However, the noise lasted for more than an hour, with some interruptions. When it was quiet again, I heard something rushing toward me from the bottom of the staircase; I saw a creature, which I took to be a cat, leap onto my bed in one bound and out the window with another, where it then vanished.

I went immediately to close the window. Imagine my astonishment to find that it was already closed on the outside by wire mesh with a third-of-an-inch screen <note>original: "wire-netting of one-third of an inch mesh"</note>. My surprise grew even greater when, after daybreak, I saw everything in order in the kitchen—not a single scrap of broken pottery!

Three days later, my mother slept in the same room and witnessed the same phenomena.

Was it a hallucination? We can find no reason to suspect one in this sixteen-year-old young man, who observed these events with such composure. This is all very complex. Yes, our first instinct is to see nothing but a hallucination in it. But the slap received by Mr. Michel was no hallucination; and if Mr. Estève’s cat was merely an illusion, and the noise of unbroken pottery in the kitchen the same, how is it that the mother received the same impression? What is the cause of this sensation?

In these latter cases, we may see personal <note>original: "subjective"</note> impressions that are nevertheless produced by external causes—the former by the dying and angry grandmother, and the latter by the spirits <note>original: "shades"</note> of the dead relative.

DEAR MASTER, <note>original: "Cher Maître," a traditional respectful address for a prominent intellectual or teacher, in this case, Camille Flammarion.</note>

After seeing your psychic trilogy <note>This likely refers to Flammarion's influential series of books on the soul and the afterlife, such as *The Unknown* and *Death and Its Mystery*.</note>, I must make my modest contribution to your research on the Unseen. The following event was witnessed by my wife and her aunt, who attest to it below.

A few days after the death of my wife's maternal grandfather, François Coudreau, on September 30, 1899, noises were heard in the house where he died. My wife, then quite a young girl, had gone to bed with her grandmother. Her aunt, now the widowed Mme. Roy, had gone to bed in the same room.

It was 10:00 p.m. They all heard something like pebbles being thrown at the windowpanes. Since there was no storm or wind, they thought it was some practical joke. The grandmother called out, "Who's there?" but there was no reply.

The noise continued intermittently for about ten minutes. They also heard a sound like a shovel stirring the heap of coal in the yard, which sounded as if the coal were being thrown against the wall.

I must tell you that the deceased had been in the habit, during his lifetime, of shoveling this heap.

Also, the latch of the door seemed to move noisily, as if somebody wanted to enter.

Greatly frightened, the three women started praying, as they believed the soul of the deceased was there. Finally, my wife's aunt called in a loud voice: "If that is you, father, speak to us!" The noise stopped immediately.

The next morning, they found everything in its place outside the house. There was no trace of impact on the windows or on the walls. The shovel was lying on the heap of coal as usual. Masses were said for the deceased, and the noises did not return.

A detail which may be important is this: On the day the event occurred, the grandmother had found a beautiful braid <note>original: "plait"</note> of hair in a trunk which the deceased had always forbidden her to open. It belonged to his first wife, whom he had loved dearly. The grandmother had burned the braid.

The witnesses maintain that it cannot have been a practical joke, since the windows would have been broken by the violence of the blows (the windows had no shutters).

She had left him to convert to a new faith, and in his fury, he had decided to kill her. He shot at her—but killed another person instead. Sainlouis, condemned to death, had been executed on the same date and at the same hour that the strange noises occurred in the house where his former partner <note>original: "concubine"</note> lived. I forgot to mention that the room in question was found locked, with all the furniture in its proper place.

Among the phenomena of haunted houses, some are objective—meaning they are material and external to the witnesses <note>original: "percipients"</note>. Others are subjective—perceived by the spirit, yet just as real as the former. These are produced by a more or less distant telepathic cause, generally an unknown death. It is necessary to pay special attention to these singular noises, for which there is no easy explanation, and which people are often inclined to dismiss.

Here are precise observations that remain, however, incomprehensible. How can these noises be produced? A paving stone rolling on the floor! These telepathic transmissions are beyond dispute. Noises are heard that vary depending on the receptivity of the witness <note>original: "percipient," a term used in psychical research for the person receiving a telepathic message</note>. These are subjective and non-physical noises. There is a projection between the cause and the effect—between the dying person and the receiver—and we are led to believe that in these cases, we are not dealing with spherical waves that spread out and grow larger, like those of sound or light. It was probably not a wave of this kind that traveled from Marseille in every direction, only to be picked up in Paris by the brother of the dying man. Rather, we suspect a psychic current, like the magnetic current produced between a bar of iron and a magnetic needle.

Such a psychic current reminds us of the link established between Captain Escourrou, who was killed in Mexico on March 29, 1863, and his mother, who was living at Sèvres, near Paris. On that day, she saw one of the eyes in his portrait destroyed and blood flowing over his face. When I published this remarkable telepathic occurrence in volume 2, page 375, I did not include the numerous testimonies <note>original: "attestations"</note> and official documents that prove its authenticity due to a lack of space. However, those interested may consult the *Annals of Psychical Sciences* <note>original: "Annales des Sciences Psychiques"</note> for 1891 (pages 148 to 156), where they will find that no doubt is possible. Here, as in Mr. <note>original: "M."</note> Riondel's observation, we clearly have subjective phenomena. The portrait did not actually have an eye destroyed, nor did blood flow over it. But at the moment of death...

Astronomy, that universal science, offers us examples which can often be applied to other studies. Here is one which I pointed out long ago. Certain spiral nebulae <note>original: "nebulæ"</note>, photographed with the help of powerful instruments, show stars symmetrically distributed along their gaseous twists, and thus indicate the secret of the formation of these bodies. The coincidences are so numerous and so consistent <note>original: "concordant"</note> that they cannot be attributed to chance, and we are led to recognize a causal connection. It is the same with these coincidences of deaths occurring alongside manifestations and apparitions. Chance plays no part here.

But let us confess that an explanation is difficult. The human soul has not yet been dissected.

Plato wrote in *Phaedrus*:
> "Do you think that the nature of the soul can be sufficiently known if we do not know the nature of the universe?"⁶ <note>original Greek: "ψύχης οὖν φύσιν ἀξίως λόγου κατανοήσαι οἴει δύνατον εἶναι ἄνευ τὴς τοῦ ὅλου φύσεως;"</note>

This maxim could be applied to all reasoning about life. The judgments passed on human beings by their equals are almost always false, because we do not know the direct or indirect springs of action. The studies we are making here have far-reaching significance.

The psychical and physical faculties of the human soul during life and after death are almost all yet to be discovered, and the observation of the phenomena of haunting sheds an unexpected light on this subject.

The story is long, and I shall only give the essential passages according to Bozzano.⁷

The scene is laid at the village of Swanland, near Hull, in England, in a carpenter’s shop, where Mr. Bristow served as an apprentice. He relates the following:

> On the morning when the phenomena took place, I was working at the bench next the wall, where I could see the movements of my two companions and watch the door. Suddenly one of them turned round and called out: “You had better keep those blocks of wood and stay focused on your work, mates.” We asked him to explain, and he said: “You know quite well what I mean; one of you hit me with this piece of wood,” and he showed us a piece of wood about an inch square. We both protested that we had not thrown it; and I, for one, was quite certain that my other companion had never stopped working. The incident was being forgotten when, some minutes later, the other companion turned round like the first, and shouted to me: “It is you, this time, who threw this piece of wood at me!” and he showed me a piece the size of a matchbox. There were two of them accusing me now, and my denials meant nothing, so I laughed and added: “Since I did not do it, I suppose that if someone was aiming at you, it is now my turn.” I had hardly said this when a piece hit me on the hip. I called out: “I am hit! There is a mystery somewhere; let us see what happens!”

We searched inside and out, but could discover nothing. This strange and unsettling incident <note>original: "embarrassing occurrence"</note> gave us much to discuss, but in the end, we set to work again.

I had barely begun when some Venetian blinds, which were held up by beams built into the wall, began shaking with such a clatter that it seemed they would be broken into pieces. We thought at once, "Somebody is up there." I grabbed a ladder, rushed up, and craned my neck to look, but I found that the blinds were immovable and covered with a thick layer of dust and cobwebs. As I climbed down and my head reached the level of the beams, I saw a small piece of wood—about two fingers thick—hop forward on a plank and, with a final jump of two feet, fly past my ear. Dumbfounded, I jumped down to the floor and said, "This is no laughing matter. There is something supernatural going on. What do you think?" One of my companions agreed with me, but the other still insisted that someone was playing a prank on us. During this brief argument, a piece of wood from the far end of the workshop near the entrance flew out and hit him on his hat. I shall never forget the sheepish look on his face.

Every now and then, a piece of wood that had just been cut and fallen to the floor would jump up onto the workbenches and begin to "dance" among the tools. It is remarkable that despite countless attempts, we could never catch a piece while it was moving; it cleverly avoided all our traps <note>original: "stratagems"</note>. They seemed alive and intelligent.

I remember one piece that jumped from the bench onto an easel standing nine feet <note>original: "three yards"</note> away; from there, it bounced onto another piece of furniture, and finally into a corner of the shop where it stopped. Another piece shot across the shop like an arrow, about three feet off the ground.

Immediately after that, a piece took flight with an undulating, wavy motion. Another moved in a diagonal line and landed quickly at my feet. While the foreman <note>original: "chief of the works"</note>, Mr. Clark, was explaining the details of a technical drawing, we were both holding our fingers on it so that there was less than an inch between them. Suddenly, a pointed piece of wood passed right between our two fingers and struck the table.

This state of affairs continued with varying intensity for six weeks, and it always happened in broad daylight.

Sometimes there was relative quiet for a day or two, during which only one or two manifestations <term>supernatural occurrences or appearances</term> took place; however, these were followed by days of extraordinary activity, as if the forces involved wanted to make up for lost time. Most of them were no larger than an ordinary box of matches, though they came in various shapes. The last flying piece I saw was made of oak, about 2½ inches square and 1 inch thick. It fell toward me from the far corner of the ceiling and followed a spiral path—like a corkscrew staircase—about 20 inches in diameter as it descended. It is necessary to add that all these objects, without exception, originated from the interior of the shop; not a single one came in through the door.

One of the strangest features of these events was that the pieces of wood we had cut, which had fallen to the ground, worked their way into the corners of the shop. From there, they lifted themselves to the ceiling in some mysterious and invisible manner. None of the workmen and none of the visitors—who crowded there in great numbers during the six weeks these manifestations lasted—ever saw a single piece in the act of rising. And yet, despite our watchfulness, the pieces of wood quickly found their way up so they could fall on us from a place where nothing had been just a moment before. Gradually, we grew used to it. The movements of the pieces of wood, which seemed to be alive and in some cases even intelligent, no longer surprised us and hardly even attracted our attention.

We worked in private houses, and the three of us who were present on the first day of the manifestations worked repeatedly and alternately outside during the period that they took place; more than once, we were all absent. Another example, backed by authentic testimony and dating from 1882 to 1889, is one recorded with confirmations by the London Society for Psychical Research <note>London S. P. R.</note>, and published in Frederic Myers’s great work, *Human Personality and Its Survival of Bodily Death* <note>original: "Human Personality"</note>, published in 1904. Here is a summary of it:

Captain Morton’s <note>A pseudonym for Captain Despard; this case is famous in paranormal research as the "Cheltenham Ghost."</note> family came to live in a house in 1882 that had been built in 1860. It was first occupied for sixteen years by an Anglo-Indian <note>A British person who had lived long-term in India.</note>, then by an old man, and was then unoccupied. One evening the Captain’s daughter, Miss Morton, heard a noise near her door, and believing it was her mother, she opened it. She did not see her, but on looking into the hallway she saw a tall woman dressed in black near the staircase. The unknown woman was afterwards seen by the whole family—Miss Morton’s three sisters, her father, a little boy, and the servant—and was even noticed by the dogs, who whimpered. 

Upon investigation, it was found that the ghost <note>original: "phantom"</note> was that of the Anglo-Indian’s second wife, who had a problem with alcohol <note>original: "who drank"</note> and often quarreled with him; they then separated, she went to live elsewhere, and died in 1878. Between 1882 and 1884, Miss Morton saw the ghost six times. One of her sisters saw it during the summer of 1882 and thought it was a nun. In the autumn of 1883, the servant encountered it. In December of the same year, Miss Morton’s father and a little boy noticed it in the dining room. On January 29, 1884, Miss Morton spoke to the ghost for the first time; but it did not reply, and seemed to be deaf. She often tried to touch it, but it always moved away. In the night its footsteps were heard, sounding very light. In fact, it appeared to inhabit the house without wanting anything, and finally they grew accustomed to it. Some twenty people saw it. Efforts were made to photograph it, but they were unsuccessful. Loud noises were heard from time to time. But let us tell the story.

That is Gurney’s <note>Edmund Gurney (1847–1888) was a psychologist and a founding member of the Society for Psychical Research.</note> story. This multiple observation, first made by children, discourages—if it does not entirely disprove—the theory of hallucination. I am well-acquainted with this theory in all its forms, for I always keep the classic work of Brière de Boismont <note>Alexandre Brière de Boismont (1797–1881) wrote an influential 19th-century study on hallucinations.</note> on my desk. Who was this strange person? Everything leads us to believe that it was a deceased lady who had once lived in the house. Let us seek another explanation that actually fits the facts!

We can apply to this apparition what we said earlier about the Morton family: “Its reality is as certain as the existence of the Obelisk on the Place de la Concorde <note>The Luxor Obelisk, a famous ancient Egyptian monument standing in a major public square in Paris.</note>.”

Let us admit without reservation that we are in the realm of complete mystery here, as we were in the case of the haunted castle of Calvados <note>A famous haunting in Normandy, France, often associated with the Cideville parsonage or the Castle of T----.</note> and all our other examples. Let us admit that we know nothing, and that we are allowed to be curious and want to learn the truth. This pursuit is worth more than all the fanciful novels published every day, which are generally based on this same fascinating subject.

Nothing should be stated as fact except what has been surely observed. However, it is neither reasonable nor honest to refuse to recognize a verified reality under any pretext whatsoever.

In 1919, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle <note>The creator of Sherlock Holmes, who became a prominent advocate for Spiritualism later in life.</note> published a remarkable book called *The New Revelation*, in which he explains that, as a member of the Psychical Research Society, he was sent with two other delegates to spend a night in a haunted house. There we have another personal observation. Inexplicable noises and blows were heard, recalling the story of John Wesley’s <note>The founder of Methodism, whose family home was famously disturbed by a spirit nicknamed "Old Jeffrey."</note> family at Epworth in 1726, and of the Fox family at Hydesville in 1848 <note>The Fox sisters’ reported communications with a spirit via "rappings" in New York are widely considered the birth of the modern Spiritualist movement.</note>, which served as the foundation of modern Spiritualism.

Not all the entities, forces, invisible causes, or spirits that reveal themselves in any way in the numerous phenomena we are studying are necessarily the souls of the dead. Besides the fact that the souls of the living can externalize themselves <note>The idea that a living person's spirit or energy can manifest outside their physical body, sometimes called "astral projection" or "bilocation."</note>, and that we can ourselves sometimes act unconsciously, we are surrounded by psychic elements, both known and unknown. Does the very curious observation that follows indicate an action of the living—the realization of a wish or a firm decision—or does it indicate the action of the dead person involved? Appearances favor this last interpretation. Let us weigh everything with absolute freedom and without prejudice.

What is the part played by our human organism in metapsychic <term>metapsychic: A term used in early 20th-century research to describe phenomena that seem to lie beyond the known laws of physics, such as telepathy, clairvoyance, or hauntings.</term> phenomena?

That night there was a bitter frost. I had taken a long walk through almost deserted parts of Antwerp, and all the way I had weighed the pros and cons of the position offered. All three of us were seated by a table moved against the wall. Our faces were toward the fire. A shelf was fixed to the wall beside the fireplace. Kitchen utensils were on the shelf, and two inches below was a lath <term>lath: A thin, narrow strip of wood used here as a rail for hooks.</term> holding some hooks, from one of which a towel hung by a loop of cord.

Nobody was walking about the room. There was not, and there could not be, even a trace of a draft <note>original: "draught"</note>.

We discussed the question that occupied me so intensely. My sisters did not wish to influence me. I was perplexed. What was I to do? The future depended on my decision.

"If only," said one of my sisters, "we could consult somebody."

"Or if father were still alive," I added, "he would give me good advice."

At the mention of our father, who was the embodiment of goodness and honesty, everyone became pensive and silent.

After some time I said again: "Should I accept?"

Suddenly the towel began to swing on its screw as if on a pivot. It moved to the right and left, all in one piece—not as if moved by a draft, but without a single fold stirring. It moved as if it were rigid and someone had, by lightly rubbing the loop with their fingers, given it a swinging <note>original: "pendulous"</note> motion to the right and left.

The towel said "No." Nothing more.

# CHAPTER XI

## HAUNTING PHENOMENA NOT ATTRIBUTABLE TO THE DEAD. RAPPING SPIRITS. POLTERGEISTS <note>The term "poltergeist" comes from the German words "poltern" (to make a noise) and "Geist" (spirit or ghost).</note>

In the previous chapter, we gathered several cases showing a connection between these phenomena and the deceased—cases where a specific goal suggested intentions, unfulfilled promises, or actions from beyond the grave. We had already noted some of these during our general survey of the topic. At the same time, we also found unique phenomena that lacked any clear sign of origin or purpose. We are left with the impression that these mysterious events are extremely diverse and likely have many different explanations, placing us on the frontier of an entirely new world to explore. In this chapter, we will only deal with phenomena that do not appear to be connected to the dead. Unlike the previous chapter, I do not say "without *association* with the dead," because we know nothing for certain and the entire supernatural <note>original: "extra-terrestrial." In this era, the word often referred to anything outside of the earthly realm, including the spiritual or celestial, rather than modern "aliens."</note> world is still being studied. We must be extremely careful; instead, I say these cases lack "any *indication* of a connection."

In our initial overview of the subject—such as the stones thrown in the Rue des Noyers <note>A famous 1849 case in Paris where stones were mysteriously thrown at a house for days without a visible culprit.</note> in Paris and several other cases—we already noted the absence of any signs of a spiritual or psychological cause <note>original: "psychic order."</note>. We also saw no such signs in the chaotic sequence <note>original: "phantasmagoria"</note> of events in Calvados <note>A department in Normandy, France, famous for the "Cideville hauntings" (1850–1851) involving a priest and accusations of witchcraft.</note>, nor in the parsonage <note>original: "vicarage"</note> where the strange noises occurred. Even though some have suggested that these events stem from the unexpected intentions of the deceased, it appears that something else is at work.

...compare some of these cases. The following case, surely a very extraordinary one, was sent to me from Cherchell (Algeria) on July 17, 1922:

In 1913, when we lived in Tonkin <note>A historical name for northern Vietnam.</note>, my wife and I went to rest for a few weeks in the town of Mong-Zen (Yunnan) <note>A province in Southwest China bordering Vietnam.</note>. We lived in an isolated bungalow in a sort of camp constituting the French concession <note>A territory within a foreign city that was governed and occupied by the French during the colonial period.</note>, the nearest house being twenty yards away. We were accompanied by our "boy" <note>A colonial-era term for a male domestic servant; it is used here in its historical context.</note>, a young Annamite <note>A historical term for a person from central or northern Vietnam.</note> of about sixteen.

A day or two after our arrival, we were startled by a massive noise, which seemed to be outside and vibrating through the roof. I thought it was a thunderclap. Looking at the sky, I found it clear, without a breeze or a cloud. However, we had found during our stay in Cambodia that thunderclaps without wind and without noticeable clouds often disturbed the atmosphere. This observation led me to inquire of my neighbors the next morning, but they had heard neither noise nor thunder.

Some days after that, there was another noise in the night. It was impossible to sleep. We passed the night waiting for the day, and I had ample opportunity to study the character of the sound. I attributed it to a rock that had broken loose from the neighboring mountain and rolled down, or to a slight earth tremor (which are so frequent in that region). Yet this explanation did not entirely satisfy me because the noise, though very loud, was, so to speak, muffled and unique. For my theory to be correct, it would have to be a rock falling perfectly flat on level ground, which is absurd. Again, nobody else in the concession had heard anything, and no seismic shock <note>An earthquake or tremor.</note> had been registered.

These two manifestations <note>Visible or audible signs of a supernatural presence.</note> might have been forgotten if a third one of the same kind had not occurred. Again, at the same hour of the night, under the same meteorological conditions of perfect calm, a noise—terrifying this time—resounded on the roof. In a second we were up, and our servant (God knows the Annamites are sound sleepers!), who slept in the next room with the door open, stood up also, stupefied.

I thought there would not be a tile left on the roof.

The owner described the property, the damage done, and the stones <note>original: "missiles"</note> which had been preserved. Furthermore, he gave detailed replies to the questions I thought necessary to ask. I spoke to him first of all about what had been told me by the public official.

"The first fact is perfectly correct," he replied. "The first stone did, indeed, hit this windowpane exactly in the middle, and the following ones struck it systematically in a spiral around the first hole."

But what surprised us most was that not one of the 300 stones thrown hit anybody. The first day, my little boy was in the garden and my little girl was sleeping in her cradle near an open window on the first floor. They were not disturbed in any way. The nurse, it is true, was struck on the head by a piece of brick, but she was not much hurt. My father-in-law was hit on the arm and cried, "Well, I did not feel anything."

That is one of the signs, I believe, by which—according to the theory—one can distinguish projectiles thrown supernaturally <note>original: "supernormally"</note> from those thrown by human hands <note>original: "human agency"</note>.

As the servant came back just at that moment, I questioned her also. It is well known how often one encounters a young woman who has reached puberty in haunted houses <note>At the time of this writing, researchers often looked for "focus persons"—typically adolescents—who were believed to unconsciously provide the energy for poltergeist activity.</note>. This girl seemed to me barely fifteen years old. The phenomena appeared to have some connection with her, for they hardly ever began until she was up and awake. She showed me the place on her head where the stone had hit her; neither her hair bun <note>original: "chignon"</note> nor her cap protected this spot. "Were you much hurt?" I asked. "Oh, yes! I have been crying with the pain during the day." "However, it did not bleed; you have had no swelling or lump?" "No, nothing like that." The projectile was about the size of a quarter of a brick. It seems to me very unnatural that it should have produced so little effect, coming from so far and consequently falling from a height.

Nothing was found, and the residents of the houses in question seemed just as mystified as Mr. Jacob Van Zanten himself.

Such is the account from the editor in Antwerp.

We agree with Bozzano <note>Ernesto Bozzano (1862–1943) was an influential Italian researcher of psychic phenomena who cataloged thousands of paranormal cases.</note>, who also reported on this case in Marcinelle, that we must consider the sheer number of objects thrown. This indicates a supernatural <note>original: "supernormal"</note> origin for these events. A human perpetrator who threw 300 stones without changing their position would have been caught red-handed by the police.

It must also be noted that when these projectiles hit anyone, they did not hurt them—or at least, they caused far less pain than they would have normally. However, when hitting inanimate objects, they caused damage consistent with their weight and size.

This peculiarity is common in *Poltergeist* <note>From the German words "poltern" (to rumble or make noise) and "Geist" (ghost). It refers to a spirit or energy that manifests through physical disturbances like loud noises or moving objects.</note> phenomena and suggests that there is a conscious will and intention directing the manifestations. These intentional acts bring to mind a commentary following a report from Sumatra, in which projectiles were said to have moved through the air in a slow-motion arc <note>original: "parabola"</note>. This phenomenon is theoretically interesting but very rare. Usually, these missiles are harmless to people but cause the most damage when hitting windows, doors, and furniture.

Cases of this kind occur to some extent everywhere. Professor Perty, from the University of Bern, published a small book in 1863 regarding the haunted house of Councillor Joller <note>Melchior Joller was a Swiss lawyer and politician whose family was famously driven from their home by persistent poltergeist activity in the early 1860s.</note> in Niederdorf, near Stans in the canton of Unterwalden. Here is a summary of that account:

# HAUNTING PHENOMENA

In the middle of August 1862, from the 15th to the 27th, tables and chairs were overturned by invisible hands. Rapping sounds occurred on the doors and floor, and doors opened and shut on their own. Finally, the noise became terrifying; bolts gave way, and it was feared the house would be destroyed. To people in the room, the noise seemed to come from the cellar under the floor. To those in the cellar, it seemed to come from above. At the same time, blows were struck as if with a hammer on tables and chairs. In spite of the most careful searching, no visible cause could be found for any of this. Yet a few days later, a Lucerne newspaper, *Der Eidgenoss* <note>German: *The Confederate*.</note>, alleged that the most obvious explanation had been discovered: rapping instruments had been found which made the noise for the purpose of devaluing the house and inducing its owner to sell it for a very low price <note>original: "sell it for a song"</note>.

Councillor Joller <note>Melchior Joller (1818–1865) was a prominent Swiss politician and lawyer whose life was ruined by these events.</note> replied to this unfounded allegation in the newspaper *Der Bund* <note>German: *The Federation*.</note> on September 4, declaring categorically that this strange phenomenon, in spite of the official inquiry and the measures taken, could not be reduced to any rational cause. The uproar continued, concentrating on a smaller area, until August 27, and then ceased for a time.

For a large family, those were days of terror which had cruel consequences.

The skeptics pretended to give a mechanical explanation, and the religious suspected the work of the Devil. The occurrence caused a great deal of noise in the press, and, as always, there was talk of illusion and trickery. In the *Allgemeine Zeitung* <note>German: *General Newspaper*.</note> of September 28, a Bern correspondent said the "last word" had been spoken; the cause of the uproar was Mr. Joller’s son, aged eighteen. It was claimed he had, among his unconventional <note>original: "Bohemian"</note> friends, learned all sorts of tricks and had practiced this one to frighten his family and amuse himself. In reply to my inquiry, Mr. Joller wrote to me as follows on October 2:

> “In reply to your esteemed letter of September 30, I beg to inform you first of all that the mysterious phenomena still continue in the house—though without the tumultuous violence they displayed in the beginning—and that the papers you mention contain not a word of truth on the subject.”

After expressing regret that the committee of inquiry <note>The official investigation launched by local authorities to find a rational explanation for the disturbances.</note> had not heard or recorded the testimony of the many honorable people who had been eye and ear witnesses of these strange phenomena, Mr. Joller added:

> “Exposed on one hand to a crude and fanatical public, and on the other to a skeptical, slandering, and mocking press, I was abandoned in my misfortune with a large family. Now, the fragile health of my wife and children forces me to find another home. At first, I wanted to keep this a secret. But the noise was so loud that I could no longer remain silent. The phenomena—of whose existence I became convinced in spite of my own skepticism and in broad daylight over the course of six weeks—were of various kinds.

> “At first, we heard raps on the walls and floor, and especially on the doors of the house. Sometimes these phenomena were so violent that the doors opened and shut, being torn from their latches. Then the noises decreased and turned into a light shaking. Tables, chairs, and pottery were overturned, sometimes loudly and sometimes silently. Pictures were taken off the walls, and vessels were taken from tables and cupboards and placed upside down on the floor. All sorts of objects were hung on nails. Finally, pictures were turned with their faces to the wall right before our eyes, and stones, fruit, clothing, and other items were thrown about and hidden in dark places, despite locks and bolts.

> “Stones were often thrown down the chimney. Nothing was broken or damaged, and strangely, the stones that hit one or another of my children after coming down the chimney did not cause any shock or noticeable pain. We were made to feel the touch of an icy hand and fingertips, and we felt a cold wind like the beating of wings, which was noticed by every inhabitant of the house. We also heard perfect imitations of a watch being wound, wood splitting, money being counted, rubbing sounds, songs, and articulate <note>original: "articulate sounds"; meaning distinct, understandable speech or vocalizations.</note> sounds like a human voice. Generally, these sounds—which were often very loud—seemed to relate to the work and conversation of the people in the house. The night before last, around 8:00 p.m., a stone wet with dew was thrown up the stairs, landing almost in front of our door. Seven weeks ago, these stories would have made...”

We might think, along with Professor Perty or with Bozzano <note>Ernesto Bozzano (1862–1943), an Italian researcher who specialized in paranormal phenomena.</note> (who comments on him), and repeat what we said before: these trivial, vulgar, and material manifestations—similar to so many others in this work—operate according to the principle of least resistance (much like lightning flashes). They might be directed by invisible intelligences with the goal of impressing witnesses, shaking their indifference, and inviting them to meditate on the possibility of a soul surviving death, along with all the moral and social consequences that implies. 

If we accept that interpretation, we also accept that a very noble aim is achieved through very modest means, adapted to the largely common nature of humanity. For we must admit that most people only understand material life; they remain deaf to philosophical and psychological arguments and are only struck by blunt facts. A hard knock on the back impresses them more than a discourse by Plato, Buddha, or Jesus Christ.

We may now state that within the total range of haunting phenomena, <term>Poltergeists</term> <note>original: "Poltergeists"; a German term meaning "noisy ghosts," used to describe spirits that move objects or make loud noises.</note>—or independent rapping spirits that have no apparent connection with the dead—are much more numerous than the cases of "association" <note>Cases where the haunting is clearly linked to a specific deceased person.</note> such as those described in the last chapter. Yet the accounts now on my table would fill some thirty pages. They are quite similar to those already published.

# HAUNTED HOUSES

It is undeniable that some invisible intelligence is at work in *poltergeist* <note>original: "Poltergeist"; from the German meaning "noisy ghost," referring to spirits that manifest through physical disturbances.</note> phenomena. Projectiles hit chosen targets, slow down so as not to hurt spectators, follow unpredictable paths, fall from nowhere, pass through narrow slits, and even penetrate into hermetically sealed rooms. Such acts belong to a supernatural world. To attribute them to strange powers of the subconscious seems to me an explanation that is hard to support. We have already pointed out that the mundane and crude nature of these manifestations may be explained by the simple goal of attracting attention and by the tendency of taking the path of least resistance. There may also be crude spirits, just as there are in our world—and probably even a large number of them. Why should there not be practical jokers on the other side of the veil as well as on this side—or even foolish and malevolent beings?

An extensive study compiled by Ernesto Bozzano <note>Ernesto Bozzano (1862–1943) was an Italian researcher famous for his systematic classification of psychic phenomena.</note> led him to the following conclusion:

> Out of 532 cases of hauntings, 374 belong to the category of “hauntings by the dead,” and 158 are *poltergeist* cases. The latter therefore make up 28 percent of the total. Examining the categories separately, we find that among the *poltergeist* cases there are 46 cases of stone-throwing, 39 of spontaneous bell-ringing, 7 involving fires, and 7 auditory cases in which unknown human voices were heard.
> 
> Among the phenomena of standard hauntings, 374 out of 532—that is, 72 percent—show a connection with a death (usually a tragic one) which took place in the building or the area haunted.
> 
> The 374 cases in question can be divided into several very distinct and telling groups. For instance, in a first group of 180 cases—mostly documented with great certainty—the start of the haunting coincided with a tragic event that had occurred there. In another group of 27 cases, the lack of historical documents was made up for by the discovery of human remains buried or walled up in those places—a clear indication <note>This sentence ends abruptly as the text continues on the next page.</note>

...of bloody tragedies enacted there and forgotten. In a third group of 51 cases, deaths are associated with the location; in a fourth group of 26 cases, the deceased person who appeared as a ghost did not die in the haunted place, but had lived there for a long time.

In 304 cases out of a total of 374, there is, therefore, a death coinciding with a haunting. There remain 70 cases without a prior death—or at least without a discoverable one. This overwhelming majority of cases following a death seems sufficient to justify the hypothesis of a link between these two types of occurrences.

The conclusion of everything we have reviewed is that these extraordinary and inexplicable phenomena certainly take place, despite the difficulties of observation and the specific illusions inevitably associated with their study. They are as certain as the existence of the sun and the moon. But it is easier to prove they happen than to explain why. Still, we must devote a final chapter to a search for an explanation, pausing first to address the matter of fake haunted houses <note>original: "Spurious Haunted Houses"; referring to cases where hauntings are revealed to be frauds, pranks, or caused by natural phenomena.</note>.

## CHAPTER XII

### FAKE HAUNTED HOUSES

Fake <note>original: "Spurious"</note> haunted houses are just as numerous as genuine ones. This subject is highly susceptible to fraud, trickery, practical jokes, illusions, hallucinations, and hysterical mistakes, as well as lies told by children of both sexes. I have taken the trouble of collecting hundreds of accounts, including those discussed some time ago by the Psychical Research Societies of England, the United States, France, and Italy, and published in various French and foreign journals. These various accounts would fill a volume nearly as large as this one, and it seems unnecessary to publish them separately. I have spent a great deal of time on this research, and I shall spare the reader's time by being brief. Those who wish for full information need only look up the files of the Paris *Annals of Psychical Sciences* <note>original: "Annales des Sciences Psychiques"</note>, the *Proceedings of the Society for Psychical Research* of London and New York, and the Rome review *Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Luce e Ombra"</note>. These are the primary periodicals on the subject, and they provide much authentic information.

The facts and events associated closely or remotely with Spiritualism <term>Spiritualism: A 19th and early 20th-century movement based on the belief that the spirits of the dead can communicate with the living, often through a person called a medium.</term> are particularly vulnerable to illusions, errors of interpretation, and especially the fraud of impostors. In spite of the shameful nature of fake mediums who cynically profit from the grief of bereaved people hungering for consolation, such vile impostors are numerous and cannot be too carefully avoided. I myself have exposed more than one, resulting in them being driven from the countries they exploited so crudely and unscrupulously. Also, there

There are people gifted with genuine psychic abilities who, when their powers fail them, do not hesitate to give things a helping hand <note>original: "give a *coup de pouce*"</note> through trickery. Researchers <note>original: "Students of the subject"</note> who value their time have frequently had to complain about this kind of behavior.

As we have seen in other cases—such as the letter from the famous astronomer Schiaparelli <note>Giovanni Schiaparelli (1835–1910) was a prominent Italian astronomer best known for his observations of Mars.</note> which I published earlier—scholars <note>original: "savants"</note> are often discouraged despite their eagerness to gather information, which is a great loss for science. Men filled with the scientific spirit are naturally honest and sincere, and they do not understand deception <note>original: "mendacity"</note>.

It is more interesting and more important to discover the causes of the genuine phenomena observed.

One thing we cannot refuse to admit—namely, that haunted houses have existed in all eras and in all countries.

## CHAPTER XIII

### THE SEARCH FOR CAUSES

->*The origin and method by which haunting phenomena are produced—*<-
->*The fifth element.*<-

"Happy is the man who is able to know the causes of things!" <note>original Latin: "Felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas!"</note> said Virgil two thousand years ago in his wonderful *Georgics* (Book II, line 489), referring to the happiness of those whose strong spirits penetrate the secrets of nature and rise above ordinary ideas. Does the material collected in this book allow us to achieve that same happiness?

In these free and independent records, which are completely without prejudice <note>original Latin: "præ-judicium," meaning a judgment made beforehand</note>, my readers know that my only goal has been to educate myself and share the results of these investigations with them. I hope they will allow me to remind them that my personal study of this occult world began in November 1861, alongside Allan Kardec <note>Allan Kardec (1804–1869) was the pen name of the French educator who founded Spiritism, a system of belief regarding the nature, origin, and destiny of spirits and their relation to the corporeal world.</note>, the founder of modern Spiritism and undoubtedly the most knowledgeable man of that era. From those distant years until now (1923), I have been in a position to know nearly all the research done on this subject throughout the entire world. Therefore, I must admit I am remarkably surprised to find these phenomena denied by people who seem otherwise intelligent, well-informed, and sensible.

As I have already said, it is usually considered "proper behavior" <note>original: "good form"</note> to claim a state of absolute skepticism with

...with regard to the facts which form the subject of the present volume. For three-quarters of the people on our planet, all the unexplained noises in haunted houses, all the movements of heavy objects without physical contact, all the tilting tables, furniture, and other objects encountered in so-called spiritualist phenomena—including messages dictated by raps or automatic writing <note>Writing produced without conscious intent, believed by some to come from a spiritual or subconscious source.</note> and all appearances of phantom forms—are nothing but illusions, hallucinations, or tricks. To these people, there is no explanation to seek. They believe the only reasonable opinion is that we are dealing with errors; that all "mediums," whether professional or not, are frauds; that these phenomena do not actually exist; and that the witnesses are fools.

The subject is indeed complicated, and the problem is like a mathematical equation with several unknown variables. But science has solved many others like it, ranging from simple algebra to the complex functions of integral calculus. To begin with, there are two elements present: human abilities to be analyzed and defined, and an invisible psychic element that exists outside of ourselves.

We may read in the book *The Unknown Forces of Nature* (Final Edition, 1906, p. 591):

> The field of Spiritualism is open to all types of explanations. It is found that the messages dictated by the tables correspond with the state of mind, ideas, opinions, knowledge, and accomplishments—even the reading habits—of the researchers. They reflect the group gathered there.

The name "medium" <note>term: "Medium" originally implied a "middleman" or intermediary between the physical world and a spirit world.</note> is quite inappropriate, because it assumes the very thing that still needs to be proven. It suggests that the person gifted with these abilities is an intermediary between spirits and researchers. Even if we admit that this is sometimes the case, it is certainly not usually so. The spinning of a table, its tilting, its levitation <note>Rising or floating in the air without physical support.</note>, the movement of a piece of furniture, the bulging of a curtain, the noises—

We certainly cannot assume that there is always a spirit responding to our whims. This hypothesis is even more unnecessary since these alleged spirits teach us nothing new. Our own psychic force is surely in action most of the time. The person exercising this force would more appropriately be called the <term>dynamogen</term> <note>From the Greek words for "power" and "to produce"; a term the author suggests to describe someone who generates psychic energy themselves, rather than acting as a "medium" for an outside spirit.</note> because he or she generates the force. In my opinion, that would be the most appropriate term for that state, and it expresses exactly what every observer witnesses.

That was an invitation to use scientific methods.

Our studies on these subjects require, perhaps, greater care than any others. As early as 1869, in my speech at the grave of Allan Kardec <note>The pen name of Hippolyte Léon Denizard Rivail (1804–1869), the founder of Spiritism.</note>, I remarked that Spiritualism must not be treated as a religion but as a science to be studied, and that the causes at play are more varied and numerous than one might suppose.

We do not know all the human faculties. The precept of the Temple of Delphi—"Know thyself" <note>original Greek: Γνῶθι σεαυτὸν</note>—is still relevant today. Our own powers certainly have something to do with the phenomena we are studying. As a faithful follower of the experimental method, I hold that we must examine every natural explanation before we resort to others.

When I attempted a first methodical classification of these very diverse occurrences in *The Unknown* <note>original title: *L'Inconnu* (1900)</note>, I started with the best-established cases of telepathic transmission and with the manifestations of the dying and the living, which were verified by credible witnesses worthy of complete confidence.

It has always seemed to me that we cannot use too much caution when interpreting the facts, especially when it is a matter of seeking scientific proof for the survival of the soul. For our normal impressions—

Are certain phenomena occurring at the moment of death to be placed before or after that moment? Mr. A. Erny wrote in the *Annals of Psychic Sciences* <note>original French: Annales des sciences psychiques</note> of 1900 (p. 22):

I never claimed or believed that the dead *could* not manifest themselves, and I have found no theoretical reason to rule it out. On the contrary, I believe that such manifestations are now proven by observed facts and that we must accept them, provided we are not misled by illusions and errors.

Mr. <note>original: M.</note> Erny was, at that time (1900), specifically reviewing my book *The Unknown* <note>original: L'Inconnu</note>, which had just been published. That book focuses primarily on telepathy and manifestations of the dead, which was to be the starting point of our studies. He cited the cases I published—including those of General Parmentier (*The Unknown*, pp. 64-67), René Kraemer (p. 70), Madame Fèret (p. 74), Clovis Hugues (p. 76), Baron Deslandes (p. 81), and Baroness Staffe (p. 82). He concluded that I was wrong to attribute these cases to dying people or to hallucinations; in his view, they were certainly caused by the dead.

I desire this conclusion as much as my critic does, but I am more demanding regarding proof. We cannot be too strict. The scientific method is relentless. I often find myself caught between two dangers—the skepticism that denies everything, and the credulity that accepts everything.

Might we not even ask ourselves if we are all mistaken? Perhaps these phenomena are produced neither by the dying nor the dead, but simply by ourselves—by human faculties that are as yet unknown. This question arises quite naturally. The comparative studies of Alexander Aksakoff have shown that more than one instance of haunting can be attributed to "action at a distance" caused by the psychic force of living people. He woke as if from a magnetic sleep <note>an early term for a hypnotic trance</note>, and when we told him what had happened, he said: "That has often happened to me. My soul is then, so to speak, outside my body."

Without occupying ourselves for the present with the theory of "ethereal bodies," let us only repeat that the human being is endowed with some as-yet-unknown faculties.

I believe Gisèle’s subconscious was driven by the desire to convert me to Spiritualism <note>the 19th-century movement/belief that the living can communicate with the dead</note>. My skepticism <note>original: "incredulity"</note> made her suffer, and to achieve her goal, she used these absurd methods derived from popular folk beliefs.

In spite of the title of *dynamogens* <note>original: "producers of force"</note>, which I previously applied to mediums, I think that term is a bit too narrow. The unknown faculties of the human being are at work, but they are not enough to explain certain manifestations after death <note>original: "posthumous manifestations"</note>. But let us not lose sight of that possibility.

Not yet convinced that it was a supernatural phenomenon, he relit the candle, thinking that a draft <note>original: "draught"</note> might have made the door bang and blown out the flame. But in order to be sure of his surroundings, he got a piece of chalk and confirmed that the door did not tend to shut on its own due to some slant in the floor, and that there was no draft in the adjoining rooms, as all their doors and windows were closed. 

Mr. H. placed the candle in front of the door several times, and it did not flicker. Then he put the door back in its original position and made a mark on the floor with the chalk to fix the position exactly. The door did not move. Then he repeated his appeal: "Albert, if that is really a sign from you, shut the door again." 

It immediately slammed just as it had the first time. His sister, who lay on a couch in the next room, asked him angrily why he had slammed the door so violently twice. He asked her if the door ever shut on its own. "Never," said the sister. The next day he performed more experiments with the door but found it did not close by itself. Also, the servant removed the chalk marks in his presence, so he was sure he had not been dreaming. The fact that his sister had been disturbed twice in her grief by the noise proved that there was no hallucination.

This very characteristic case was reported in *Light* <note>a prominent British Spiritualist newspaper first published in 1881</note> on February 27, 1894, from which I translate it. I ask Mr. Flammarion <note>Camille Flammarion (1842–1925), a French astronomer and researcher into psychic phenomena</note> to consider it, for as the case comes from a materialist, it is all the more striking.

I am far from being opposed to assuming that deceased persons can act. On the contrary. If I began by considering the actions of the dying and the living, it is because it seemed best to first prove their reality. From there, we might naturally move to a discussion of the actions of the dead, following a methodical order that should be observed in making claims of such importance. Let us not forget that to satisfy our own convictions, we must use positive psychical observations to counter the major objection: the parallel between the birth and development of an infant's intelligence and the physical evolution of its brain.

And let us not lose sight of the physical and psychological faculties of the human being, especially the possibility of "doubling" <note>the theory that a person can manifest a second, independent personality or presence</note>. Everyone knows the great discovery made in Bordeaux by Dr. Azam regarding the two alternating mental states of Félida.³

---

³ It will be remembered that this girl, born in 1843, suffered in 1858 from violent hysterical fits that seemed to predict <note>original: "presage"</note> insanity, and for which Dr. Azam was consulted. She was observed falling into cataleptic <term>a physical state characterized by muscle rigidity and a lack of response to external stimuli</term> trances that lasted several minutes. Afterward, she would wake up in a completely different state—as a different person: cheerful instead of sad, with a lively character. This second state, which initially lasted only a few hours, eventually divided her life into two nearly equal periods; the second state formed a life almost entirely distinct from the first. It went so far that, while in her second state, she fell in love with a neighbor, became pregnant, and gave birth to a child—all without being aware of it when she was in her first state. By 1875, when Dr. Azam published his study, that child was sixteen years old. The second state gradually grew longer at the expense of the first, eventually covering her entire existence. Naturally, this story was met with widespread skepticism <note>original: "a general smile"</note>. The girl was accused of acting, and the distinguished observer was thought to have been fooled. In response to this general ignorance, Dr. Azam published his observations under the title *Hypnotism, Double Consciousness, and Alterations of Personality* <note>original French: "Hypnotisme, Double Conscience et Altérations de la Personnalité"</note>. Félida was then forty-four years old and had been married for a long time to the father of her first child; she was the mother of a lovely family, and her second state had ultimately completely replaced the first.

As we become familiar with these examples, we can guess how vast the unexplored territory of the human psychological and physical world is. At the International Congress of Psychical Research held in Copenhagen from August 28 to September 2, 1921—for which we have an excellent official report edited by Mr. Carl Vett—Dr. von Schrenck-Notzing presented a report titled *The Ghost in Hopfgarten* <note>original: *Der Spuk in Hopfgarten*</note>. This was a legal verification of the phenomenon of telekinesis <term>the movement of objects by mental power without physical contact</term>. My learned colleague, Mr. Louis Maillard, has provided a scientific summary of this case in the journal *Psychica*, which shows how uncertain the explanation for haunting phenomena still is.

This case of haunting presents a dual perspective: first, because it suggests certain hypotheses concerning its cause, and second, because it was the subject of a legal inquiry that established its authenticity in an unquestionable way.

In Hopfgarten, a village near Weimar, there lives a clockmaker named Sauerbrey. He is married for a second time and has a son from his first marriage. This son, who lives in a neighboring area and studies the occult sciences <note>the study of supernatural or hidden knowledge, such as magic or spirits</note>, visited his father around February 10, 1921.
