The author of the pamphlet summarized here concludes that the animistic hypothesis <note>the theory that such events are caused by the unconscious power of a person's own soul or mind rather than external spirits</note> fully accounts for the manifestations, which, by the way, did not at any time acquire a religious or spirit-like <note>original: "spiritoid"</note> character.

But he hastens to add that this explanation is far from being applicable to all manifestations of this kind. There are several which are produced in the absence of any person who can be considered an agent, and which seem to be more dependent upon a locality than upon a person, and so on.

If, then, in the present example we can, so to speak, catch the mode of production of the phenomena "on the wing," we must not generalize hastily. It is wiser to recognize that the etiology <note>the study of causes or origins</note> of the phenomena of haunting is still surrounded by deep mystery.

This reasoning of Monsieur Maillard is exact and judicious, and agrees with numerous cases brought forward in this book. The living human being enters largely into the production of these phenomena. But they are not yet explained.

We do not know how they are produced. There are, no doubt, fantastic stone-throwings and the actual destruction of buildings committed unconsciously by women and hysterical girls through the externalization of their nerve force. I shall mention another case, still more amazing, published by the *Annals of Psychical Sciences* <note>original: *Annales de sciences psychiques*</note> (1899, pp. 302-309), a case which is almost incredible and yet sufficiently verified.

The Malayali had left the house at 11:00 p.m. We used the same small roll, blowing the smoke into her nose, and she seemed to recover completely and drank a cup of tea.

On Friday, April 30, stones began to be thrown at noon and continued until 11:00 p.m. She fainted once, though not as deeply, even though she looked terrible. On Saturday, the 1st of May <note>original: "1st inst.," meaning the first of the current month</note>, she told us that she went to fetch a plate from the dining room, and that it had been pulled away from her. That evening she was in a much better state of mind, but glasses were still broken. She went for a walk that same evening, and as she re-entered the house, a single window pane which was still in one of the frames <note>original: "casements"</note> broke near her head and fell to the ground. Talking to one of us about her misfortune, she said every night she could see two headless women. Some time afterward, a large cobblestone flew into the room, and a glass broke on its own.

The father was sent for by telegram, and he arrived at Gudalur <note>original: "Goodalur"; a town roughly 132 miles from the hill station of Ooty (Ootacamund)</note> the following Monday evening. On that day, the damage to the windows was extensive, but fortunately, the girl did not lose consciousness.

Wijk, of Gothenburg, Sweden, published a remarkable work on these phenomena in 1904. It is described as "an experimental study of inexplicable noises and movements." This account can be read in the *Annals of Psychic Sciences* <note>original: "Annales des sciences psychiques." A prominent French journal of the era dedicated to the study of paranormal and psychological phenomena.</note> from September 1905, and it is useful to summarize it here. The conclusion drawn from this case is that the rapping noises were caused by the unconscious actions of a specific person whose presence was necessary for them to occur.

In the spring of 1904, the residents of a villa in southern Sweden noticed noises that seemed to be produced by vigorous blows from inside the floors and the walls. These sounds were impossible to explain by any known cause.

The occupants were a forest inspector, identified as N., his wife, their servant, and a German official. Before long, it was observed that the phenomena were connected to the person of Madam N. by some indefinable link. The blows were only produced when she was in the house and always occurred in her immediate vicinity; however, they were in no way influenced by the presence of the other residents.

The following is a brief description of Madam N. who, for the sake of brevity, is referred to by her given name, Karin.

Karin is twenty-seven years old. She has a delicate constitution, and there is something childlike in her face and her whole being. She has lost some of her natural gaiety and lightheartedness due to disappointments and sorrow, though her original personality remains unchanged. She has a frank and trusting nature and quickly expresses her innermost feelings.

Her whole person seems healthy, and one gets the impression that the nervous attacks she has suffered during the last few years are not the result of an underlying medical condition <note>original: "pathological condition."</note>. There seems to be no history of hereditary illness in her family. Karin has been married since 1897 and has no children.

Her first experiences with these phenomena date back ten years. At that time, she had several experiences of auditory sensations in the form of...

Mr. N. was away on business. Karin, who had gone to bed early, was kept awake for a long time by the noisy conversation of the guests. At last, toward midnight, she heard the party break up. Two of them, who were to sleep at the manager's house, left to find their lodgings. The third, who was staying at the villa, locked the door and retired to his room. Silence reigned, and Karin was on the point of going to sleep when she heard heavy footsteps mounting the steps of the veranda <note>veranda: a roofed, open-air gallery or porch attached to the outside of a building.</note>. They had not been able to find their way in the dark and wanted a lantern. Karin gave him a lantern and went back to bed. 

She was falling asleep when three more knocks—just like those which had recently frightened her—made her start. She got up, went to the door, and found nobody there. Back in bed, she heard the same three knocks ring out repeatedly for about an hour; then all was quiet until three o'clock in the morning. The three knocks then came once more, the last for that night.

Karin had no thought but that these knocks were a practical joke played by the guests from the evening before, or by some other person, so she did not worry about them much.

The case appeared exceptionally interesting to us. We were dealing with a person who seemed to exhibit, to a slight degree, several of the psychic <note>original: "psychical"</note> traits of mediums, and one of these traits appeared in an unusually pure and distinct form. The many similarities between trance states and mediumship on one hand, and deep hypnosis and hypnotic suggestion on the other, had already led us in previous research to believe that hypnotism provided the best way to study such events. It allowed us to use the ultimate <note>original: "*par excellence*"; French for "of the highest degree" or "the archetypal example"</note> tool of the exact sciences—namely, experimentation. Mediumistic activities are most often—like the unusual knocks in this case—expressions of an intelligence that is rooted (as is generally accepted) in the subconscious life of the medium. Could we not, thanks to hypnosis, reach this subconscious life and shape it as we liked through suggestion? And by doing so, could we even bring the physical activities that manifest from it under our control—triggering them, stopping them, or modifying them at will?

The details mentioned take up many pages and can be summarized as follows:

1. In this case, there seems to be a direct link between a known nervous condition (hysteria <note>In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, "hysteria" was a broad medical diagnosis for various nervous and emotional disorders, often associated with physical symptoms like tics or phantom pains.</note>) and the mysterious phenomenon of raps. These raps have been closely tied to psychic experiences that perhaps stem from the same nervous condition, such as hallucinations and the imaginative associations created by subconscious "psychography" <term>psychography: a term used for automatic writing or the supposed recording of spirit messages</term>. Additionally, external psychic influences—such as ghost stories and the general atmosphere of a "haunted" house—have also played a role.
2. The raps can be controlled through the will using hypnotic suggestion.

If the results of our research are accurate, they imply significant consequences because of the practical importance of raps in Spiritualism and their probable connection to other mediumistic events. These results would provide a solid foundation for judging the psychic value of spiritualistic "typtology" <term>typtology: a method of communicating with spirits through a code of raps or knocks</term> and their reliance on the medium and the people present (the "circle"). This would confirm conclusions already reached through less certain methods. The current work is less about documenting a specific case than it is about showing that it is possible to use experimental scientific methods in this new field of study. The importance of such a method cannot be overstated. It is only by basing our theories on experimental evidence that we can hope to explain these mysterious phenomena, which still deserve to be called "occult."

We can only applaud the efforts of the Swedish scholar <note>original: "savant"; referring to Hjalmar Wijk</note>. Everyone can see that the gullible believers in Spiritualism do more harm to it than the skeptics, as the unverified claims of believers are often naively simple. It is time to conclude. Everywhere in nature—in the guiding force of life on Earth, in the instincts of plants and animals, in the general spirit of things, in humanity, and in the cosmic universe—there is a psychic element. This element reveals itself more and more in modern studies, especially in research regarding telepathy and those unexplained phenomena dealt with in the present volume. This element, this principle, is still unknown to contemporary science; but, as in many other cases, it was sensed by the ancients. I am inventing nothing new.

In addition to the four elements—air, water, earth, and fire—the ancients did, in fact, assume a fifth element of an immaterial kind. They called it the *animus* <note>original: "animus"; the world soul or animating principle</note>, or the world soul, the ether. Cicero writes in his *Tusculan Disputations* <note>original: "Tusculan. Quæst." (Tusculanae Quaestiones)</note> (Book 1, Section 22): "Aristotle, having listed the four kinds of material elements, felt compelled to assume a fifth essence, a *fifth nature* <note>original: "quinta natura"</note>, which gives rise to the soul. Since thought and the intellectual faculties cannot reside in any of the material elements, we must admit a fifth kind. It had not yet received a name, so he called it *entelechia* <term>entelechia: an ancient Greek term for "entelechy," meaning the realization or complete expression of a potentiality</term>—that is to say, eternal and continuous movement." The four material elements of the ancients have been broken down by modern analysis. This fifth element is perhaps more fundamental.

Virgil wrote these admirable verses in the *Aeneid* (Book VI), which everyone knows:

Let us repeat for the thousandth time: the essential nature of the human soul, both in life and in death, is still entirely unknown to us. What is immortality?

"The idea that souls might not be equal has already occurred to me," I replied to Naquet. "It seems worth considering. No, it is not pride in Victor Hugo; it is a sense of justice, for he knows well that his works prove his personal individuality."

That conversation took place around 1880. More than forty years later, I still hold the same opinion, strengthened by my psychic studies. No soul seems to be destroyed. But are many souls conscious of their spiritual existence? Are only those who were aware of it before death still conscious of it afterward? Diversity continues. We see the educated and the ignorant, the intelligent and the simple, the good and the evil. The guillotine <note>A reference to the French method of execution; the author argues that the sudden death of a criminal does not automatically refine or change their character in the afterlife.</note> does not turn a criminal into a saint. The chaotic phenomena of haunted houses align with this view.

We conclude: if the universe is a system of dynamic forces <note>original: "dynamism"; the theory that all phenomena in the universe can be explained by energy or force rather than just inert matter.</note>, if the cosmos deserves its name (which implies "order"), if the unknown world is more important than the known world, and if there are intelligent forces and invisible beings—then we must reject the denials of Naquet, Berthelot, Le Dantec, Littré, Cabanis, Lalande, Voltaire, and the anatomists <note>These figures represent a tradition of French rationalism, materialism, and skepticism that sought to explain the world through physical matter alone.</note> in favor of the convictions of Victor Hugo, Pasteur, Ampère, Goethe, Euler, Pascal, Newton, and the spiritualists <note>This list includes iconic scientists and philosophers who believed that the laws of nature pointed toward a higher spiritual or divine intelligence.</note>. For these thinkers look beneath the surface of appearances and discover, in the final analysis of things, the fundamental invisible energy.

# EPILOGUE

## THE UNKNOWN OF YESTERDAY IS THE TRUTH OF TOMORROW

->*Progress surrounded by obstacles—Lavoisier's Report to the Academy of Sciences on meteorites.*<-
<note>Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794) was a central figure in the 18th-century chemical revolution. He famously helped draft a report for the French Academy of Sciences in 1772 which argued that stones could not fall from the sky, dismissing reports of meteorites as delusions or lightning strikes.</note>

What was unknown yesterday becomes the truth of tomorrow.
We must study everything, discuss everything, and analyze everything without prejudice. The history of science shows us a great number of eminent men and superior minds who were stopped in the path of progress by the idea that science had spoken its last word. In astronomy, physics, chemistry, geology, and all branches of human knowledge, it would be easy to fill several pages with the names of famous people who thought science would not surpass the limits attained in their own time, and that there was nothing left to discover. Among the scholars <term>savants</term> <note>original: "savants"; meaning learned scientists or experts</note> of the present day, it would not be difficult to cite a number of distinguished men who are firmly convinced that in the fields they have mastered, there is nothing more to be found.

We must only admit that which has been proved. We must be neither too ready to believe nor too ready to doubt. We must study without prejudice and, above all, we must remain free and independent. It is quite natural that official institutions should be conservative. The important thing for the progress of ideas is that we should not be closed off, and should not be blinded by a traditional <note>original: "classical"</note> attitude toward the evidence of facts. This same resistance has happened in astronomy, physics, chemistry, and medicine—in all the sciences—concerning the "phlogiston" theory <note>original: "phlogistics"; phlogiston was a debunked 18th-century scientific theory that proposed a fire-like element was released during combustion.</note>, steam power, electricity, and the existence of meteorites. A great and noble spirit, the immortal Antoine Lavoisier himself—who disproved the phlogiston theory and created modern chemistry—remained bound by the limited ideas of his time during the eighteenth century. Tasked by the Academy of Sciences to prepare a report on a meteorite fall that had been clearly witnessed, he wrote the following document in 1769. It serves as a lesson for us all. I provide here a word-for-word extract worth preserving for our own education. This document is historical and teaches us much. It is taken from the official edition of the *Works of Lavoisier* (Paris: Imperial Press, 1868, vol. IV):

### *Report on a Stone Alleged to have Fallen from the Sky during a Thunderstorm*

> Monsieur Fongeroux, Monsieur Cadet, and I have been tasked with submitting to the Academy an account of an observation shared by Monsieur Abbot <term>Abbé</term> <note>original: "l’Abbé"; a title for a member of the clergy in France</note> Bachelay regarding a stone alleged to have fallen from the sky during a thunderstorm. There is probably no object with a longer history than the "thunderstone" <note>An old folk term for meteorites, which were often believed to be the physical remains of lightning strikes.</note> or thunderbolt, if we were to collect everything written by various authors. We can judge this by the large number of substances called by that name. Yet, despite the beliefs of the ancients, true physicists have always doubted the existence of these stones. We can find some details in a report written by Monsieur Lémery, printed among other Academy proceedings in 1700.
>
> If the existence of thunderbolts was regarded as doubtful at a time when physicists had hardly any idea of the nature of lightning, their skepticism seems even more reasonable today, now that they have discovered that lightning is identical to electricity. However, we shall faithfully report the facts communicated to us by Monsieur [Bachelay]...

On September 13, 1768, at half-past four in the afternoon, a storm cloud appeared in the direction of the castle of La Chevallerie, near Lucé, a small village in the province of Maine. A sharp thunderclap was heard which resembled the report of a gun. Then, over a distance of about two and a half leagues <note>original: "two leagues and a half"; a league was a measurement of distance roughly equal to 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers.</note>, a considerable whistling sound was heard in the air, without any sign of fire. It resembled the lowing of a cow so closely that several people were fooled by it. Several crofters <term>crofters</term> <note>original: "crofters"; tenant farmers who worked small plots of land.</note> who were harvesting in the parish of Périgué, about three hours from Lucé, heard the same noise. They looked up and saw an opaque body describing a curve and falling into a meadow near the main road to Le Mans, right beside where they were working. They all ran to the spot and found a sort of stone about half-buried in the earth, but it was so hot and burning that it was impossible to touch it. They were all seized with terror and ran away. But upon returning some time later, they saw that it had not moved, and it had cooled down enough to allow them to examine it more closely. 

The stone weighed about seven and a half pounds and was triangular in shape—that is, it had three more-or-less rounded points, one of which had pierced the turf at the moment of impact. All the portion that had entered the ground was a gray or ash color, while the rest, which had been exposed to the air, was extremely black. Monsieur the Abbot <term>Abbé</term> Bachelay, having obtained a piece of this stone, presented it to the Academy and expressed a wish that its nature might be determined.

We shall now give an account of the experiments we have conducted with this goal in mind. They will help us determine what we should think of such a singular occurrence.

The substance of the stone is a pale ash-gray. Looking at the grain with a magnifying glass, one can see that it is studded with a multitude of small, bright metallic points of a pale-yellow color. The part of its outer surface which, according to Abbot Bachelay, was not embedded in the ground, is covered with a very thin layer of a...

The conclusion, based on the facts reported by the Abbé Bachelay <note>Abbé: a title for a member of the Catholic clergy in France.</note> and our own experiments, is that this stone—which was perhaps covered by a thin layer of earth or turf—was struck by lightning and thus exposed. The heat would have been intense enough to melt the surface of the struck part, but it would not have lasted long enough to penetrate the interior; therefore, the stone was not decomposed. The large amount of metallic material it contained, offering less resistance than other objects to the electric current, may have even helped determine the path of the lightning flash.

It is known that lightning tends to strike objects that are most easily electrified by contact. We must not overlook a remarkable fact: Mr. Morand, Jr., sent us a piece of stone from the area of Coutances, which was also claimed to have fallen from the sky. It was found to be very similar to Abbé Bachelay's stone. It is also a sandstone permeated with <term>iron pyrites</term> <note>original: "iron pyrites"; a shiny yellow mineral also known as "fool's gold," composed of iron and sulfur.</note>, and only differs from the other stone by not producing the smell of <term>liver of sulfur</term> <note>original: "liver of sulphur"; a chemical mixture of potassium sulfides known for its distinct rotten-egg smell.</note> when treated with <term>spirits of salt</term> <note>original: "spirits of salt"; an archaic name for hydrochloric acid.</note>. We believe we can only conclude from this similarity that lightning strikes metallic substances by preference, especially those containing pyrites.

However legendary <note>original: "fabulous"; in this context, meaning "seeming like a fable" or "unbelievable."</note> this class of occurrences may seem, we consider it appropriate to report them to the Academy, as they may help clarify the history of lightning strikes through the observations and experiments detailed above.

This report by Lavoisier to the <term>Academy of Sciences</term> <note>original: "Académie des Sciences"; the prestigious French national scientific institution founded in 1666.</note> prompts reflections closely connected with the research discussed in this book. Witnesses *saw the stone fall* in broad daylight on September 13, 1768, in the open countryside. It is true that they picked it up. However, after it was examined and analyzed, the conclusion drawn was that it did not fall from the sky. Preconceived notions prevent the recognition of the truth. Human testimony is dismissed as worthless, and, even in our day, a certain school of thought drawn to paradoxes continues to teach that witnesses, whoever they may be, can prove nothing.

Certainly, human testimony is unreliable, as anyone may be mistaken, and it is not scientific to trust it blindly; but there is a great gap between that and the attitude of denying everything. Now, this was not the first time that one or several stones were seen to fall from the sky, picked up, and preserved. To cite but one instance (the most celebrated): On November 7, 1491, at Ensisheim (in the <term>Haut-Rhin</term> <note>Haut-Rhin: a department in the Grand Est region of France, bordering Germany and Switzerland.</note> region), an enormous stone fell in front of a whole army, near Maximilian I, the Holy Roman Emperor. They are seen nearly every year somewhere or other. Even in 1768 another one fell at Aire (in the <term>Pas-de-Calais</term> <note>Pas-de-Calais: a department in northern France, named after the Strait of Dover.</note> region), and another at Maurkirchen in Bavaria. Lavoisier knew this, and yet he wrote that “true physicists have always regarded the existence of these stones as doubtful.” This perennial blindness toward all that is unknown has constantly hindered the progress of science. We see at the same time how imprudent it is to form premature explanatory theories, for this explanation of meteorites has to some extent invalidated the judgments of the *Academy of Sciences* <note>original: "Académie des Sciences"; the prestigious French national scientific academy founded in 1666.</note>.

Let us be wary of premature theories; this historical case compels us to do so.

Human beings of all degrees of intelligence who still think that metapsychical phenomena <note>metapsychical phenomena: an early 20th-century term for what is now called parapsychology or the study of supernatural events, such as telepathy or hauntings.</note> are inadmissible, because to admit them throws doubt on certain principles of traditional teaching, should also remember that all discoveries began by being denied.

For thousands of years, meteorites had fallen from the sky before hundreds of witnesses. A great number had been picked up, and several were preserved in churches, museums, and collections. But until 1794, there was still no independent mind willing to confirm their origin. This man arrived in 1794: it was <term>Ernst Chladni</term> <note>Ernst Chladni (1756–1827) was a German physicist and musician often called the "father of meteoritics" for his radical—and correct—claim that meteorites came from outer space.</note>.

I am not throwing stones at <term>Lavoisier</term> <note>Antoine Lavoisier (1743–1794), the famous chemist who previously dismissed meteorites as terrestrial rocks struck by lightning.</note>, nor at the *Academy of Sciences* <note>original: "Académie des Sciences"</note>, nor at any individual, but rather at the oppressive nature of prejudice. They did not believe—they *would not* believe—that minerals could fall from the sky. It seemed contrary to common sense. For example, <term>Pierre Gassendi</term> <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655) was a renowned French philosopher and astronomer.</note> was one of the most independent and learned intellects of the seventeenth century. In 1627, a meteorite weighing sixty-six pounds fell in Provence from a clear sky. Gassendi saw it, touched it, and examined it, yet he still attributed it to some volcanic eruption on Earth.

The *Academy of Sciences* finally recognized the reality of meteorites following the report of its own commissioner, <term>Jean-Baptiste Biot</term> <note>Biot was a physicist sent by the Academy to investigate a massive meteorite shower, providing the evidence needed to end scientific skepticism.</note>. This occurred after the fall at Laigle, in the <term>Orne</term> <note>Orne: a department in Normandy, France.</note> region, on April 26, 1803. The stones had been picked up while still hot by a number of witnesses who had narrowly escaped being killed by this hail of stones from the heavens. Since that time, the Academy has very often had to engage in the study of meteorites.¹ In spite of everything, the world moves forward, and the truth eventually forces itself upon us.

->Deny nothing beforehand <note>original: "a priori"</note>.<-

In 1831, Dr. Castel said at the *Academy of Medicine* <note>original: "Académie de Médecine"</note>, after the reading of a report by a commission of this Society on <term>animal magnetism</term> <note>Also known as Mesmerism, this was a theory of an invisible natural force possessed by all living things; it was a precursor to modern hypnotism.</note>:

The advice of the Medical Faculty of Bavaria against the introduction of <term>railways</term> offers a classic example of this hostility toward everything new. That learned body supposed that such rapid movement would inevitably cause brain disorders in the travelers and dizziness in the onlookers. They recommended that at least a wooden wall should be built on each side of the railway track to block the view.

After explaining her husband’s apparent mental instability <note>original: "aberration"</note>, she added with tears in her eyes that the most convincing proof of Daguerre’s insanity was his firm belief that he would succeed in "nailing his own shadow to the wall" or fixing it onto a "magical" metal plate. The doctor listened carefully and replied that he had also observed symptoms in Daguerre that served as undeniable proof of lunacy. He ended the conversation by advising her to quietly and quickly send her husband to <term>Bicêtre</term> <note>A famous hospital in Paris that, in the 19th century, served as an asylum for the mentally ill.</note>. Two months later, an exhibition of pictures created by the new process sparked intense interest in the worlds of science and art, and photography—already discovered by Niépce—was officially recognized.

# HAUNTED HOUSES

And the great physicist, <term>Lord Kelvin</term> <note>William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin (1824–1907), was a preeminent Scotch-Irish physicist and engineer known for his work in thermodynamics.</note>, wrote the following:³

> I make a point of firmly rejecting even the slightest inclination to accept this miserable superstition of <term>animal magnetism</term> <note>A theory proposed by Franz Mesmer suggesting an invisible natural force possessed by all living things; a precursor to hypnotism.</note>, table-turning, <term>Spiritualism</term> <note>A religious movement based on the belief that the spirits of the dead can communicate with the living.</note>, <term>mesmerism</term> <note>Another term for hypnotism or the therapeutic use of "animal magnetism."</note>, clairvoyance, and spirit raps. There is no mystical sixth sense. Clairvoyance and the rest are merely the result of bad observation, combined with a touch of intentional self-deception, acting upon simple and trusting souls.

This shows the level of narrow-mindedness to which even one of the greatest intellects of the era could be reduced. He did not deign to notice, examine, or even try to understand the subject.

We can add the name of <term>Ernest Haeckel</term> <note>Ernst Haeckel (1834–1919) was an influential German biologist and philosopher who promoted Charles Darwin's work in Germany.</note> to the list of scholars blinded by a false pride, who have denied the existence of unexplained phenomena. On one unfortunate page of his interesting work *The Riddle of the Universe* <note>Original: *Die Welträthsel* (1899), a best-selling book that argued for a purely materialistic explanation of the world.</note>, after lightly and hastily touching on mediumistic phenomena—which he classifies as the delusions of overworked minds—he speaks of thought-readers in these terms:

> "What is called telepathy (or the transfer of thoughts without a physical medium) does not exist any more than spirits or ghosts do."

In spite of Haeckel and his colleagues, thought-transference, hypnotism, and many other psychic manifestations are now acknowledged by eminent men. Psychologists have found the courage to take an interest in problems arising in a field of study previously dismissed as nothing but trickery and fraud. Let us instead reason as <term>Jaurès</term> <note>Jean Jaurès (1859–1914) was a prominent French Socialist leader and intellectual who advocated for a more open-minded approach to spiritual and philosophical questions.</note> did just now.

We must remark again, along with <term>Ch. Richet</term> <note>Charles Richet (1850–1935) was a Nobel Prize-winning French physiologist who coined the term "ectoplasm" and studied paranormal phenomena.</note>, that the—

# EPILOGUE

The understanding of psychic phenomena is beyond the capacity of many people.

First, there are leading scientists and high-ranking officials in education or administration. These individuals are highly competent in certain subjects, possess integrity, and usually have mature and well-founded judgment. However, they never venture outside their specific fields of expertise, believing that science has already spoken its final word on every subject. They are convinced that all the laws of nature are already known! Throughout history, this class of people has opposed every new discovery: the movement of the earth, the telescope, the circulation of the blood, meteorites, vaccination, electricity, gas lighting, railways, photography, undersea telegraph cables, the phonograph, the <term>cinematograph</term> <note>An early term for a motion picture film camera and projector.</note>, aviation, and more. They would never devote their time to these developments *because they were certain they were impossible*, and they obstinately cling to a skepticism that they believe to be rational.

Next, there are the shrewd business types—the dishonest, deceitful, and crooked people who make a living by exploiting others. Convinced that it is better to rob than to be robbed, they set unscrupulous traps for their neighbors. Because of their own nature, these people can see nothing in psychic phenomena except clever trickery, falsehood, and deception.

Finally, from a different perspective but equally incapable of judging these events, there are the simpletons and the gullible. These individuals lack a critical mind and turn <term>Spiritualism</term> <note>A movement based on the belief that the living can communicate with the spirits of the dead.</note> into a matter of blind faith—a religion, in fact. They are unable to accurately analyze the effects they observe.

Yet, there are also the "Free" <note>likely referring to "free-thinkers" who are not bound by dogma or prejudice</note>, and they surely represent a significant portion of the human species.

In any case, let us acknowledge that people in general are incapable of sustained attention, and that within the human race on Earth as a whole, in—

# HAUNTED HOUSES

Indifference to the knowledge of truth is almost universal. This indifference perpetuates the amazing ignorance that every shrewd observer encounters in all scientific and historical fields. After so many centuries of progress and so many discoveries, this universal ignorance is truly fantastic. Nobody wants to learn. The inhabitants of our planet live without knowing where they are and without having the curiosity to ask.

The columns of <term>the Press</term> <note>A collective term for newspapers and journalism.</note> are occupied with material pursuits: races of all kinds, millions in bets, speed tests, sports, boxing, <term>pugilistic matches</term> <note>Boxing or prize-fighting matches.</note>, financial speculations, the theater, the cinema, films, new dances, the nude in the <term>music-halls</term> <note>Popular 19th and early 20th-century entertainment venues featuring a variety of acts, including music, comedy, and theater.</note>, adulteries, crimes of passion, assassinations, political speeches, and advertisements. As for scientific progress and general instruction, they are conspicuous by their absence.

It is particularly in psychic matters that this ignorance is remarkable and regrettable, for we are all personally concerned with them. The psychical world is vaster and more immense than the physical world.

A last word: it is well to know this psychical world. We are far from having exhausted its study in this or the preceding volumes. We have not been able—as we had hoped to be—to include the numerous and incontestable observations concerning apparitions of the dead to the dying. These are evidence of the survival of those who have died and have their own special value. Neither have we been able to concern ourselves with the phantoms themselves—those which have been seen and heard. In those, we have a whole field of complex studies that opens unexpected horizons. It seems to me that the time has come to devote—in spite of the apparent paradox—a special volume to ghosts, discussed methodically.

<summary>The author concludes that a general indifference to truth and a media focus on trivial entertainment keep society ignorant of psychic realities. He notes that the study of the psychical world is far from finished and proposes a future volume dedicated to the methodical study of ghosts.</summary>
